News.title: Great-gran, 101, arrested for dealing drugs after ‘being found with bags of skunk she was selling to locals’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

GRANJA DEALER Great-gran, 101, arrested for dealing drugs after ‘being found with bags of skunk she was selling to locals’

A 101-YEAR-OLD great-gran has been arrested for allegedly dealing drugs after she was found “selling bags of skunk”.

Esther Ogunmabo was taken in on Saturday after being caught selling Cannabis in Nigeria, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency said.



The old lady was found carrying “retail sachets of skunk, a strain of cannabis weighing 90 grams, which she claims she sells to locals” according to Femi Babafemi – the agency’s director.

According to officials, Esther began selling the contraband after her local shop was burnt down in a fire.



They also claimed one of her daughters, who lives in Lagos, was the key supplier of the drugs.

It is believed the centenarian would receive a batch of drugs every four days and sell it in smaller quantities to paying customers.



Shortly after being arrested, Esther was bailed and provided with counselling due to her age.

Her daughter has also since been arrested.

The case has quickly caught widespread attention due to the OAP’s age, with some labelling her “Granny Escobar”.

One person said: “Serious Retirement plans.”



Another joked: “Grandma only thought she was selling vegetables.”

A third said: “101 yrs and still hustling them streets.”

A final simply put: “Free Great Grandma.”

The agency claims this is part of a wider crackdown on drugs across the country’s coast.

It claims to have intercepted a wooden boat last Friday, believed to be transporting drugs to Cameroon.



It reports having arrested three individuals onboard and seizing more than 42kg of contraband.

News.title: It is irresponsible for social media giants to allow teens to glory in driving at shocking speeds on wrong side of road
News.content:
Video nasties

SOCIAL media sites have no business making money from allowing teens to glory in driving at shocking speeds on the wrong side of the road.

It is wholly irresponsible for the likes of TikTok to encourage reckless law-breaking with such fatal consequences.

Two brave armed officers — one an Iraq war hero — were killed by a runaway car in Middlesbrough.



Two of the “joyriders” were thugs who previously posted videos of high-speed chases for mindless “likes”. Other social media accounts linked to the car’s passengers show men in balaclavas on motorbikes and speeding cars.



That investigators say there is no evidence of filming in this particular case doesn’t lessen the shattering senselessness of the deaths of PCs Tom Clough and Matthew Blades.

How social media giants respond to public outrage over algorithms that push such violent content will tell us whether they prize profit over responsibility.

Breaking Vlad

ANDY Burnham’s steadfast support of Ukraine might be the most welcome move of his premiership so far.



Providing the blueprints so Kyiv can make its own long-range Storm Shadow missiles will worry Putin, even if they will take time to build.

But Burnham must also realise how much Britain is at risk, too.

So far he has been less than clear over spending plans for our Armed Forces.

It’s no use handing cash to Ukraine while leaving our own defence well short.



Gas blast

BRITAIN’S dash for Net Zero has made our country worse than the economic basket case of Venezuela.

So says Jim Johnson, boss of one of the country’s oldest energy firms Hunting, who says “crazy” Government policies mean he’ll never invest in the UK again.

He said: “The reality is that Britain has become uninvestable. Everything your politicians have done has shown me that we cannot trust them.”

Johnson’s words make for grim reading for Chancellor John Healey, desperate for growth to balance the books.

It’s also another reminder of the folly of smashing our North Sea gas and oil industry with massive taxes.



Free enterprise

ANDY Burnham must understand he will never fix soaring youth unemployment without freeing up businesses to grow.

Labour seems to think only State schemes and subsidies are the answer.

But cutting the sky-high taxes that stop firms hiring youngsters would be faster, cheaper, and far more likely to work.

News.title: Labour lefties must stop bleating and back benefit & immigration cuts or they’ll be off to Jobcentre after the election
News.content:
LORD AUSTIN Labour lefties must stop bleating and back benefit & immigration cuts or they’ll be off to Jobcentre after the election

PARLIAMENT’S summer holiday finishes next week and Andy Burnham’s honeymoon could end with it.

Labour have gone ahead in the polls since he took over, but there’s a long list of problems piling up on his desk that could bring it all crashing down again.



And one of the biggest headaches is immigration, which has caused every other recent Prime Minister huge problems.

More than 100 Labour MPs are already demanding he drops Shabana Mahmood’s plans to make migrants wait for ten years before claiming benefits or applying for social housing.



They must be mad. Opposing the Home Secretary might make them feel virtuous but, if anything, the rest of us think her changes don’t go far enough.

Instead of listening to his backbenchers, the PM should pay attention to former Labour Home Secretary Alan Johnson, who has urged Ms Mahmood to stick to her guns.



The more she listens to out-of-touch MPs, “the worse it will be” because it is a “very big issue” for voters, he said.

“Pictures of people coming illegally into this country, people feel really, really strongly about it.

“Don’t listen to your Labour colleagues — press ahead,” he told her.

“When you’re doing something that really needs to be done, particularly on illegal immigration, you always get a kickback, and she’s got to carry on.”



And he warned that if they block her plans, voters will quickly lose patience and back a party with a plan to get a grip of immigration.

He said: “We need to have the right policies to address it, or someone else will. This is Shabana’s main argument — ‘If we don’t do it there’s a very, very different approach from a very different party and they’ll end up in government’.”

Wise words.



But if they don’t believe him, they should just remember what happened to the last Tory government.

The country lost confidence when they crashed the economy, but voters were absolutely furious when they broke their promise to stop the small boats — let alone allowing 3.5million people to come here legally in just four years.

That changed our country for good and is one of the biggest reasons the Tories are still struggling to get a hearing.

With numbers like that, it’s impossible to know who was allowed in, what they believe or how they’ll behave.

The result is the shocking news that the Government has had to start handing out leaflets telling migrants not to rape women, that sex with children is illegal and domestic violence is a crime.



And it’s why the Home Secretary knows she’s got to press ahead and sort the system out — no matter how much her backbenchers complain.

Her changes so far have seen the number of criminals and immigration offenders booted out hitting its highest level for a decade.

More than 80,000 foreign criminals, immigration offenders and failed asylum seekers have been deported since the election, but just 6,000 of them had arrived on the small boats, which is why she now wants to strike deals to send those refused asylum to other countries.



That obviously makes sense, but we also need stronger rules to keep out those who don’t share our values — let alone people who support terrorism and extremism, racist bigots or anyone who believes women are second-class citizens.

Labour MPs need to wake up and smell the coffee when it comes to welfare too.

Anyone who looks at the numbers can see the country is going broke and we need to cut the cost of benefits if we’re going to avoid a terrible reckoning.

The economy is barely growing, rising energy bills have increased inflation, unemployment is increasing, too, and the benefits bill drove up government borrowing by £1.8billion last month.

Taxes are sky high and we’re mortgaged to the hilt with national debt approaching a whopping £3trillion.



Lenders have such little confidence in our ability to pay our way that our borrowing costs are the highest of any major economy.

That means we’re wasting well over £100billion on interest payments alone — almost as much as we spend on education.

In fact, we’re spending billions more on benefits than on education, defence and policing put together.

Pat McFadden, the Work and Pensions Secretary, knows we can’t carry on like this and he’s appalled that a million young people are out of work, not at college and don’t have a training place.

That will ruin their lives, cost the rest of us a fortune and he’s determined to do something about it by getting them off the dole, on to apprenticeships and into work.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Labour lefties bleat when anyone tries to curb the benefits bill or dares to tackle immigration, but Burnham reappointed Mahmood and McFadden and must back them now.

Labour MPs need to get behind them too, or they’ll be off to the Jobcentre as well after the next election.

News.title: Boy, 5, who fell to death from ‘faulty’ 15th floor kitchen window ‘believed he could fly’
News.content:
PLUNGE TRAGEDY Boy, 5, who fell to death from ‘faulty’ 15th floor kitchen window ‘believed he could fly’

A FIVE-YEAR-OLD boy who fell to his death from an allegedly faulty 15th floor kitchen window “believed he could fly”, an inquest has heard.

Aalim Ahmed died instantly after falling from the residential block in Plaistow, East London.



His distraught father Makail Ahmed rushed from the top-floor flat and discovered the youngster’s body shortly before 6am on May 16 2024.

Aalim’s mother, Sahra Osman, described their son’s death as “preventable” and blasted Newham Council, claiming she had reported safety concerns about the top-floor flat in Jacobs House on multiple occasions.



But contrasting accounts about the condition of the windows were heard at the inquest into the boy’s death.

The inquest heard that an engineer sent by Newham Council to carry out an inspection in December 2023 said they were functioning when he saw them.

In contrast, Ms Osman had a list of complaints spanning several months which included her fears the windows were opening too wide and she did not have a key.

She told the court how she was “scared” and “horrified” when the council put her young family in the flat, which needed repairs, saying Aalim was autistic with “no sense of danger”.



Assistant coroner Ian Wade, sitting at East London Coroner’s Court, said the windows “were not used appropriately”.

He delivered a narrative conclusion on Monday, in which he said: “Aalim was an active five-year-old boy who suffered from a diagnosed condition called autism, such as to render him incapable of making reliable judgments about his personal safety and abilities.

“In the early hours of May 16 2024, he awoke and went from his bedroom to the kitchen, he climbed onto a chair and then onto the windowsill of an insecure double turn and tilt window.

“He opened the window and in a naive belief that he could fly or alternatively could come to no harm he leapt from the open window… he died at the scene.”

Mr Wade added that while the window had “become compromised”, he believed there was “no compelling reason a landlord should’ve considered that placing this little boy on the 15th floor was inappropriate”.



The court previously heard a young child’s voice is twice heard counting down “three, two, one” followed a few seconds later by “a loud clang” was captured on grainy audio, which was taken from CCTV outside the apartment block.

Detective Constable Joe Linton previously said “it is most likely from the footage available” that Aalim had “jumped out” of the flat at the building in New City Road “of his own accord without the presence of a third party”.

Ms Osman denied any suggestion she may have “forced” the window open to cope in hot weather.

She said Aalim could have been reaching for a biscuit when he fell and that her ongoing complaints to fix “faulty” restrictors – a type of safety device – only led to a series of workmen who did not sort the problem.

Window engineer Charlie Mann said the windows were “all working”, including the handles and restrictors, when he tested them in December 2023.



Having spoken to the mother, who said her son had autism, he decided the restrictors should be changed to a lockable version rather than one that can be worked by a button.

He ordered nine restrictors and contractors came to fix them in January 2024.

Charlie Mann’s father, James Mann, who is managing director of ABC Ltd the firm where the window engineer works, watched videos of police operating the window from which Aalim fell.

In the video, the court saw that the restrictor did not engage every time the police officer tested the window.

He said that “there needs to be an adjustment, something is not quite right” but he added he needed to see more of the window to have a clearer idea of the problem.



Detective Inspector Jamie Humm, who investigated the incident, said there was “no evidence or suspicion he (Aalim) had been forced”.

“The flat was well furnished and it was clearly a loving environment for a child,” he noted.

He added that soon after arriving at the scene he was satisfied “there was no evidence of a crime, not that I thought there would be”.

John Gray, cabinet member for housing, Newham Council, said: “This was a tragic accident which resulted in the heartbreaking death of a young five-year-old child.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Our thoughts continue to be with Aalim’s family and friends during this incredibly difficult time.



“We are grateful to the coroner Ian Wade KC for his thorough and fair hearing of the facts of this case, which have at times been very difficult to hear and revisit.”

News.title: Man, 46, charged with manslaughter after ‘wonderful’ woman, 75, killed during ‘burglary’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

'BURGLARY' HORROR Man, 46, charged with manslaughter after ‘wonderful’ woman, 75, killed during ‘burglary’

A MAN has been charged following the death of a 75-year-old woman in an alleged burglary.

Police were called to a property in North London on the evening of Tuesday, August 11 to reports of a burglary.

75-year-old Rose Smith was taken to hospital shortly after, where she tragically died the following day.

It is believed an 81-year-old man was also treated at the Finsbury Park location before being taken to hospital.





Jeffrey Dean Rose, 46, was arrested in connection with the investigation, cops said.

He has since been charged with manslaughter and aggravated burglary with intent and will appear at Barkingside Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday, August 25.

Paying tribute, Rose’s heartbroken family said: “This is the most devastating loss our family could ever have imagined.

“Rose was a truly wonderful, outgoing woman who was loved by so many people.

“She loved bingo, going to cafés with her friends and, above all, spending time with her family.

“She treasured the time she spent with her children, grandchildren and great-grandchild.

“We want people to remember Rose for the person she truly was — loving, fun, kind, sociable and full of life.”

News.title: Brexit betrayal fears grow as Burnham vows to be ‘bolder’ in bringing Britain closer to the EU
News.content:
ANDY Burnham sparked fears of a Brexit betrayal yesterday as he promised to be “bolder” in bringing Britain closer to the EU.

He told European Council chief Antonio Costa the UK must seek “greater co-operation” with Brussels across all areas as the pair both visited Kyiv.



The PM ruled out rejoining but previously said he wanted to see Britain back inside the EU in his lifetime.

His comments come ahead of a delayed UK-EU summit set to take place later this year, aimed at delivering a “step change” in relations.



Downing Street said: “Turning to the UK’s relationship with the European Union, the two leaders underlined the importance of being ambitious to drive a step change in relations.

“The UK had to be bolder in terms of getting closer to the bloc, the Prime Minister said.”

Shadow foreign secretary Priti Patel accused Mr Burnham of wanting to reopen old wounds by fighting the battles of the Brexit years all over again.

Ms Patel said: “Labour should be focused on reversing the terrible damage done by Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves.

“Their tax rises and red tape have hammered business, destroyed jobs and driven bills up for hardworking families.

“Instead of trying to take our country back to 2016, he should lay out a coherent, costed plan to take Britain forwards.”



The PM blasted Brexit as “damaging” in his by-election campaign in June but warned against re-running the old arguments.

Reform said: “The British people voted to leave not slowly hand back powers to Brussels bureaucrats.”

Mr Burnham visited war-torn Ukraine after Britain agreed to hand Kyiv blueprints to long-range missiles.

News.title: Inside the terrifying balaclava-clad TikTok joyride gangs terrorising Britain’s streets after horror A66 head-on crash
News.content:
STARING into the eyes of a balaclava-clad gang, I saw not a shred of remorse.

They laughed as they told how they broke into people’s homes to find car keys – taking along weapons they were willing to use – before taunting cops to chase them in high-speed pursuits.



The gang even boasted of rigging up MOBILITY SCOOTERS, swapping out engines to make them go up to 70mph in a bid to mock police.

Their dangerous antics could easily kill – as evidenced by the weekend deaths of two hero police officers when a car carrying five young men smashed into them.



Yet they simply don’t care.

One gang member casually told us: “It gets the adrenaline going, dunnit?”



Their attitude is the culmination of a toxic culture in which cravings for TikTok likes override everything else.

A quick look on the site – in fact any social media platform – is sobering.

In one clip, a man films himself on his phone with just one hand on the wheel, the driver’s speedometer hits 178mph and the motorway becomes a blur.

In another video, the same motorist hits 109mph while a small child strapped into a toddler seat beside him rubs his tired eyes and drinks from a baby bottle.



When grown adults are prepared to put their pre-school children at risk for a little bit of kudos on social media, society has hit a new low.

As part of a month long investigation into ‘balaclava boys’ terrorising Britain I saw first hand just how nonchalant these young men have become.

They boasted to me of ‘ragging’ cars and bikes – driving them as fast as possible – before ‘decamping’, or dumping vehicles before running off.

They wear balaclavas in the hope they won’t ever be prosecuted, with a ‘no face, no case’ motto.

One told us: “I’ve got about 700 followers. You can just rag a car and annoy the cops and you get loads of people watching on TikTok.



“It gets the adrenalin going.”

Scarily, one of the youths produced a serrated weapon he kept down his trouser leg, telling me it was for “protection” against anyone who caught him up to no good.

Another teen told me how they sell cars to organised crime gangs for as little as £300, with Nissans and Audis their vehicle of choice.

They said: “There’s nowt better to do and this is a way to make money, innit?

“If you get a good car you can sell it for fo £300 or £400 and motorbikes for about £200.



“That’s good money for us. Nissan Qashqai is a good’un to sell easily.”

Yet cops are reluctant to chase those on powerful bikes if kids remove their helmets – a fact gangs are well aware of.

One senior officer told us: “No traffic officer is going to chase some teenager without a helmet because they’d be to blame if there was a fatality.”



The antics of these gangs is dangerous beyond belief but ‘flexing’ (showing off) their ‘skills’ has more value than any innocent life.

Under hashtags such as #smoked and #chased, social media videos reveal blue-light night pursuits through residential areas while other drivers are brazen enough to torment police during the day, driving past them at ridiculous speeds.

It’s become a dangerous game in a world where validation on TikTok is the norm for Generation Z.

The Government has now warned social media giants to take down clips of dangerous drivers after horrendous A66 crash in MIddlesborough at the weekend.

In Ireland last month, five teenagers were killed and three sisters and a child left fighting for their lives in hospital after a similar horrendous crash.



Downing Street today said it had raised the problem of the “glorification of dangerous driving” with social media giants since the A66 smash – warning it will take “tough action” if platforms fail to get a grip.

Defence minister Luke Pollard called on firms like Meta to step up, saying: “They’ve argued for many years they don’t need to be regulated, that they can police themselves. So this is the challenge for them.

“Remove that content.

“They know exactly what content is on their site. They know how their algorithm works. They also know that people post content to get views.”

He said content creators were being given a “financial incentive” to post “outrageous content.”



Statistics reveal that one in seven drivers aged 17 to 24 use mobile phones to record videos or take pictures while driving. The research, from charity IAM RoadSmart, also show that one in six go on social media while behind the wheel.

Policy director Nicholas Lyes said kids are also trying to use a loophole to stop their content being taken down.



He said: “Social media companies have a duty to ensure that dangerous criminal activities are not circulated for likes and shares.

“Many of the accounts label content ‘AI generated’ in an apparent attempt to reduce the risk of removal by moderators.”

At least one of the five young men who died in the Middlesbrough crash, Jakub Matusiak, 23, had posted apparent dangerous driving content on TikTok. The other four dead passengers were named as Makai Saddington, 18, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Theo Rae, 17 and Cole Robert Worthy, 17.

Police had been chasing their Volkswagen Passat for almost seven minutes before aborting the pursuit when it started travelling down the wrong side of the road.



Seconds later the Passat hit a second police car, killing innocent PC’s Matthew Blades, 37, and Tom Clough, 38, an ex-soldier who served in Iraq and Afghanistan.

It’s since emerged that Saddington was awaiting trial on charges of racially abusing and assaulting officers.

His social media activity has also since come under scrutiny, with clips appearing to show him taking part in high-speed police chases months before the crash.



Matusiak also posted a video of himself apparently driving erratically through a housing estate in May, with the caption: ‘Unfortunately I’m not a nonchalant boyfriend’.

The clip, seemingly filmed by the driver himself, shows a car speeding through a residential area in broad daylight, before veering onto a green in the middle of a housing estate. The vehicle appears to head down a path as the driver steers with the hand not holding the camera.

In Ireland, three sisters and a young boy are still fighting for survival after a BMW driving the wrong way down the M9 hit their car.

Ella Hendricken, who is in her 20s, and Niamh and Alma Kinsella, in their 30s, and Alma’s seven-year-old son Yemi were badly injured in the crash near Moone, Co Kildare on August 16.

The BMW driver and passengers were also killed and named as Joey Carthy, 15, Alex McCarthy, 16, Jack Kennedy and Kamil Pustkowski, both 17, and Jeremy O’Brien, 18.



Jeremy’s mum Margaret Berry, 36, told the Irish Sun: “This tragedy should never have happened.

“I’m not proud of what happened and I don’t condone what they did – I wish my son had never got into that car.

“I also hope that the family who remain in hospital can find some kind of forgiveness some day . I will continue to pray for them. My son and those other boys didn’t set out that night to intentionally hurt people and my heart will always break for everyone who’s involved in this nightmare.”

The boys apparently identified with the so-called “Lucky Dip” gang, a loosely organised group police believe is behind a large number of carjacking and dangerous driving incidents near Dublin.

Like the young men killed in Middlesborough, some had posted clips of themselves being pursued by blue lights as loud music blared.



They uploaded videos weaving in and out of traffic with one including the caption ‘wrong way’.

Some had written Lucky Dip onto their social media profiles – alluding to a gang operating in Ireland which pick an area at random, break into houses and steal cars.

It’s a trend that is expected to spread across the UK.

Retired Scotland Yard DCI Mick Neville said: “It’s a contagion so I’ve no doubt that some idiots somewhere are thinking, ‘we’ll have a go at that’.

“For the criminals they get to pass their tips on how to do it, and they get the bravado effect of people liking it.”



TikTok today removed content flagged by The Sun and said it removes harmful content. The site said it was also monitoring content related to the smash that killed two police officers.

Snapchat said reckless driving had “no place” on its platform while Meta said it bans damaging content and restricts under 18s from seeing some posts.

Social media dangers Unbelievably, there is no automatic duty for social media giants to take down dangerous driving posts. Platforms like TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat must remove content that comes under a criminal offence such as child sex abuse, terrorism or non-consensual intimate images such as AI deepfakes under the new Online Safety Act. Otherwise it is up to firms themselves to assess what is inappropriate content and take it down fast. But there are duties on providers to protect children against content deemed to be harmful, even if it is not classed as illegal. Dangerous stunts and challenges sit alongside bullying and abusive or hateful content in the “priority” category of harmful content. Regulations, published alongside the Act which passed into law in 2023, listed “content which encourages, promotes or provides instructions for a challenge or stunt highly likely to result in serious injury to the person who does it or to someone else”. Online platforms must minimise children’s exposure to such content, online safety regulator Ofcom said. However some providers, such as TikTok, said their own policies strictly prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving. It said it actively removes any videos and accounts that break its rules. TikTok removed some of content The Sun sent today, including the 78mph driver. According to a spokesperson, between January and March this year the site removed 99.1percent of harmful violent and criminal content before it was flagged to them. A Snapchat spokesperson said: “Our deepest sympathies are with the families who are grieving this devastating loss. “Content depicting dangerous or illegal activity, including reckless driving, has no place on Snapchat and is prohibited by our Community Guidelines. We’ve removed content that we located related to this incident for violation of our policies.” Meta said it bans people from “promoting” high risk challenges and dangerous driving, taking down content. It also restricts under-18s from viewing “content that isn’t suitable for them” including posts by reckless motorists.

Bereaved family members have warned about the dangers of drivers filming reckless stunts for social media.

In May, Denise Doyle spoke publicly after her partner, Sylvester Abayomi, 50, was killed in Manchester. The two men responsible had filmed themselves inhaling nitrous oxide and driving at up to 139mph.

“Sylvester was simply on his way to work,” Denise said.



“An ordinary hard-working man. He should have returned home to me safely that day. Because of your actions he never did.”

Addressing the defendants in court, she added: “You left Sylv to die alone. You did not show him even a shred of compassion or humanity.”

Dafydd Hughes, 18, also lost his life after getting into a car with an unlicensed and intoxicated friend in Wales in May 2022, who posted his reckless driving on social media.

Snapchat footage showed driver Ricky Davies drinking cider and smoking drugs behind the wheel.

His mum Emma later urged other youngsters to learn from the tragedy.



“Dafydd, like most young boys, thought he was invincible, and made the wrong choice getting in the car that morning,” said mum-of-six Emma, 35.

“But it wasn’t Dafydd’s choice for Ricky to drink all day, to speed or be on the wrong side of the road. I’ll never forgive Ricky.”

Months earlier, 17-year-old Nadia Yusuf was killed in Manchester. Rohail Jillani had filmed himself for Snapchat while inhaling nitrous oxide and driving at up to 98mph.

But while these incidents used to be rare, campaigners warn that they have dramatically increased in recent months.

Youth justice figures show that 11percent of ‘proven offences’ committed by 15 to 17-year-olds are linked to motoring – around 3,500.



It appears a surprisingly low number but perhaps not when you consider how many car thefts police solve – with around just one in every 40 resulting in a charge or court action.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Whatever the real figures, the reality is that this deadly trend fueled by social media is likely to result in even more tragedies.

News.title: Kids looking for clicks & dying for likes is tip of the digital iceberg – how many more will die before decisive action?
News.content:
TEENAGERS, as both Shakespeare and worrying parents have long testified, have always been inveterate risk-takers.

But where once upon an innocent time 17-year-olds got their thrills from a quick fumble in the back row of the cinema, or drinking cider in a park, now the stakes are so much higher. And lethal.





Take the awful, awful case of the fatal car crash which killed two police officers and five young men on Saturday.

PC Tom Clough and PC Matthew Blades died when a Volkswagen Passat, which officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.

Two brave, decent men killed so cruelly and so utterly needlessly. My thoughts are with their friends, family and colleagues — victims, all of them.

The young men’s car had been speeding the wrong way down a dual carriageway. Two of the youngsters in the car had shared high-speed police chase videos.

Kids looking for clicks, dying for likes.

The Government has urged social media companies to remove such posts, as Andy Burnham branded sharing them “truly reprehensible”.

It was, quite literally, an accident waiting to happen.

Because filmed high-speed car chases have become a terrifying “thing” on this app, one which averages around two BILLION users monthly.





Other current or recent trends include “bridge jumping”, which is every bit as dangerous as it sounds, “chroming”, which sees youngsters inhaling from household objects to get high, and a challenge which involves consuming excessive amounts of over-the-counter allergy medication to trigger hallucinations.

Of course, parents have a responsibility in all of this, to do all they can to monitor their children’s online viewing.

But that is easier said than done.

Stateside, a landmark trial against Meta — the owner of Facebook and Instagram — started last Tuesday.

According to prosecuting lawyer Megan O’Neill, the company’s business model can be boiled down to four words: Hook, hold, harvest and hide.

It is alleged the world’s largest social media company “hooks” in users, “holds” them on its platforms for as long as possible, “harvests” their data and then “hides” the truth from the public. If proven, sinister stuff, for sure.

California — where its HQ lies — has joined 28 other US states in suing the £1trillion company for allegedly designing addictive products that lead to children being harmed.

The reckoning for social media over here surely follows. Not if, but when.



Social media, something that started out as a way of bridging long-lost friends and making our online world ever smaller, has so many positives.

Community, charity en- deavours, humour and irreverence. It has allowed anyone, irrespective of class, colour or sex, to forge a career path that simply did not exist 20 years ago. In that sense, it is meritocratic and should be lauded.

But now so many kids see influencing as their get-out-of-jail-free card, a means to make millions from the comfort of their smartphones.

Not surprisingly, we are also seeing a mental health epidemic, with young people glued to their phones, seeking validation from strangers.

Dangerous driving is the tip of the digital iceberg.

How many more people must die before decisive action is taken?

PYJAMA DRAMA THOUGHTS and prayers with John Barrowman at this difficult time. The former Doctor Who star launched into a tirade about his recent business-class flight from LA to London . . . bemoaning the lack of free pyjamas. “The tickets were very expensive and we get on thinking we’d get pyjamas with the flagship service,” he whined on X. “Then you apparently only give them to the first two rows in business class. What’s that all about?” That’s about time you lost your entitlement, pal.

Beckhams – from salad scoffer to the veneer-ly normal



IF David Attenborough had been narrating the Beckham family last week, he’d have had a field day.

First up, we were treated to a very rare sighting of Victoria Beckham eating.

A creature infrequently spotted before food, here she was heartily tucking into a salad while on holiday. Granted, this is largely the same meal she has apparently eaten daily for the past 25 years, but still, eagle-eyed watchers rarely get to see the process.

Indeed, the number of times she has been pictured actually consuming food can probably be counted on one hand.

And then, three days later, almost an equally unheard-of phenomenon: Man with normal teeth.

Youngest Cruz, who is rapidly proving to be the funniest member of the clan, took to social media to plug his new record, and DIDN’T have gleaming white veneers.

Something, as Attenborough would surely testify, that is a sight to behold in the modern animal kingdom. And long may it continue.

BEES' BUZZ, I GIT IT IF I had my time again, I’d come back as a Brentford supporter. On Saturday afternoon I took my father to watch Spurs get trounced 3-0 at Brentford’s Gtech Community Stadium. Tottenham were terrible, but absolutely everything about the Bees was first-rate. Chatting to a member of the backroom staff in the corporate lounge at half-time, he told me the club had a “no d***head-signing policy”. Alas, unlike my own club. Another highlight was meeting this gent. After homing in on his Old Git shirt, I asked this local legend where I could get a similar one made for my poor dad. “Not in the official Brentford shop,” replied Mr Git (I’d had three pints by the time we started chatting so failed to ask the lovely man his name). “They told me ‘Old Git’ was discriminatory, so I had to go to Snappy Snaps to get it printed.” Brilliant.

A HIGH KICK BY GIO

GIOVANNI PERNICE’S recently serialised autobiography couldn’t have made for fun reading for BBC bosses.

The Sicilian dancer, let go from Strictly Come Dancing in the wake of his torrid falling-out with Amanda Abbington, lashed out in spectacular fashion.



Effectively accusing the corporation of failing in its duty of care to him, he also threw the current crop of pros under the bus.

“There are still people on Strictly whose behaviour is far worse,” he writes.

“Others drink before the live show. Yet I’m paying the price because I danced with a woman I don’t think should have been on the show in the first place, who didn’t like my teaching style.”

A gentleman scorned. . .

Harry and Meg heading back CAN’T say I shared the same breathy excitement as much of the population upon discovering Meghan and Harry are headed back to these shores. Certainly, in the past – and on this page – I’ve questioned some of their motives, and haven’t always been an uber-fan. But times move, and people change. And Harry’s Invictus Games is a truly brilliant and worthy initiative, one that deserves all the plaudits. Here’s to them making a fresh start, reconciling with Charles, and generally new beginnings.

Meme of the week





10

BACK in my day we had Trolls: Little creatures with furry, bright colours, upturned hair, stocky, plasticky bodies and smiling faces.

Thirty odd years later, here we are again.

Apparently, this purple- haired K Pop doll, below left, is on Gen Alpha’s Most Wanted Christmas list.

The resemblance is sort-of uncanny.

News.title: Organised crime arrests as police investigate A66 crash that killed two officers
News.content:
Twelve people have been arrested as part of the investigation into the A66 crash that killed seven people, including two police officers.

Nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61, have been arrested across Teesside on suspicion of a range of offences including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.

In the early hours of Saturday, a Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by police travelled the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough and crashed into an oncoming police car - two PCs and all five Passat occupants died.

Cleveland Police said it was investigating "serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident".

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and 17-year-old Cole Robert Worthy.

Earlier, Cleveland Police released more details of its investigation into the lead-up to the crash and information about the 12 people it had arrested.

The force said:

It received several reports of two vehicles "being driven dangerously" on Saturday morning

The first vehicle, believed to be a Volvo XC60, was seen "ramming properties" in the Middlesbrough area

The second vehicle, a Passat, is believed to have been associated with this activity

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology

The Volvo has been recovered in Middlesbrough

Four of the five people in the Passat had previous convictions

Assistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said the investigation had been "fast moving and complex".

He said: "The events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect.

"We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident and to bring all those responsible to justice."

News.title: How the deadly A66 crash unfolded leaving seven dead
News.content:
Two police officers and five people within a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way down the A66 motorway were killed after the car collided with a marked police car around 03:30 BST on Saturday.

Using doorbell footage, pictures of the scene and police reports, we can now piece together exactly how this fatal incident unfolded.

We also know that four of the five people in the car had previous convictions. One of them, Makai Saddington, 18, previously pleaded guilty to assaulting a police officer.

PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were the two police officers who died in the crash.

The BBC's UK correspondent Daniel Sandford explains what we know so far.

More on this story.

News.title: Is UK's Storm Shadow missile a game changer for Ukraine?
News.content:
The UK has handed secret blueprints to Ukraine that will allow the country to build its own long-range cruise missiles.

The announcement came during Andy Burnham's first visit to Kyiv as prime minster, where he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

But faced with an almost daily barrage of Russian ballistic missiles, correspondent Joe Inwood explains why the offer may not be enough to win the war.

News.title: Charity? Acting? The Cotswolds? What will Harry and Meghan's UK life look like?
News.content:
Within the next few days, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex and their two children will have departed California and become residents of the UK.

Since news broke of the move, there has been some confusion as to what British life for Harry and Meghan will look like - but a picture is emerging of the family's priorities.

Over the weekend, there was a deluge of stories about Meghan's return to acting with speculation she would have a role in the next series of The Gentlemen on Netflix, created by British director Guy Ritchie.

Talks are still said to be in the early stages and we understand filming for the third series of the show is imminent - but Netflix has made no comment on who will star, leaving the way open for a former working member of the royal family with an acting background to be cast.

The comedy is about a duke turned drug baron and is mostly filmed in the Cotswolds.

What is clear is that a return to acting more broadly is very much on the agenda for Meghan. It would be financially lucrative for the family in a world of expensive homes, school fees and international travel.

News.title: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows
News.content:
The world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from human-caused climate change and the growing El NiÃ±o weather phenomenon.

The average surface temperature of the planet's seas outside the polar regions hit 21.1C (70F) on Saturday, according to figures from the European Copernicus climate change service.

That edges past the 21.09C recorded on three separate days in March 2024, and is far above average for the time of year.

Warmer oceans can have wide-reaching consequences, including supercharging extreme weather, raising sea levels and harming marine life.

"This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress," said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus.

"El NiÃ±o is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming," she added.

News.title: Briton fighting for Russia killed in Ukraine
News.content:
A British national has been killed in Ukraine while fighting for Russia.

Bradley Townsend is said to have died following an attack by a remote-controlled FPV drone in Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region. His death, on 10 June, is believed to be the first of a British citizen fighting for Russia in the conflict.

The 33-year-old left his home in Barnsley, South Yorkshire, earlier this year after telling his family he was going to Romania, according to the Yorkshire Post, external.

The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was aware of reports a British national had died in Ukraine, adding it was in contact with his family.

The news emerged as Andy Burnham arrived in Kyiv for his first foreign trip as UK prime minister.

The visit coincides with the 35th anniversary of the country's independence from the Soviet Union.

The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.

News.title: Police pass Mohamed Al Fayed case file to prosecutors
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police have sent a file of evidence to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) relating to a man in his 80s as part of its investigation into claims of sexual assault against Mohamed Al Fayed.

A man and a woman, both in their 80s, were interviewed under caution last month on suspicion of aiding and abetting rape and sexual assault, and assisting the commission of sexual offences.

The CPS will now decide whether a charge can be made.

Earlier this year, three women, aged in their 40s, 50s and 60s, and one man in his 60s were also questioned. The former Harrods owner died three years ago aged 94 having never faced any charges.

Al Fayed was accused by more than 20 women of sexual assault in a BBC document and podcast that aired in September 2024.

Since those allegations more than 400 alleged victims or witnesses have come forward to lawyers.

A Met Police spokesperson said "detectives submitted a full evidential file" to the CPS for a "charging decision".

"The file relates to one suspect, a man in his 80s, and relates to two indecent assaults on two women in London. Officers will continue to work closely with CPS prosecutors as the case progresses.

"To date, seven suspects have been interviewed under caution on suspicion of offences including aiding and abetting rape and sexual assault, assisting in the commission of sexual offences, and human trafficking for the purposes of sexual exploitation."

Co-chairs of the Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors, Jen Mills and Lindsay Mason, welcomed the latest development.

"The submission of a full evidential file to the CPS is a significant step, and it matters most of all for the two women whose allegations are at the centre of it," the statement said.

"Both are members of Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors and, as with all those impacted by this scandal, we stand alongside them with love and empathy."

A spokesperson from another Fayed survivor group, No One Above, said: "We call on the Met to confirm it is securing evidence on all perpetrators and co-conspirators - including the financial and documentary evidence of how victims were recruited, screened, moved, harboured and silenced."

Harrods - which was sold by Al Fayed in 2010 - previously told the BBC it was in the process of settling more than 250 claims for compensation.

News.title: US-Canada trade war escalates as Trump threatens tariff hike on autos after Carney vows to retaliate
News.content:
President Donald Trump has threatened to hike US tariffs on automobiles originating in Canada, as the trade war between the two neighbours continues to heat up.

Trump said on Monday that he will increase tariffs on Canadian cars and trucks, as well as auto parts, from 25% to 50% as of 1 January.

It comes after US-Canada trade talks collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of making unreasonable last-minute demands.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called Trump's latest levy threat unsurprising and accused the president of wanting to destroy Canada's auto industry. He added that Canada is ready to resume talks if the US comes with the "right attitude".

The war of words followed several US and Canadian officials saying that talks are suspended with no set date to resume.

Trump's threat was the latest escalation after Canada walked away from trade negotiations late Friday night, moments before a US-imposed deadline that would add a 50% levy on nearly $20bn (C$28bn; Â£14bn) of Canadian imports.

The collapse in talks marked a significant change in tone from earlier in the week, when both sides appeared optimistic that a new US-Canada trade deal could be reached.

Canadian officials have said that the US introduced last-minute demands that were "unacceptable", including a clause limiting which countries Canada could sign trade deals with.

US officials, meanwhile, said that it was Canada that introduced last-minute changes. "They wanted more," US trade representative Jamieson Greer said in an interview with CNBC on Monday.

The breakdown led to growing tensions as both sides publicly dug in their heels.

On Monday, Trump's tariff threats to Canada's auto industry followed Carney declaring the country would counter his levies with reciprocal tariffs on US goods "dollar for dollar".

Carney said he was focused on supporting Canadian businesses impacted by new 50% US tariffs after the Friday deadline expired, as well as building infrastructure to diversify Canada's trade, which historically has relied heavily on the US.

Carney announced funding of C$11bn ($7.95bn; Â£5.83bn) to build six icebreakers at a Quebec shipyard for the Canadian Coast Guard that will replace its medium and heavy ageing fleet.

The icebreakers will be used to open winter shipping routes through Canada's northern and Atlantic waters.

News.title: Man charged with murder after house fire
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder, attempted murder and arson following a fire in west London that left a woman dead and eight others in need of hospital treatment.

Pawel Kulpa, 34, faces one count of murder, eight counts of attempted murder and one count of arson with intent to endanger life.

The charges come after a fire at a residential address on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow, at about 01:15 BST on Wednesday, 19 August.

A 48-year-old woman died in hospital while another woman, 40, remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. Kulpa is due to appear at Willesden Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

News.title: Teenager arrested after four viable devices found in security alert
News.content:
A 16-year-old boy has been arrested under the Terrorism Act after a security alert in Omagh, County Tyrone.

Police carried out a planned search on Monday at an address in the Gardenville Avenue.

Police said four viable explosive devices were found and removed from the property for forensic examination.

Nearby residents who had been asked to leave their homes during the alert have since returned.

Det Insp Winters urged the public not to speculate about the incident.

"It's important to stress that, while the suspect has been arrested under the Terrorism Act, our investigation to establish a motive remains very much ongoing."

News.title: Prince Harry steps down from African wildlife charity board
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses against indigenous people.

A spokesman for Prince Harry confirmed he was stepping down after being president for the charity, African Parks, for six years before becoming a member of its board of directors in 2023, but said he remains a "supporter of its mission".

Last year the organisation admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.

Prince Harry's resignation comes shortly after it was announced he was relocating with the Duchess of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet from California to the UK.

Prince Harry's spokesman said "the Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board.

"His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks' mission."

African Parks manages around 20 national parks and protected areas across 12 countries.

It was subject to an independent human rights investigation into allegations guards managed and paid by the charity had beaten, raped and tortured indigenous people in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park.

The charity said in 2025 it had improved its safeguarding processes both in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park and institutionally.

Announcing a "governance refresh of its board of directors", the charity thanked Prince Harry for his association, saying he had "brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa".

It added: "The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks' work."

The charity's website says Prince Harry served as part of the expert team that helped implement the first phase of the 500 Elephants project, which was "one of the largest and most significant elephant translocations in conservation history".

It saw wildlife experts move elephants from a park in Malawi to help increase population in areas where they have been heavily poached.

Prince Harry has said helping move elephants to safer homes was an "amazing" experience.

The Sussexes are back in the spotlight after the revelation last week they were returning to the UK this month after enrolling their children to start at a British school in September.

No change is expected to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.

Their pending return to the UK has raised questions on their security arrangements.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.

It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.

The couple's plans while they are in the UK are also unclear.

The BBC learned the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, which would be her first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

In early 2020, the Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties before settling in California in March that year.

News.title: Snooker champion Graeme Dott guilty of child sex abuse
News.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of child sexual abuse.

The 49-year-old denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010.

During a trial, the High Court in Glasgow heard that Dott had exposed himself and inappropriately touched a primary school girl in the 1990s and attacked a young boy between 2006 and 2010.

Lord Harrower told Dott, who won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, he would be sentenced at a separate hearing in Edinburgh on 29 September.

Dott, from Glasgow, covered his face with his hands and shook his head while the verdict was delivered by jurors following a five-day trial.

He previously called the allegations made against him "disgusting".

News.title: Drugs dug up at Creamfields site ahead of festival
News.content:
Huge stashes of illegal drugs have been found buried underground at a festival site days before the event was due to begin.

More than 80,000 music fans will head to Creamfields Festival in Daresbury, Cheshire, from Thursday.

About 204 canisters of nitrous oxide - known as laughing gas - and large bags containing ecstasy, MDMA and ketamine tablets were dug up by police during a pre-event search of the grounds, Cheshire Police said.

Supt Andy Blizard said: "Every year, we counter a number of brazen individuals who think they can outsmart us by concealing drugs from view or burying them at the site months in advance."

"There is a zero-tolerance policy regarding drugs," he said.

News.title: Man charged with manslaughter in burglary case
News.content:
A man has been charged with manslaughter after a 75-year-old woman died following a suspected burglary in north London.

Police were called to Tollington Park in Finsbury Park on the night of 11 August after reports of a burglary.

Rose Smith was taken to hospital, where she died the following day. An 81-year-old man was also taken to hospital and was discharged the next day.

Jeffrey Dean Rose, 46, of Apsley Close, North Harrow, has been charged with manslaughter and aggravated burglary. He is due to appear at Barkingside Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

He was arrested on Friday, 21 August.

In a statement released earlier on Monday, Smith's family described her as an "outgoing woman" who loved "bingo, going to cafÃ©s with her friends and, above all, spending time with her family".

They described their loss as devastating, adding: "She was the life and soul of every party. She had a wonderful personality, a big heart and a way of bringing laughter and happiness wherever she went.

"We want people to remember Rose for the person she truly was - loving, fun, kind, sociable and full of life."

News.title: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
News.content:
The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.

Jobs website Adzuna said it had just 8,383 graduate vacancies listed in July, down from 15,397 at the same point last year.

Adzuna also found competition among job seekers across all levels is rising, with an average of 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July, up from 1.93 a year earlier.

However, some have said the data might not be reflective of the whole graduate job market and may instead suggest a shift in the way the roles are advertised.

Businesses have said employer national insurance and minimum wage hikes have made hiring more expensive, particularly for junior staff.

The number of graduate vacancies listed hit its lowest level since Adzuna started recording such data in 2016. The firm pointed to a peak for graduate roles in 2017, when it had more than 55,800 listed on its website. That is more than six times the number of roles listed on the site in July.

Andrew Hunter, the co-founder of Adzuna, said the figures show "employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring" for recent graduates.

But graduate jobs expert Charlie Ball said the numbers might not be as bad for graduates as they first appear.

He said they could instead suggest that firms are advertising fewer roles specifically for graduates, even if the roles themselves still exist and end up being filled by graduates.

From his experience in the sector, Ball said the graduate market has "not collapsed" but added: "We know the graduate jobs market is weak. We know it's not in great shape."

Official figures show the UK's youth unemployment rate - which covers 16-to-24-year-olds - was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026. The number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is now over one million.

Young people have told BBC News previously they have applied for hundreds of jobs before even receiving a response.

They also expressed frustration at the growing number of employers using AI to screen applications.

Former government minister Alan Milburn is leading a major review of the youth unemployment crisis. He has previously said the number of entry-level jobs is shrinking, as is the number of part-time jobs traditionally filled by teenagers and students.

The Adzuna data also showed vacancies for jobs in travel, teaching and construction rose in recent weeks.

But sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently changed the rules for public contracts so that companies bidding for them have to show how they will create jobs and training opportunities.

A government spokesperson said on Monday: "The latest figures show there are 253,000 more people in work than this time last year with unemployment continuing to fall.

"We are determined to go further to restore opportunity for young people through our Â£2.5bn youth employment package which will deliver almost one million opportunities to earn or learn."

News.title: Race Across the World star dies year after son
News.content:
A former Race Across the World contestant has died, a year after her son and co-star's death in a car crash.

Jo Gardiner, 61, died "following a long and courageous battle with cancer", her family said.

Gardiner, a physiotherapist from Manchester, travelled across South America with her son Sam in the second series of the BBC show, which aired in 2020.

Her family said she was "one of a kind" who "lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves".

News.title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez reveals she paid nearly $10,000 to freeze her eggs as she criticises US healthcare system
News.content:
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has shared more about the financial realities of egg freezing, saying she paid roughly $9,000–$10,000 for the process, including clinic fees and prescription medications.

The US congresswoman pointed to France, where "egg freezing is free for women between 29 and 37”.

In a video released on Monday (24 August), she said: "It is criminal how horrifically our healthcare system treats women."

AOC first revealed in a previous video that she decided to freeze her eggs at 36, saying it helped her "feel more in control of my life."

News.title: Man charged with murder and eight attempted murders after London house fire
News.content:

A man has been charged with murder after a house fire in west London which left a woman dead and hospitalised eight others.

Pawel Kulpa, 34, has been charged with one count of murder, eight counts of attempted murder and one count of arson with intent to endanger life.

Officers were called to reports of a fire at a property on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow, at about 1.14am on August 19.

The London Fire Brigade and London Ambulance Service were also in attendance.

Nine people were taken to hospital as a result of their injuries.

A 50-year-old woman who died in hospital has been named by the Metropolitan Police as Anna Kowalska, and the force said her next-of-kin has been informed, and are being supported by specially trained officers.

Another woman, 40, remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition.

The remaining seven people – six men and one woman – have since been discharged after receiving treatment for minor injuries, the Met said.

Officers were called to reports of a fire at a property on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow, at about 1.14am on August 19 ( PA )

A murder investigation was launched soon afterwards and the Crown Prosecution Service said on Monday that Kulpa had been charged.

He will appear at Willesden Magistrates’ Court on August 25.

Images from the scene show a light-coloured terraced house that has been blackened on the outside, with the window panes peeling.

Lisa Ramsarran, chief crown prosecutor in London North said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute Pawel Kulpa for murder, attempted murder and arson following a fatal fire in Hounslow, west London which resulted in the murder of a 48-year-old woman and the injury of eight others at approximately 1am on Wednesday 19 August.

“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to pursue criminal proceedings.

“We have worked closely with the Metropolitan Police to bring this case to court, and we will continue working with them as their investigation progresses.

“Mr Kulpa will appear at Willesden Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday 25 August.

“We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial.

“It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in any way prejudice these proceedings.”

News.title: Supreme Court rules Trump’s mail-in voting restrictions can stay, for now, before fast-approaching midterms
News.content:

The Supreme Court will let Donald Trump implement a sweeping executive order for new mail-in voting rules that could significantly restrict voters’ access to ballots in high-stakes midterm elections this fall.

Federal courts have repeatedly blocked the U.S. Postal Service from further implementing Trump’s executive order that sought to create a national voter registration list that would be used to decide who is eligible to cast a ballot.

On August 21, the U.S. Postal Service published its new certification requirements, changes that could not go into effect until federal courts lifted an injunction against them.

Monday’s 6-3 decision — with the court’s liberal justices dissenting — appears to leave room for legal challenges to continue, which could further slow or block Trump’s order altogether with critical registration and ballot deadlines fast approaching before Election Day. The issue could end up right back at the Supreme Court for oral arguments this year or in 2027.

But dozens of election officials and voting rights groups have warned that Trump’s order would cause chaos before midterms without enough time to ensure eligible voters aren’t wrongly removed from voter rolls — errors that could disenfranchise millions of Americans.

open image in gallery The Supreme Court will allow the Trump administration to implement sweeping changes to mail-in voting rules before midterm elections while legal challenges play out again what state officials and voting rights groups fear will chaos ‘chaos’ before high-stakes elections ( Getty )

“The consequences of allowing such transformative changes to take effect so close to this fall’s elections would be extreme,” nearly two dozen state attorneys general wrote to the court earlier this month.

“Because of the high risk of errors and the limited window for correcting mistakes, many of the millions of voters who rely on mail voting — especially voters with disabilities and those in rural areas — would likely be denied mail ballots and, as a result, disenfranchised,” they added.

A bipartisan coalition of 118 current and former election officials tasked with running the nation’s elections said the results will be “chaos.” And a group of 53 judges — most of whom were appointed by Republicans — called Trump’s order “a recipe for confusion among voters” that will “strain” election officials.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani previously rejected the government’s argument that courts cannot rule on the legality of the new Postal Service process before it’s finalized, stating that it would be “prudent” to step in now with “millions of citizens who rely on mail voting” needing “clarity as to how or whether they will vote in November,” she wrote earlier this month.

Trump’s executive order, even if it hasn’t been implemented, “is thus causing irreparable harm” to states and voting rights groups “through the confusion it has engendered as to how they may vote in the fast-approaching midterm elections,” Talwani wrote.

The Supreme Court’s conservative majority appeared to disagree, saying that Trump’s executive order itself is not causing any harm to the states that sued to stop it, and any further injunction will “irreparably harm the government if it remains in place while the appellate process runs its course.”

But Monday’s decision does not mean that the Trump’s implementation of the order will “necessarily be lawful,” the court’s majority wrote.

“On that score, time will tell,” the ruling states.

The decision merely postpones a decision on whether Trump’s attempts to “interfere” with elections are lawful, liberal Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan noted in their dissent. But a “common sense” reading of Trump’s executive order “makes clear” that it will cause irreparable harm to the states.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was more to the point. Monday’s decision “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections,” she wrote.

Jackson accused the court’s conservative majority of creating a “Kafkaeqsue nightmare” for election lawsuits.

“Today’s revelation is that such claims can also come too early — never mind that an election is looming and related harms are presently occurring,” she wrote. “States administering elections and the voting public that relies on them to do so deserve clarity, not caginess or confusion.”

open image in gallery Trump’s executive order would require states to compile lists of eligible voters based on information from his own administration but could disenfranchise millions of eligible voters if they information is not correct, election administrators have warned ( Getty )

Trump — who has spent years baselessly insisting that voting by mail is ripe for fraud, and that manipulated ballots were “rigged” against him in elections he lost — is simultaneously demanding the Senate pass his SAVE America Act, which would also restrict mail-in voting and require ID to vote, among other changes.

Voting rights groups fear the president’s efforts to centralize control over election administration, which is left to the states under the Constitution, is an attempt to boost Republican candidates and suppress Democratic turnout.

In March, Trump issued an executive order that would require states to compile lists of eligible voters based on information from his own administration. The Postal Service would then be blocked from mailing ballots to anyone who did not appear on those lists, and election officials could remove eligible voters from state voter rolls without first getting a chance to see whether they made a mistake,.

“The cheating on mail-in voting is legendary,” Trump said during a signing ceremony at the White House earlier this year. “I think this will help a lot with elections.”

Democratic officials in 23 states and Washington, D.C. sued to block the order, fearing the administration would needlessly upend election administration and chill participation with its baseless threats to prosecute election officials for doing their jobs.

Keely Hodgkinson has withdrawn from this week's Diamond League event in Zurich where she had been set to feature in a blockbuster 800 metres showdown.

The 24-year-old was due to race against Audrey Werro, who narrowly beat her to European gold earlier this month, as well as in-form fellow Briton Georgia Hunter Bell, who recently took the 1500m title in Birmingham.

But Hodgkinson said in a short statement: “Unfortunately the body isn’t quite ready to race again after the European Championships. We’ve made the decision to skip this race and get ready for the next one, sad to miss it, hopefully see you next year!”

Werro beat Hodgkinson by two tenths of a second in the European final in Birmingham – snapping a championship record that had stood since 1982 in the process – as she crossed the line in one minute 54.81 seconds.

But despite the defeat, Hodgkinson had relished the chance to take on the world’s best again in Zurich.

As well as Werro, who has gone unbeaten throughout the outdoor season, and Hunter Bell, the field also originally included European bronze medallist Femke Broeders-Bol and world champion Lilian Odira.

The latter also pulled out of the event on Monday, citing medical advice in her statement on Instagram.

Hailing the dawning of a generational women’s 800 metres cohort, Hodgkinson said earlier this month: “I hope everyone enjoys watching the level of athletes that we have because that’s difficult to come across in generations.”

She added: “I signed myself up for Zurich because I knew everyone was in it but me.

“I want to be in with the best and I think that’s going to bring out the best in me.

“There’s no point in me going to a race and time-trailling at the front. The more fun is when you’ve got everyone together, everyone’s going at it and you don’t know which way it’s going to go.”

Hodgkinson has battled numerous injuries over the last two years.

She struggled with a hamstring issue throughout 2025 and also suffered a setback when she sustained a knee injury in a freak accident in June.

The Trump administration is reportedly planning to rescind up to 200,000 business and tourism visas, the Associated Press reports.

The alleged plan could amount to the largest mass cancelation of visas in U.S. history.

“We are coordinating with [the Department of Homeland Security] to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott told The Independent in a statement. “These types of visas are issued with the clear understanding that they are for those who intend to return home. Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud — which is grounds for visa revocation.”

The mass cancelation would apply to individuals who were issued B1 and B2 visas between 2016 and 2026 then sought asylum, according to the AP.

The visas, respectively, cover business trips and voyages for other common reasons such as tourism, family visits and medical care.

open image in gallery The Trump administration reportedly plans to cancel as many as 200,000 business and tourism visas held by asylum seekers ( Getty )

“It’s shocking from an historical perspective,” Yael Schacher, director for the Americas and Europe at the humanitarian group Refugees International, wrote on Bluesky, arguing the “crazy” policy was part of the “delegalization of people who applied and were given permission to enter” the country.

The visa plan would likely face strong challenges in court, as have many of the Trump administration’s immigration efforts.

Last week, a federal judge struck down a Trump administration policy that suspended visa processing for nationals from 75 countries whose citizens were deemed likely to need public assistance upon coming to the U.S.

open image in gallery The president and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have moved to aggressively limit immigration to the U.S. while revoking the status of thousands of people already in the country ( AFP/Getty )

The Trump administration has moved aggressively to tighten immigration requirements, halt refugee resettlement and cancel scores of existing visas.

Since Trump took office, his administration has revoked more than 175,000 visas from foreign nationals, according to the State Department.

That’s quadruple the pace of the final year of the Biden administration, an analysis by The Guardian found.

The president has also sought to revoke the legal status of hundreds of thousands of people who came into the U.S. legally under a Biden-era immigration parole program.

The White House is pushing to permanently impose a $100,000 fee on businesses seeking H-1B visas for high-skill workers, despite a federal judge previously striking down a similar plan.

The areas in line for a multi-billion pound boost in housing funding have been revealed as the government promises the “biggest council housebuilding revival in decades”.

Around £10bn has been pledged to deliver 70,000 homes across England, the Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) has announced.

This will spread between 33 ‘strategic partners’, including councils, housing associations and other providers. Six local mayors outside of London will receive around £2.5bn.

The funding is being delivered as part of the government’s £39 Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP). The ten-year sum was first agreed by Sir Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves in 2025, alongside housing secretary Angela Rayner during her first term in the role.

Ms Rayner said: “Families can’t be left raising children without a place to call home, and none of us should spend years waiting for somewhere safe and affordable to live.

“That’s why the Prime Minister and I are doing everything we can to get councils building once again – it’s fundamental to turning the housing crisis around, helping families out of temporary accommodation and into a secure home.”

Around 134,000 households housing over 176,130 children are currently living in temporary accommodation, as of the latest statistics.

At the same time, over 1.3 million households are on their local authority’s waiting list for social housing.

Through the SAHP, 60 per cent of homes built are expected to be for social rent. This is the most affordable form of rented housing, typically costing 50 to 60 per cent of local market rates for long-term tenancies.

Andy Burnham’s previous mayoralty, Greater Manchester, will receive the largest share of funding at £529m to support around 4,400 new homes.

The other mayoral authorities which have had funding announced through this first wave are West Midlands, North East, West Yorkshire, Liverpool, and South Yorkshire.

Announcing the pledge, the prime minister said: “No child should be raised in a hostel room and no family should wait ten years for a front door of their own. I have said from my first day in this job that everything starts with a good home.

“Councils built this country out of a housing crisis once before. Backed properly, and trusted to get on with it, they will do it again.”

Mr Burnham said: “Councils built this country out of a housing crisis once before. Backed properly, and trusted to get on with it, they will do it again.” ( PA )

Council housebuilding across the UK has faltered in recent years, with just 2,000 completions annually in the five years leading up to 2025.

This compares to a postwar peak of an average 103,000 homes every year in the late 1970s.

Earlier this month, local leaders and house builders told The Independent that increased costs in the sector and a lack of support from central government was stifling ambitions to build more council homes.

Today’s announcement comes after Mr Burnham pledged in June – shortly before becoming prime minister – to oversee the “biggest council housebuilding drive since the postwar period”.

However, experts have said that reaching levels seen in the 60s and 70s is almost impossible under current conditions.

Through the SAHP, the government intends to deliver 300,000 homes for mixed affordable rent by 2036.

It would require an £8bn funding boost to make all of these social rent homes, research from the Resolution Foundation has found, which would still only be delivered at a rate of 30,000 a year – far below the postwar peak.

A final funding settlement for London has not been announced by MHCLG. However, the Greater London Authority is expected to offer at least £6bn through the programme, with councils expected to deliver half the homes built.

Responding to the latest funding announcement, mayor of London, Sadiq Khan said: “Thousands of Londoners will benefit from this new wave of new social and affordable homes, which will help people out of temporary accommodation and provide good, affordable homes to live in for the long-term, as we build a fairer, better London for everyone.”
