The bill removes the five functions added to the institution's mandate by the 2012 reform — among them promoting employment and economic development with social equity — and replaces them with a single objective. It also prohibits the purchase of national, provincial or municipal government bonds on the primary market, the mechanism through which the central bank has historically financed the Treasury.

Central bank governor Santiago Bausili and deputy governor Vladimir Werning defended the initiative before the budget and finance committees. They argued the purpose is to shield the institution from the political pressures of successive administrations and to consolidate a structure aimed at preventing a return to high inflation.

The same session will take up the bill known as Fiscal Innocence II, which expands a simplified scheme designed to bring undeclared assets into the formal system, estimated by the government at some 170 billion dollars. It removes the annual income and asset ceilings that limited access to the scheme and cuts by 25% the penalties for individuals and small and medium-sized companies that sign up. Opposition lawmaker Victoria Tolosa Paz, of Unión por la Patria, has called for an article barring officials of all three branches of the state from accessing those benefits.

The special session was called for midday by La Libertad Avanza bloc leader Gabriel Bornoroni, with backing from nine parliamentary groups including PRO, the Unión Cívica Radical and blocs answering to provincial governors. The governing coalition believes it has the votes to secure approval in the lower house.

The debate comes against a backdrop of deteriorating financial indicators. In August the country risk premium passed 470 basis points and sovereign bonds gave up much of their first-half performance, in a move not mirrored in other emerging markets. Arrears on credit to individuals reached 17.5% of total lending in June, according to a study by Universidad Austral and the consultancy Eco Go. A recent survey puts the share of Argentines identifying as opponents of the government at 52%.

Milei will chair a cabinet meeting on Monday, the first since July 9, and will receive deputies and senators on Tuesday ahead of the vote.

World.title: The Mercosur-Singapore trade agreement reaches Argentina's Congress
World.content:
The Mercosur-Singapore trade agreement reaches Argentina's Congress

23rd Sunday, August 2026 - 22:32 UTC Full article

The request carried signatures from nine groups, among them PRO, the Unión Cívica Radical, Provincias Unidas, Innovación Federal, Por Santa Cruz, La Neuquinidad and Adelante Buenos Aires

Argentina's Chamber of Deputies will on Wednesday take up ratification of the free trade agreement between Mercosur and Singapore, signed in December 2023 and still awaiting parliamentary approval. It is the first trade treaty the bloc has concluded with a Southeast Asian country.

The text appears on the agenda of a special session called for midday by La Libertad Avanza bloc leader Gabriel Bornoroni, alongside a reform of the central bank's charter and an expansion of the scheme for regularising undeclared assets. The request carried signatures from nine parliamentary groups, among them PRO, the Unión Cívica Radical, Provincias Unidas, Innovación Federal, Por Santa Cruz, La Neuquinidad and Adelante Buenos Aires, suggesting sufficient backing to secure approval in the lower house.

The Singapore agreement was negotiated over several years and signed under Brazil's pro tempore presidency of Mercosur. It requires ratification by the parliaments of all four member states — Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay — to enter into force.

The same agenda includes Argentina's accession to the Patent Cooperation Treaty, an instrument administered by the World Intellectual Property Organization that allows protection for an invention to be sought simultaneously in multiple jurisdictions through a single filing. Argentina is one of the few countries in the region not yet part of the system.

The session also covers a series of domestic measures: a reduction in the value added tax rate on cassava starch, promoted by lawmakers from Misiones province; the creation of additional chambers in the federal appeals courts of Tucumán and Mar del Plata; and a dozen bills designating various towns as national capitals of different productive and cultural sectors.

Consideration of the Singapore agreement comes at a moment of tension within the bloc. Brazil on August 4 downgraded its diplomatic relations with Argentina to chargé d'affaires level, after President Javier Milei took part in a campaign event for Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro at which he referred to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in terms Brasília considered offensive. Paraguayan President Santiago Peña said on August 14 that the differences between the two leaders had not affected how Mercosur functions.

The bloc, made up of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, also has Bolivia's full accession process under way. Brazil's presidential elections on October 4 are the next political milestone bearing on the regional agenda.

World.title: Colombia's earthquake toll rises to 329 dead and more than 300,000 affected
World.content:
Colombia's earthquake toll rises to 329 dead and more than 300,000 affected

22nd Saturday, August 2026 - 08:47 UTC Full article

Records of material damage have also risen substantially: 171,273 homes damaged, 31,183 destroyed and 553 buildings collapsed, mainly in Cali and Pereira, the two worst-hit cities

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western and central Colombia on August 10 has left 329 dead, 4,600 injured and 247 missing, according to the National Disaster Risk Management Unit's assessment as of Friday. The number of people affected stands at 314,751, from 154,014 families, across 481 municipalities in 16 of the country's 32 departments.

Records of material damage have also risen substantially: 171,273 homes damaged, 31,183 destroyed and 553 buildings collapsed, mainly in Cali and Pereira, the two worst-hit cities. Damage has also been recorded at 367 health centres, 3,710 schools, 5,584 community centres and 427 roads. The number of people rescued alive remains at 364.

The figures have varied considerably between the agency's successive reports. On August 12 the toll stood at 239 dead and 49,214 people affected; on August 16, at 289 and 185,016; on Friday, at 329 and 314,751. The number of missing has fluctuated between 143 and 379 depending on the day, and collapsed buildings rose from 66 in the August 14 assessment to 553 on Friday.

The agency has attributed these variations to three factors. The first is the cross-checking of initial reports, mostly verbal, against official records held by the attorney general's office and the forensic service, in order to remove duplicates. The second is the progressive incorporation of surveys compiled by municipal governments: the jump recorded on August 16 was largely due to the integration of data from Pereira. The third is the on-site assessment of each building by engineering teams, which corrects the count of homes and structures in both directions.

The epicentre was located in San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, one of those with the highest poverty rates in the country. The worst-affected departments are Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Caldas and Quindío. The Colombian Geological Service described it as the strongest seismic event recorded in Colombia this century and had counted 325 aftershocks one week after the quake.

Search operations gave way last weekend to body recovery and debris clearance, after several days without anyone being pulled out alive. President Abelardo de la Espriella declared an economic emergency on August 12, a constitutional mechanism subject to Constitutional Court review that empowers the executive to issue decrees with the force of law, and announced the creation of a fund to channel reconstruction resources.

World.title: Another major bust nets weapons, drugs and 20 CJNG-related arrests
World.content:
Federal authorities dismantled a major criminal cell over the weekend, arresting 20 people and seizing weapons and exotic animals.

The joint operation targeted a network allegedly linked to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) and featured simultaneous raids on 36 properties in the states of Hidalgo, Jalisco and Michoacán.

In an official statement, the Security Ministry said the Aug. 21-23 operation was the result of intelligence and investigative work by the Defense Ministry, the Navy, the Security Ministry, the Federal Attorney General’s Office and the National Guard.

The statement said that the operation resulted “in the arrest of 20 individuals linked to the CJNG,” adding that “authorities seized 10 firearms (seven handguns and three rifles), drugs, 113 vehicles, tigers, panthers, as well as other animals and birds kept in inadequate conditions.”

Officials also confiscated cash and jewelry, communications equipment, a drone and a drone jammer, while specifying that in addition to the firearms seized, agents gathered up magazines and cartridges of various calibers. The drugs confiscated were said to be unspecified doses of fentanyl and methamphetamine, as well as marijuana.

The Defense Ministry said the 20 detainees were transferred in a Mexican Navy aircraft and placed at the disposal of the Attorney General’s Office (FGR) in Mexico City “to continue with the corresponding investigations and expert analyses to determine their legal status.”

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said the goal of these operations is not only “to stop those who generate violence, but to steadily weaken the operational, logistical and financial capabilities of criminal organizations.”

García Harfuch said the authorities will “continue with coordinated intelligence, investigation and territorial presence efforts” to protect and defend the public interest.

The outcome of this latest tactical operation brings to 32 the total number of alleged CJNG members apprehended by security forces in less than a week.

On Aug. 19, the Army led a major security operation in Michoacán targeting CJNG leader Heraclio Guerrero Martínez, alias “El Tío Lako.” The 15-hour raid resulted in nine to 12 arrests — including the target’s partner and daughter.

With reports from Excelsior, Milenio and Aristegui Noticias

World.title: Why Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya returned to office for only 48 hours
World.content:
Rubén Rocha Moya, the Sinaloa governor who is accused of drug trafficking by U.S. prosecutors, returned to office on Friday — only to ask to go on leave again the very next day.

The 77-year-old governor’s submission of a request to take indefinite leave came after representatives of his own party — Morena — rejected his decision to return to the governorship of Sinaloa almost four months after he first left office. The Sinaloa Congress approved his leave request on Sunday.

In a social media post on Saturday, President Claudia Sheinbaum also indicated that she didn’t agree with Rocha’s decision to return to office. The president — the leader of the “fourth transformation” (4T) movement with which Rocha is also affiliated — explicitly expressed that position on Monday.

Rocha, who became governor of Sinaloa in late 2021, first decided to take leave in early May shortly after the unsealing of a U.S. indictment accusing him and nine other current and former Sinaloa-based officials of drug trafficking in league with the Sinaloa Cartel.

The U.S. Justice Department said on April 29 that the governor allegedly attended meetings with “the Chapitos” — sons of convicted drug trafficker Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán — and allowed the Sinaloa Cartel faction they lead to “operate with impunity in Sinaloa.”

Rocha, who is also accused of weapons offenses, promptly rejected the accusations against him. To date, he has avoided extradition to the United States as — according to the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) in Mexico — U.S. authorities have not presented sufficient evidence against him. Sheinbaum has endorsed the FGR’s view and stressed that Mexican legal processes and sovereignty must be respected. However, now, more than ever, she is seeking to distance herself and her government from Rocha, whose indictment has raised serious and broader questions about alleged corruption and alleged collusion between Morena and organized crime.

The governor’s decision to return to office on Friday surprised — and in some cases outraged — millions of Mexicans, including members of the federal government. His brief return to office restored his constitutional immunity from prosecution, according to experts, but he presumably lost that immunity (called fuero in Mexico) by going on leave once again.

Here is a timeline of relevant events between Friday. Aug. 21 and Monday, Aug. 24.

Friday morning: Rocha announces his return to office

In a social media post shortly before 10 a.m. on Friday, Rocha announced that he had resumed his position as governor of Sinaloa.

“It is my duty to fulfill the mandate of the people of Sinaloa, who elected me as head of the executive branch to govern until October 31, 2027,” he wrote.

“During the period of my temporary leave from office, which I requested from the State Congress on May 1 of this year, I placed myself at the disposal of our country’s justice system in order to be investigated regarding the false accusations … that a U.S. government office leveled against me without any evidence, seeking to undermine our national sovereignty through its statements and slander,” Rocha wrote.

The governor wrote that he had personally appeared before the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) during his leave of absence. That institute, he said, determined that there was no evidence against him.

“In other words, I haven’t committed any crime,” Rocha wrote.

“… Today I return to fulfilling my duties as Governor of Sinaloa with a clear conscience, with my head held high, and with the power of the truth on our side.”

Early Friday afternoon: SEGOB says that Rocha’s decision to return to office was a ‘personal’ one

In a statement issued early Friday afternoon, the federal Interior Ministry (SEGOB) sought to distance the federal government from Rocha’s decision to return to office.

“The Interior Ministry reports that the decision of Dr. Rubén Rocha Moya to resume his duties as governor of the state of Sinaloa is exclusively a determination of a personal nature,” SEGOB said.

The ministry noted that the FGR opened investigations into the 10 people accused of drug trafficking and weapons offenses by U.S. prosecutors, among whom is Rocha, a Morena senator and the mayor of Culiacán.

SEGOB highlighted that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has asked the U.S. Department of Justice on repeated occasions to “provide the evidence that supports the accusations.”

“In that sense, it is up to the Federal Attorney General’s Office, within the domain of its powers and in accordance with the advance of the investigations, to provide additional information it considers pertinent,” the Interior Ministry said.

Late Friday afternoon: Morena lawmakers speak out

Later on Friday afternoon, Morena deputies expressed their opposition to Rocha’s decision to return to office.

In a statement, Morena deputies called on the governor to “reconsider his decision” so that the FGR and “other authorities” can continue and conclude their investigations “with full autonomy.”

Comunicado del Grupo Parlamentario de Morena pic.twitter.com/5S3wYRYkB7 — Arturo Ávila. (@arturoavila_mx) August 22, 2026

Morena senators echoed SEGOB’s sentiment, saying in a statement that Rocha’s decision to return to office was a “personal and individual action.”

Friday evening: Morena governors weigh in

The Morena governors of 22 states as well as Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada and the Green Party governor of San Luis Potosí released a statement on Friday evening expressing their opposition to Rocha’s return to office in Sinaloa.

“In the fourth transformation, individual decisions will never be above the collective project or the citizens’ mandate,” said the 4T political leaders.

“… No authority is empowered to act at the margin of the law or to take unilateral decisions that threaten constitutional order or republican dialogue,” they said.

“Personal or group political projects have no place when they counteract the well-being of the nation. We call on Dr. Rubén Rocha Moya to act with maturity and responsibility,” said the 23 governors and Brugada.

“Politics is an exercise of congruence. Excess and factional decisions go against principles of honesty and loyalty that we swore to uphold.”

Saturday morning: Sheinbaum enters the fray

In a social media post on Friday morning, Sheinbaum announced that she was sick with the flu and therefore didn’t perform any public duties that day, and didn’t comment on Rocha’s return to office.

The president returned to social media on Saturday morning to publish a message that was clearly aimed at Rocha, although she didn’t mention the governor by name.

“No personal interest can ever be above the interests of the people and the nation,” she wrote.

“And certainly not when what is being placed above Mexico is not the well-being of its people, but the naked ambition of power for power’s sake,” Sheinbaum said.

“… Power without principles becomes arrogance; power without limits becomes abuse; and power that forgets the people ultimately finds itself at odds with history,” she wrote.

Ningún interés personal puede estar jamás por encima de los intereses del pueblo y de la Nación. Y mucho menos cuando aquello que se pretende colocar por encima de México no es el bienestar de su gente, sino la ambición desnuda del poder por el poder.

Porque el poder sin… — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) August 22, 2026

“Mexico deserves public servants who understand that positions are temporary, but the responsibility to the nation is eternal. The people are not here to feed personal ambitions: they are here to demand that their dignity, their future, and their hope be defended. Above any name, any group, and any personal interest stand the people and the nation.”

In a separate social media post on Saturday morning, the director of the Sinaloa-based Noroeste newspaper, Adrían López Ortiz, wrote:

“I see many outsiders saying that Sinaloenses are speaking out against Rocha. I’ll give you a fact. Yesterday, @noroestemx tried to ask people in the center of Culiacán what they thought about his return [but] they were scared to respond on camera.”

Sinaloa is a violence-plagued state where the Los Chapitos and Los Mayos factions of the Sinaloa Cartel are engaged in a long-running and extremely bloody civil war. Cartel violence has ravaged the Sinaloa economy and led many residents to take extra safety precautions, such as limiting their movements at night.

Saturday evening: Rocha heeds Sheinbaum’s words

In a social media post on Saturday evening, Rocha published a letter addressed to the president of the Sinaloa Congress in which he requested “temporary leave” of an “indefinite nature” from his job as governor.

Above the letter, he wrote: “Sinaloa, the nation and the transformation movement are above everything.”

Sunday morning: Sinaloa Congress approves Rocha’s leave request

In an extraordinary session on Sunday morning, Sinaloa state lawmakers unanimously approved Rocha’s request to go on indefinite leave.

Monday morning: Sheinbaum says Rocha’s decision to return to office was ‘imprudent’

At her Monday morning press conference, Sheinbaum said that she found out about Rocha’s decision to return to the governorship of Sinaloa via his social media post on Friday.

“I didn’t have any prior knowledge that he wanted to return to his duties in the state of Sinaloa,” she said.

“The truth is that I didn’t think it was appropriate, to say the least,” Sheinbaum said.

Later in the press conference, the president explicitly said she didn’t agree with Rocha’s decision to return to the governorship of Sinaloa.

“At the very least, I thought it was imprudent,” Sheinbaum said.

“… Nothing personal can be above the interests of the people of Sinaloa and the people of Mexico,” she said.

Sheinbaum said on Sunday that Rocha’s decision to once again leave the governorship was “the best thing for Sinaloa.”

On Monday, she noted that the Sinaloa Congress has to appoint an interim governor until a new governor takes office in late 2027 following the Sinaloa gubernatorial election in June of next year. She said that the interim governor should be a person who is honest, professional and dedicated to “the people of Sinaloa.”

Sheinbaum subsequently described claims that former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador told Rocha to return to the governorship of Sinaloa as “political fiction.”

World.title: MND Local: Flight cuts and water relief in Guadalajara, and Jalisco’s tequila economy
World.content:
This week brings another round of international flight schedule changes at Guadalajara International Airport. Also in this week’s update, the government clarifies who is eligible for 80% discounts from SIAPA due to poor-quality tap water, plus an update on Jalisco’s tequila economy.

Aeroméxico suspends flights from Guadalajara to Northern California, Chicago

Last week, Aeroméxico suspended several important routes between Guadalajara and the U.S., including nonstop flights to San Francisco, Sacramento, Fresno and Chicago, according to schedule filings tracked by AeroRoutes.

The route suspensions are in effect from now until mid-December, with no clarity on whether they might resume after that.

Aeroméxico’s suspended routes and dates in effect

Route Dates of suspension Guadalajara to Chicago (ORD) Aug. 17, 2026 – Dec. 16, 2026 Guadalajara to San Francisco (SFO) Aug. 17, 2026 – Dec. 16, 2026 Guadalajara to Fresno (FAT) Aug. 17, 2026 – Dec. 16, 2026 Guadalajara to Sacramento (SMF) Aug. 17, 2026 – Dec. 16, 2026

Under Aeroméxico’s disruption rules, ticketed customers on canceled routes are entitled to a route and schedule change or a refund. Before calling the airline to request rebooking, it is a good idea to confirm that your itinerary is no longer available on its website.

It is also wise to keep any receipts for hotels, ground transport and nonrefundable side bookings tied to your original Aeroméxico itinerary. Those costs can influence whether the airline grants a reissue, refund or full cancellation of the original ticket.

Competing carriers such as United Airlines and the ultra-low-cost carriers Volaris and Viva Aerobus still service these cities to and from Guadalajara, so travelers have a few alternatives left that eliminate the need to connect in Mexico City.

Who is eligible for 80% discounts from SIAPA due to poor water quality?

A hot topic in Guadalajara lately has been the question of who is — and is not — eligible for a discount on their water bill from SIAPA (the Intermunicipal Water and Sewerage Services System in Jalisco) stemming from chronic water quality issues in the Guadalajara metropolitan area.

After weeks of speculation, we finally have some answers.

As of Aug. 17, an 80% discount will be applied to water bills in 203 neighborhoods in Guadalajara, Zapopan, Tlaquepaque and Tonalá affected by serious water quality problems. The initiative aims to compensate users who have reported various problems with water coming from their taps, including foul-smelling, dirty or discolored water.

The Jalisco Congress formalized the benefit, and the SIAPA Governing Board approved the first list of beneficiary neighborhoods, with details published on Aug. 14 in the Official Gazette of Jalisco.

Popular expatriate neighborhoods such as Ladrón de Guevara, Santa Teresita and Providencia in Guadalajara, as well as Chapalita and Seattle in Zapopan, are all eligible for the discount. To see the full list of neighborhoods, check Annex A of this document.

How to claim the SIAPA discount

Economic relief is aimed at residential users and small businesses in the designated neighborhoods who consume up to 25 cubic meters of water per month. Those who consume more than this amount are ineligible.

To qualify, households and businesses must also demonstrate that they are up to date on all of their payments to SIAPA to receive the discount. In other words, those who stopped paying for contaminated water out of frustration and are still in arrears cannot obtain a discount.

There are also 32 neighborhoods still under review for eligibility, so if your neighborhood is not on the current list, it may still be added later as SIAPA makes adjustments.

Residents can access the discount until Dec. 15, 2026.

Tequila exports showed signs of recovery in the first half of 2026

Despite the trade uncertainty surrounding negotiations of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), the tequila business appears to be resurgent in 2026, following sluggish results in 2025.

According to figures from the Tequila Regulatory Council (CRT), total tequila exports during the first half of this year reached 215 million liters, up 3.4% from the 208 million liters exported abroad in the same period of 2025. The U.S. remains the largest export market for Mexican tequila by far (taking roughly 81% of the total).

Following a period of explosive growth in demand from 2020 to 2024 where growth averaged 8.5% per year, demand for Jalisco’s most famous beverage has leveled off. The slowdown stems mainly from reduced demand for super-premium tequila in the U.S., as consumers traded down or explored sobriety following the coronavirus pandemic’s well-documented drinking binge.

In response, Jalisco’s producers have been working to correct an agave oversupply problem (too many fields were planted during boom times) and develop new business in Europe, Latin America and Asia to reduce their dependence on the U.S. consumer.

Based on the trend year to date, the Tequila Regulatory Council is cautiously optimistic for better times ahead for the state’s 229 authorized producers and more than 3,400 registered brands.

MND Writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Profepa clears 6 dolphins for relocation from shuttered Cancún dolphinarium
World.content:
Six of the nine dolphins living at the now-shuttered Dolphin Discovery installations, located within the former Ventura Park in Cancún, Quintana Roo, are considered candidates to begin a preparation process for a possible relocation, according to a report by the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Profepa).

The move comes amid concerns about the health and safety of the animals, which remain under the care of Mexico’s environmental authority following the closure of the dolphinarium in October last year after videos surfaced of the dolphins displaying extreme distress.

Profepa stated that the nine dolphins – two females and seven males – are in delicate clinical condition, meaning their transfer cannot be immediate and each animal will require an individual protocol.

Since May, Profepa has been working to medically stabilize the dolphins through veterinary checkups, laboratory tests and monitoring of their behavior, feeding and response to treatment, the agency told Mongabay.

However, activist groups in defense of animal rights, including Veeleaf and Tide Breakers, have shared images and videos criticizing the care of the nine dolphins that remain in captivity. Reportedly, the dolphins are in small pools where they can barely move, are fed smaller portions of food than required and spend all their time in the sun, with no shade.

The future of these dolphins is tied to a reform that sought to transform the operations of dolphinariums in Mexico.

In July 2025, the Mexican Senate unanimously approved a nationwide ban on dolphin and other marine mammal shows, as well as the breeding of marine mammals in captivity except for conservation purposes.

The new regulations mandate the transfer of cetaceans to marine pens, or fenced-off ocean enclosures that slowly reintroduce the dolphins to their natural habitat, and limit interactions with those already under human care, prohibiting practices that could compromise their well-being.

However, the regulations needed to establish the application criteria have not been published yet; hence, the nine dolphins remain in the same pools where they have spent a good part of their lives.

The organization Empty the Tanks is demanding that the dolphins be temporarily transferred to existing marine pools at the Dolphin Discovery facilities in Isla Mujeres and Chankanaab, Cozumel. “We are not asking that they be released into the ocean. We are asking for a responsible, feasible measure backed by scientific evidence: that they be allowed to live in a much more natural environment while receiving the care they need,” the organization said in a statement.

According to a statement by Profepa, “All the decisions that have been made aim to ensure the best possible well-being of the dolphins, to help them survive in the best way possible and to alleviate their suffering.”

“We know that moving them to a semi-open enclosure at sea would be an improvement, but first we must guarantee that this move does not cost them their lives,” the statement continues.

With reports from Infobae, Por Esto! and Reportur

World.title: Aura farming battles make their debut in Mexico
World.content:
With a nod to the “You got served” hip-hop dance battle craze of two decades ago, kids and young adults in Mexico have begun to stage “aura farming” battles in public squares across the country.

What the heck is aura farming, you ask? Fair question …

Aura farming is a viral internet slang trend that describes doing intentional, effortless things to look confident or charismatic. Gen Alpha and Gen Z use the term to describe doing something to improve your “vibe,” your style or your perceived social status, without seeming like you’re trying too hard.

It even warrants a definition in Merriam-Webster: “the act of doing something to look cool, impressive, stylish, etc., especially — and importantly — without trying too hard.”

The concept grew on TikTok and Instagram, combining the video game concept of “farming” (carrying out repetitive actions for points), before dancing was attached to it, eventually evolving into physical “aura battles” in parks and streets across Latin America.

In Mexico City, three notorious aura farming battles took place last week: on Friday at the esplanade of the Palace of Fine Arts in Mexico City; on Saturday at the Monument to the Revolution; and on Sunday in the Condesa neighborhood (where there was even a prize of 3,000 pesos, or US $177).

The craze has reached beyond the capital, too.

Aura battles have recently been staged in Juárez Park in Xalapa, the capital of Veracruz, and children as young as six years old participated in a competition in Torreón, Coahuila.

Compiten en Concurso para "Farmear Aura" en Veracruz

Watch this video on YouTube

The “battles” attract massive crowds who watch participants compete symbolically with poses, dances, gestures and meme references to demonstrate who has more “aura.”

A winner is determined by crowd reaction (the volume of cheers, applause, laughter) and by the general impact made during the face-off. Essentially, the social presence displayed is “scored” like an imaginary video game.

Unfortunately, the events also have their detractors. The municipal council of Ignacio de la Llave, Veracruz, officially prohibited aura battles in public parks, arguing that it was not due to the theme or content of the competition, but rather “a strict matter of administrative procedures and regulations for public spaces.”

CNN traces the origin of aura farming to 2024 and said it gained international attention last year through viral videos of 11-year-old Indonesian Rayyan Arkan Dikha dancing at the front of a boat in a traditional rowing competition. Social media users commented on the high levels of “aura” the boy possessed and it took off from there.

The trend has become particularly popular in Latin America: A “championship” was staged at the University of Costa Rica in San Juan on Aug. 18 and several tournaments were organized in São Paulo, Brazil, this summer.

With reports from CNN, LatinUS, Infobae and Telediario

World.title: Several storm systems, including a potential hurricane, are dumping rain across much of Mexico
World.content:
Mexico’s National Meteorological Service (SMN) is monitoring three simultaneously occurring and potentially cyclonic tropical storms that are expected to continue to bring rain to much of the country, along with lightning, hail and strong winds.

One of the storms is Tropical Storm Iselle, safely offshore but expected to reach Category 1 hurricane force as it moves further out into the Pacific.

The atmospheric instability over northwestern Mexico will lead to continued showers and heavy rain. As a result, heavy rainfall of between 50 and 75 mm is expected on Monday in the western states of Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima and Michoacán, along with strong waves in Baja California Sur.

At the same time, low-pressure troughs will interact with a cyclonic circulation at middle and upper levels of the atmosphere to bring rain to many areas of Mexico.

Further south, winds of between 50 and 70 km/h are expected in Campeche and Oaxaca, with waves of between 2 and 3 meters (6 to 10 feet) in the Gulf of Tehuantepec.

The SMN warns that strong wind gusts in any of the affected areas, north or south, could knock down trees and billboards, while heavy rainfall could cause flooding and fog banks could reduce visibility on highways and in urban areas.

All the rain is not expected to alleviate the ongoing heat wave in the border states. Highs of 45°C (113°F) or higher are predicted for Baja California on Monday, with maximum temperatures of between 40 and 45°C expected in Sonora, Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas, as well as in Sinaloa.

As for Iselle, the SMN reported that the tropical storm was located approximately 920 km southwest of Cabo San Lázaro, Baja California Sur, at 6 a.m. on Monday. Though it is expected to intensify into a Category 1 hurricane by Monday evening, the SMN has emphasized that the projected distance and trajectory of Iselle do not pose a direct risk to Mexico.

With reports from UNOTV, Proceso and N+

World.title: Cattle trade with US reopens as Sheinbaum weighs in on Rocha’s status in Sinaloa: Monday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🐄 Sonora-Arizona border reopens to cattle trade: Sonora Governor Alfonso Durazo joined the mañanera via video link from Agua Prieta, where the Douglas, Arizona, port of entry reopened to Mexican cattle on Monday, more than a year after the U.S. closed its border over New World screwworm concerns. Sheinbaum said the ban had shifted more Mexican beef to the domestic market but still hurt cattle sectors nationwide.

Sonora Governor Alfonso Durazo joined the mañanera via video link from Agua Prieta, where the Douglas, Arizona, port of entry reopened to Mexican cattle on Monday, more than a year after the U.S. closed its border over New World screwworm concerns. Sheinbaum said the ban had shifted more Mexican beef to the domestic market but still hurt cattle sectors nationwide. 🏛️ Sheinbaum calls Rocha’s return “imprudent”: The president said she learned of Rubén Rocha Moya’s decision to return to the Sinaloa governorship via social media and didn’t think it was appropriate. She said his decision to leave again a day later was “the best thing for Sinaloa.” Rocha is accused of drug trafficking by U.S. prosecutors.

The president said she learned of Rubén Rocha Moya’s decision to return to the Sinaloa governorship via social media and didn’t think it was appropriate. She said his decision to leave again a day later was “the best thing for Sinaloa.” Rocha is accused of drug trafficking by U.S. prosecutors. ⚖️ Interim governor still to be named: Sheinbaum said the Sinaloa Congress must appoint an interim governor to serve until a new governor takes office in late 2027, following June’s gubernatorial election. She said the pick should be honest, professional and dedicated to Sinaloa’s people.

Sheinbaum said the Sinaloa Congress must appoint an interim governor to serve until a new governor takes office in late 2027, following June’s gubernatorial election. She said the pick should be honest, professional and dedicated to Sinaloa’s people. 🗣️ Sheinbaum dismisses AMLO rumor: Asked if she’d discussed Rocha’s situation with former president López Obrador, Sheinbaum said she had not and called claims that he told Rocha to return to office “political fiction.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

Last Friday, Rubén Rocha Moya announced he had returned to his position as governor of Sinaloa more than three months after he went on leave following the unsealing of a U.S. indictment accusing him and nine other current and former Sinaloa-based officials of drug trafficking in league with the Sinaloa Cartel.

Rocha’s decision to return to the governorship of the northern state was described as “personal” by the federal Interior Ministry and opposed by lawmakers and state governors affiliated with the ruling Morena party, which Rocha also represents.

His return to the governorship didn’t last. On Saturday, Rocha asked to go on leave once again and that request was approved by the Sinaloa Congress on Sunday. His decision to leave the governorship — for a second time — came after President Claudia Sheinbaum wrote on social media that “no personal interest can ever be above the interests of the people and the nation.” She didn’t mention Rocha by name, but her message was clearly aimed at him.

The most significant aspect of today’s mañanera was that the president spoke in more detail about Rocha’s decision to return to the governorship of Sinaloa. Sheinbaum has endorsed the view of the Federal Attorney General’s Office that U.S. authorities have not provided evidence that warrants the extradition of the governor to face drug trafficking charges. While she has defended Rocha’s right to the presumption of innocence, she evidently doesn’t believe he should be at the helm of the Sinaloa government and thus serve as the foremost representative in that state of the “fourth transformation” (4T) political movement she leads.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was a live cross to Sonora, where Mexican cattle exports to the United States are resuming more than a year after the U.S. closed its border to Mexican livestock due to concerns over the spread of the New World screwworm in Mexico.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture announced the Aug. 24 reopening of the Douglas, Arizona, port of entry to cattle trade last month.

Sonora-Arizona border reopens to cattle trade

Sonora Governor Alfonso Durazo joined the mañanera via video link from the northern border city of Agua Prieta, where the Douglas port of entry into Arizona reopened to Mexican cattle on Monday.

“We’re here at the quarantine station in Agua Prieta with the extraordinary news of the reopening of cattle exports to the United States,” Durazo said.

“We thank you and your team, president, … for all the steps you have taken to achieve this goal,” he said.

“We recognize and appreciate your commitment to agriculture in Sonora and those who make their living from it,” Durazo said.

The governor said that the cattle trade across the border between Agua Prieta and Douglas is resuming with an “enhanced health-screening capacity.”

Sheinbaum noted that the U.S. closed its border to Mexican livestock for an extended period due to screwworm concerns.

“There was an economic impact, although, believe it or not, meat production in Mexico increased,” she said.

“While [Mexican beef] wasn’t sold in the United States, it was sold in the domestic market. But the [ban on exports] obviously affected different cattle sectors across the whole country,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum: Rocha’s decision to return to the governorship of Sinaloa was ‘imprudent’

Sheinbaum told reporters that she found out about Rocha’s decision to return to the governorship of Sinaloa via his social media post on Friday.

“I didn’t have any prior knowledge that he wanted to return to his duties in the state of Sinaloa,” she said.

“The truth is that I didn’t think it was appropriate, to say the least,” Sheinbaum said.

The president said on Sunday that Rocha’s decision to once again leave the governorship was “the best thing for Sinaloa.”

On Monday morning, Sheinbaum noted that the Sinaloa Congress has to appoint an interim governor until a new governor takes office in late 2027 following the Sinaloa gubernatorial election in June of next year. Yeraldine Bonilla Valverde served as interim governor until Rocha’s surprise return last Friday.

Sheinbaum said that the interim governor should be a person who is honest, professional and dedicated to “the people of Sinaloa.”

Later in the press conference, she said that she didn’t agree with Rocha’s decision to return to the governorship of Sinaloa.

“At the very least, I thought it was imprudent,” Sheinbaum said.

“… Nothing personal can be above the interests of the people of Sinaloa and the people of Mexico,” she said.

“So I thought his decision was imprudent,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum rejects claims that AMLO told Rocha to resume his governorship

A reporter asked the president whether she had discussed Rocha’s situation with former president Andrés Manuel López Obrador (AMLO), the founder of Morena and the 4T political movement.

“No, no, no, no, no,” Sheinbaum responded.

She went on to describe claims that AMLO told Rocha to return to the governorship of Sinaloa as “political fiction.”

“… Political fiction is the order of the day,” Sheinbaum said.

World.title: When frequent family visits start to look like US residency: A legal primer
World.content:
For millions of Mexican families, a trip to the United States is not tourism in the ordinary sense. It may mean spending time with children in Texas, helping a daughter after a baby is born in California, attending a graduation in Arizona or staying with a son recovering from surgery in Chicago.

Those ties are unusually deep. Roughly 40 million people of Mexican origin now live in the United States, and U.S. immigration law expressly allows B-2 visitors to travel to see family and friends.

The shifting landscape of B-visas

One of the most difficult questions in visitor-visa law is also one of the most human: When does a family visit stop looking temporary and begin to look like residence?

That question is becoming more important for Mexican travelers. The State Department’s adjusted B-visa refusal rate for Mexican nationals rose to 21.36% in fiscal year 2025, up from 13.87% the previous year.

Since October 2025, the State Department has also generally required applicants under 14 and over 79 to appear for an in-person nonimmigrant-visa interview, subject to limited exceptions.

That latter change matters especially to families. A Mexican grandmother hoping to spend time with grandchildren in Houston may now face more scrutiny before the trip even begins.

There is no rule stating that someone admitted to the U.S. for six months has been invited to live in the country for six months every year. Nor does leaving for several weeks automatically reset the clock.

What constitutes a temporary visit?

A B-2 visa is for a temporary visit. Each admission is considered separately, and the fact that U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) allowed a lengthy stay once does not promise the same result the next time.

Imagine a retired mother from Guadalajara who spends four months in Dallas after her daughter gives birth. She returns to Mexico for six weeks and then flies back for another four months because her daughter still needs help.

Her explanation may be entirely genuine. She may own her home in Guadalajara, receive her pension there and have no intention of immigrating. But the CBP officer sees another fact: For much of the year, she has spent more time in the United States than in Mexico.

The officer may reasonably ask where she actually lives.

Why legitimate travel may not always look legitimate

That does not make long visits unlawful. A parent caring for a seriously ill child may have a perfectly legitimate reason to stay for months. There is also no rule requiring visitors to spend twice as much time in Mexico as in the U.S.

What matters is the larger pattern: how frequently the person travels, how long the stays last, whether a genuine home and life remain in Mexico, and whether each trip is actually temporary.

This is where immigration law can collide with completely ordinary Mexican family life.

There is nothing suspicious about a grandmother cooking meals, helping after a new baby arrives or spending time with grandchildren. Ordinary family assistance does not automatically turn a visitor into an unauthorized worker.

But if someone spends month after month in the U.S., returns briefly to Mexico and then comes back to resume the same arrangement, the larger issue may become whether the U.S. has effectively become a second residence.

Words can matter as well. A retired parent may casually say, “I live with my daughter in Houston half the year.” To the family, that may simply describe retirement. To an immigration officer, the words “I live in Houston” can raise the precise issue a visitor visa is designed to avoid.

Owning property in the U.S. is not automatically prohibited. Neither is having American children, grandchildren or bank accounts. But when those circumstances are combined with repeated lengthy stays, immigration officers may look more closely at where the traveler’s real life is based.

Visiting the US while obtaining a green card

Families sometimes make the opposite mistake when an immigrant petition has been filed. They assume that once a U.S. citizen child or spouse begins the green-card process, the Mexican beneficiary can no longer visit at all.

That is not automatically true.

The State Department’s own Foreign Affairs Manual recognizes that visitor visas may be issued even when an immigrant petition or immigrant-visa application is pending, provided the person can establish that the immediate trip is temporary.

Wanting to immigrate legally in the future does not necessarily mean someone intends to remain unlawfully today.

A Mexican mother waiting for an immigrant visa may still want to attend a granddaughter’s birthday in Chicago. A spouse waiting for consular processing may have a legitimate reason to temporarily visit a husband or wife. But the pending immigration case gives the government an obvious reason to examine whether this particular trip will really end with a return to Mexico.

Telling the truth about your travel history

The traveler should also assume that the government can see a history of prior entries and departures. Foreign visitors can themselves retrieve recent arrival and departure information through CBP’s I-94 system, so repeated lengthy stays are hardly invisible.

In appropriate circumstances, CBP can also search phones and other electronic devices during a border inspection. Most travelers will never experience such a search, but a phone or social media account describing a “move to Texas” can create obvious problems if the person tells an officer the trip is nothing more than a short family visit.

The answer is not to erase a phone or invent a better story. It is to tell the truth and make sure the truth supports temporary travel.

Most Mexican visitors who receive additional questioning are ultimately admitted. But when CBP concludes that someone is using a visitor visa to live in the U.S., the consequences can extend far beyond a missed vacation.

Depending on the facts, a visa may be canceled, a traveler may be allowed to withdraw the application for admission and return to Mexico, or a more serious immigration action may follow.

That is why someone who has already been warned about lengthy stays, refused admission or had a visa canceled should not simply try another airport or land crossing hoping for a different answer. The next inspection does not necessarily begin with a clean slate.

When family life collides with immigration policies

None of this means Mexican parents and grandparents should become afraid to visit their families.

Family visits are a legitimate use of a B-2 visa. The difficulty is that behavior that feels completely natural within a family can gradually collide with an immigration category built around temporary presence.

A daughter has a baby. A son becomes ill. Parents retire. Grandchildren grow up. The natural instinct is to spend more time together, particularly when Mexico and the U.S. are separated by little more than a flight or a drive.

But a visitor visa is not a residence permit, nor is it a substitute for the family-based immigration process.

With Mexico’s visitor-visa refusal rate rising and older applicants generally facing in-person interviews again, families should think about that distinction before an immigration officer asks them to explain it.

There is no magic number of days that guarantees a traveler will have no problem. The better question is much simpler: Is this genuinely a visit, and does the traveler still have a real life to return to in Mexico?

A tourist visa can connect Mexican families across the border for many years. Understanding where a visit ends and residence begins is one of the best ways to protect it.

Richard T. Herman is an award-winning U.S. immigration attorney and founder of Herman Legal Group. He has practiced immigration law for more than 30 years and is the co-author of “Immigrant, Inc.: Why Immigrant Entrepreneurs Are Driving the New Economy.” He writes about various immigration law topics, including tourist visas, student visas, work visas and immigration enforcement.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Mangroves Face Growing Threats From Pollution and Development
World.content:
Costa Rica’s mangrove forests protect coastal towns, support fishing communities and provide breeding grounds for marine life. Researchers warn that pollution, construction and changes to rivers are slowly weakening these important coastal ecosystems. Mangroves are forests that grow where rivers meet the sea. Their tangled roots create sheltered areas where young fish, crabs, shrimp and other marine animals can grow before moving into open water.

Those roots also hold soil in place and absorb some of the force from waves, flooding and storms. Without mangroves, coastal areas can become more vulnerable to erosion and rising water. Costa Rica’s 2021 mangrove ecosystem map estimated that Costa Rica has approximately 52,802 hectares, or 130,477 acres, of mangrove environments. Most are found along the Pacific coast, including the Gulf of Nicoya, the Térraba-Sierpe wetlands and the Osa Peninsula.

Despite legal protections, many of these forests remain under pressure. The main threats include garbage and polluted water flowing down rivers, construction near the coast, agricultural runoff, sediment buildup and the clearing or filling of wetland areas. Some of the waste begins far from the coast. Plastic, sewage, chemicals and other pollutants from communities in the Greater Metropolitan Area can travel through rivers before reaching mangroves and the ocean.

Research from the University of Costa Rica has found pesticides, detergents and pharmaceutical substances in mangrove environments. These pollutants can damage water quality and affect the animals living among the roots. Changes to rivers create another problem. When a river is straightened, diverted or surrounded by farms and construction, the natural movement of water and sediment can change. Too much sediment may bury mangrove roots or block the normal exchange between fresh water and seawater.

Researchers have raised concerns about the Aranjuez River in Puntarenas, where changes to the river and years of sediment buildup have affected the nearby mangrove. Environmental specialists warn that further deterioration could leave parts of Puntarenas more exposed to coastal erosion and flooding.

The effects are already visible in some locations. Monitoring around Punta Flor on Isla Chira has found fewer crabs and other small marine animals in degraded sections of the mangrove than in healthier areas. A 2025 study of the Morales mangrove in Puntarenas found that the forest lost approximately 24 hectares, or 59 acres, between 1944 and 2020. Researchers linked much of that decline to changes in how surrounding land was used.

The loss of mangroves can also hurt the local economy. Fish, shrimp, crabs and shellfish depend on these forests during part of their life cycle. When mangrove habitats decline, fishing communities may eventually find fewer animals available to catch and sell. This is especially important around the Gulf of Nicoya, where families have long depended on small-scale fishing and the collection of shellfish. Damage to the mangroves can therefore affect jobs, household income and local food supplies.

Mangroves also store large amounts of carbon in their soil and roots. When the forest is destroyed or the soil is disturbed, part of that carbon can be released into the atmosphere, adding to the problem of climate change. Costa Rica has promised to protect and restore thousands of hectares of coastal wetlands as part of its international climate commitments. Scientists say restoration can help, but preventing pollution and further damage is usually easier and less expensive than trying to rebuild a mangrove after it has collapsed.

The warning is not that every mangrove in Costa Rica is disappearing at the same rate. Conditions vary considerably from one location to another. The larger concern is that damage has continued for decades while many coastal communities depend on these forests for protection and income.

World.title: Fewer Humpback Whale Sightings Reported in Costa Rica’s Golfo Dulce
World.content:
Tour guides in Costa Rica’s Golfo Dulce say humpback whales have been more difficult to find this season, raising questions about whether warmer ocean water is changing their normal movements. Guides have said August usually brings regular whale sightings inside the gulf but this year, however, this year they have experienced days when dozens of tour boats searched the area but very few whales were seen.

On one recent morning, guides said that only one of approximately 30 to 40 boats reported seeing a whale. The observations do not prove that Costa Rica has fewer humpback whales this year but there has been no official population count showing a decline. The whales may simply be spending more time outside Golfo Dulce or moving between different parts of the southern Pacific coast.

Still, guides with years of experience say the change has been noticeable. Captains and guides, who has worked in the area for more than 12 years, said the whales previously remained inside the gulf for longer periods. This season, they appear to leave the protected waters more frequently and stay outside for longer.

The guides believe warmer ocean water could be influencing that behavior. They say they have personally noticed higher water temperatures while swimming and snorkeling. Some have also reported seeing coral with signs of partial or complete bleaching, which can occur when the ocean becomes unusually warm.

Golfo Dulce is one of Costa Rica’s most important whale-watching destinations and humpback whales from the Southern Hemisphere travel thousands of kilometers from waters near Antarctica to Costa Rica’s warm Pacific coast. The whales come north to mate, give birth and care for their calves before beginning the long journey back toward their feeding grounds. The southern whale season normally runs from July through October, with sightings often reaching their highest point during September.

Conditions inside Golfo Dulce are usually well suited for mothers and young calves. It’s warm, relatively calm water gives the animals a protected place during the first weeks of a calf’s life. Scientists have found evidence that water temperature and food availability can affect when humpback whales begin migrating.

A study published in 2025 followed 42 humpback whales traveling from breeding areas in Costa Rica, Panama and Ecuador toward feeding grounds near Antarctica. The researchers found that the whales used information from their surroundings, including water temperature and the amount of marine life in the water, to help decide when to leave.

Warmer water and El Niño conditions were connected with changes in the timing of their southward migration. The research suggests that humpbacks can adjust their movements when ocean conditions change. However, that study used tracking information collected between 2009 and 2016. It does not establish that warmer water is responsible for the sightings reported by Golfo Dulce guides in 2026.

Confirming such a connection would require current water-temperature measurements, whale counts and comparisons with previous seasons. For local tourism businesses, fewer sightings can create a difficult situation. Whale watching supports boat operators, guides, hotels, restaurants and other businesses across the Osa Peninsula and southern Puntarenas.

Guides sometimes remain at sea longer than usual while searching for whales because they know that visitors may have traveled a considerable distance for the experience. But sightings are never guaranteed, even during the busiest part of the season. Visitors can still encounter dolphins, sea turtles and other marine wildlife in Golfo Dulce. Tours in the area also commonly include snorkeling, mangrove visits and trips along the coast.

The guides’ reports offer an early warning worth examining, rather than proof of a permanent decline. Continued monitoring will be needed to determine whether this is an unusual season or part of a larger change in humpback whale migration.

World.title: Rincón de la Vieja Erupts Twice Ahead of Free National Parks Day
World.content:
The Rincón de la Vieja volcano erupted twice today and the Observatorio Vulcanológico y Sismológico de Costa Rica (Ovsicori-UNA) reported no ashfall and no lahars from either event. The larger of the two came at 7:38 a.m. and lasted under a minute. Ovsicori classified it as moderate. A smaller eruption had already occurred at 12:30 a.m.

Neither eruption was visible on the observatory’s webcams. Cloud cover sat over the summit all morning, so nobody got a look at the column. That happens often during the rainy season, and it is one reason the seismic and infrasound networks matter more than the cameras this time of year.

The volcano stays at caution, which is level 3 on Ovsicori’s four-step scale. Ovsicori moved it up from level 2 in early August after counting 48 eruptions in roughly a month, including 23 in a single week. Volcanologist Cyrill Müller said at the time that a volcano at level 3 can produce eruptions, lahars and ashfall — a plain description of the range, not a forecast that any of those will happen on a given day.

Several dozen phreatic eruptions have hit the mountain this year. Some of them sent primary and secondary lahars down the slopes in July and August. Phreatic is worth understanding, because it explains why this volcano behaves the way it does. Groundwater seeps down until it meets hot rock, flashes to steam, and blows out through the crater carrying mud, rock fragments and gas.

There is no fresh magma rising to the surface. That is why these eruptions are usually short, usually small, and almost never announced in advance — the trigger is water, and water moves fast.Lahars are the part that reaches beyond the crater. They are slurries of volcanic debris and water that run down river channels, and they are far more likely when heavy rain falls on loose material the volcano has already deposited. Ovsicori has repeatedly flagged the rainy season as the higher-risk window for exactly this reason.

That matters right now as the Instituto Meteorológico Nacional forecast gusts reaching 80 km/h (50 mph) in northern Guanacaste today, with afternoon downpours and thunderstorms across the region. Rivers draining the massif, including the Pénjamo and the Azul, have discolored after past eruptions as material washed downslope.

If you are near those drainages during heavy rain, move away from the channel and onto higher ground. Do not wait to see the water rise. Lahars travel faster than people expect and arrive without warning. The summit trail has been closed for years and remains closed, and SINAC will keep it shut until eruptive activity drops enough for access to be considered safe.

That route climbs about 8 kilometers (5 miles) one way with roughly 1,000 meters (3,300 feet) of gain, and it ends at the active crater — the single worst place to be standing when a phreatic eruption fires with no warning. The rest of the park operates on its own schedule.

Rincón de la Vieja National Park covers 14,300 hectares (35,300 acres) and splits into two visitor sectors, Las Pailas and Santa María. Las Pailas takes most of the traffic and centers on a 3-kilometer (1.9-mile) loop past mud pots, fumaroles and steam vents, well below the summit. Entry tickets must be booked through SINAC’s online reservation system before you arrive.

Tomorrow is National Parks Day, and entry to Costa Rica’s national parks is free. That comes from Decree 16847-MAG-MEP, signed in 1986, which waives admission for every visitor on 24 August regardless of nationality. SINAC has confirmed the waiver applies countrywide this year, with the national celebration centered in Puntarenas. Free does not mean the volcano rules change, and there are two things worth sorting out before you drive to Guanacaste.

The first is the calendar as Rincón de la Vieja normally closes on Mondays — the park runs Tuesday through Sunday, and the Monday shutdown exists so crews can maintain the Las Pailas trails. This year 24 August lands on a Monday. SINAC has not published whether it is waiving that closure for the free-entry day, so do not assume the gates open just because admission is waived. Call the Las Pailas sector or check sinac.go.cr before you commit to the drive from Liberia or the coast.

The second is the summit trail, and this one is not ambiguous. Free entry does not reopen it and that trail is closed on volcanic grounds and stays closed until Ovsicori’s activity level supports reopening it, which is a separate decision from anything to do with ticket prices. You still need a reservation even when the ticket costs nothing. Parks inside SINAC’s online system, and Rincón de la Vieja is one of them, release free tickets through the same platform and cap them the same way.

The cap is about how many people the trails can carry safely, not about revenue. Free days draw crowds, and slots go. Nothing Ovsicori reported today changes the park’s status on its own as the volcano sat at level 3 before those two eruptions and it sits at level 3 after them. What changes access is a closure decision, and those arrive on their own schedule — rain on a mountain that has been shedding loose material for two months is the likelier trigger.

Check the park’s status the day you go rather than the week before since sector and trail access shifts with volcanic activity and with weather, and a closure decided on Saturday will not appear in a tour operator’s brochure. The volcano rises to 1,916 meters (6,286 feet) roughly 25 kilometers (16 miles) northeast of Liberia. Ovsicori monitors it continuously through seismic, gas and deformation instruments, and publishes updates as events occur.

Costa Rica lives with six active volcanoes, and Rincón de la Vieja has been among the busiest of them for the better part of a decade. Level 3 is not an emergency but it is a standing instruction to pay attention to where you are and what the sky is doing.

World.title: Hattieville student reports losing $550 in Facebook marketplace phone deal
World.content:
Hattieville student reports losing $550 in Facebook marketplace phone deal

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old student from Hattieville has reported an alleged online scam after paying BZ$550 for an iPhone that he says was never delivered.

Police said Giovanni Ortiz reported that on August 4, he was browsing Facebook Marketplace when he saw a post from a person identified as Jared Franklin advertising a black iPhone. Ortiz said he agreed to purchase the phone for BZ$550.

According to the report, Ortiz initially deposited BZ$250 into an Atlantic Bank account in the name of Renan Blake.

The seller allegedly demanded the remaining BZ$300, claiming the phone would not be sent unless the full payment was made. Ortiz said he subsequently deposited the balance after receiving a photograph of what appeared to be a Caribbean Sprinters package receipt.

Ortiz later contacted Caribbean Sprinters Water Taxi to inquire about the shipment and was reportedly told that the receipt was an old document from 2023. Police said Ortiz had not received the phone at the time of his report and had been unable to contact Renan Blake despite several attempts.

World.title: Pregnant woman’s boyfriend choked her and applied pressure to her stomach
World.content:
Pregnant woman’s boyfriend choked her and applied pressure to her stomach

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 27-year-old pregnant woman in San Pedro has reported an alleged assault by her boyfriend, telling police that she was bitten, choked and had pressure applied to her stomach during an incident at her home.

Police said that the woman reported that on Friday, August 21, at approximately 10:30 p.m., she was in her room with her boyfriend when a message from another woman appeared on his cellphone.

The man then attempted to take the phone back after she refused to hand it over, and he allegedly became aggressive.

According to the report, the pregnant woman said that her boyfriend bit the left side of her back and placed both hands around her neck, choking her while she shouted for help.

She also reported that he placed both hands on her stomach and applied pressure, causing her pain.

The woman told police she was 27 weeks pregnant and became fearful for her life. Police observed bite marks and a bruise and issued her a Medico-Legal Form.

The boyfriend was detained and later formally arrested and charged with Wounding.

World.title: Man charged after alleged attempt to snatch gold chain at Seine Bight Restaurant
World.content:
Man charged after alleged attempt to snatch gold chain at Seine Bight Restaurant

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 28-year-old Seine Bight man has been arrested and charged with attempt theft after a Canadian businessman reported that someone tried to take his gold chain at a restaurant.

Police said Bryan Newton, 46, a Canadian national and businessman from the Maya Beach area, reported that on Saturday, August 22, at approximately 8:30 p.m., he went to Me N U restaurant in Seine Bight Village to purchase food.

While waiting, Newton said he stepped outside to smoke and was approached by an unknown man who asked him for a cigarette.

Newton reported that after returning inside the restaurant, he noticed the same man standing close to him.

He alleged that the man suddenly grabbed his gold chain, which was worn around his neck. Newton said he grabbed the man’s wrist and managed to prevent the chain from being taken.

Police said surveillance footage from the restaurant was viewed and the suspect was identified as Akeem Joseph, 28, of Seine Bight Village.

Joseph was detained and formally arrested and charged with attempt theft.

World.title: Motorcyclist dies following crash on George Price Highway
World.content:
Motorcyclist dies following crash on George Price Highway

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 55-year-old motorcyclist died following a road traffic accident on the George Price Highway between miles 76 and 77 on Saturday evening.

Police reported that the accident occurred at approximately 7:15 p.m.

At the scene, police found a National Bus Company passenger bus parked on the right side of the highway facing Succotz Village, with damage to its front driver’s-side headlamp and bumper.

A black Meilum motorcycle was also found on the roadway with damage to its front portion and handle.

The motorcyclist, identified as Patrick Joseph Chun, 55, of Duck Run 1 Village, was found motionless in a ditch approximately nine feet from the motorcycle.

Police said the scene was secured and processed, while the bus driver, Marcos Santos, 57, of Benque Viejo Town, was escorted to the Benque Viejo Police Station pending investigation.

Police issued Santos a Notice of Intended Prosecution and requested a blood or urine sample which he provided.

World.title: Motorcyclist dies after crash between Duck Run 1 and Billy White, Cayo
World.content:
Motorcyclist dies after crash between Duck Run 1 and Billy White, Cayo

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 46-year-old man from San Marcos Village died following a motorcycle collision between Duck Run 1 and Billy White Village in the Cayo District early Saturday morning.

Police said the accident was reported shortly before midnight on Friday, August 21.

The deceased was identified as Jaime Haroldo Catalan, 46, who was found motionless in the middle of the road. His motorcycle was located nearby with damage to the front headlamp, front fork, handlebar and rear light.

Police investigations indicate that Catalan was travelling toward Billy White when another motorcyclist, identified as Javier Pinelo, 26, of Bullet Tree Village, allegedly overtook him.

Due to oncoming traffic, Pinelo swerved in front of Catalan, causing Catalan to collide with the rear of Pinelo’s motorcycle.

Catalan sustained head and bodily injuries and later succumbed to them.

Pinelo also sustained injuries and was taken to the San Ignacio Community Hospital.

Police subsequently obtained a blood specimen from Pinelo.

He was detained under police guard, issued a Notice of Intended Prosecution and remained at the hospital.

World.title: Boat recovered in San Pedro Lagoon, outboard engine missing
World.content:
Boat recovered in San Pedro Lagoon, outboard engine missing

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 25-foot fiberglass boat has been recovered from a lagoon in San Pedro after it was reported missing, but its owner was left without the vessel’s outboard engine.

The owner , Kimberly Carrillo, 32, reported that her white fiberglass skiff named “Boat Ride,” fitted with a dark-gray Yamaha E60 HMHDL two-stroke outboard engine was missing.

The boat is valued at approximately BZ$9,000.

According to Carrillo’s report, the boat had been parked on the lagoon side of Coral Brain Street in the San Thelmo area under the care of someone she knows.

However, her relative reportedly last saw the boat around midnight on Saturday, August 22.

On Sunday morning, Carrillo was informed that the Belize Coast Guard had recovered the boat floating in the lagoon at approximately 11:30 a.m.

However, the outboard engine was missing.

Carrillo subsequently contacted the Coast Guard and was advised to make a police report before the boat could be released to her.

World.title: Ex common-law husband punches Salvapan woman; took her documents
World.content:
Ex common-law husband punches Salvapan woman; took her documents

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 31-year-old woman from the Salvapan area of Belmopan has reported an alleged domestic dispute involving her former common-law partner, whom she accused of assaulting her and later taking a bag containing important personal documents from her home.

The woman told police that on Saturday, August 22, between 3:00 and 4:00 p.m., the man went to her home and became involved in an argument with her. She said she told him that he had already moved out and that she no longer wanted to continue their relationship. She alleged that the man then moved aggressively toward her son, prompting her to intervene.

According to her report, the man attempted to punch her in the face, but she raised her hands to block the blow, causing it to strike her left wrist. She further alleged that he kicked her on the left foot above the ankle before leaving the residence.

The woman reported that the man later returned and, after taking a shower, allegedly punched her in the face, striking her left ear and the center of her nose. She also told police that he later returned and took a black bag belonging to her containing important doc

World.title: BEL says if you can’t afford your bill this month, they can put you on a payment plan
World.content:
BEL says if you can’t afford your bill this month, they can put you on a payment plan

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) says customers who have been hit with unusually high electricity bills this month and simply cannot afford to pay them in full can contact the company to be placed on a payment plan.

That was among BEL’s responses on Monday as the utility and the Ministry of Public Utilities faced the media following days of widespread public outrage over the latest billing cycle, with Belizeans reporting increases of hundreds of dollars and, in some cases, bills that have doubled, tripled or even quadrupled.

The issue comes as Belizeans are already grappling with broader cost-of-living pressures, including high fuel prices and concerns over transportation costs. Last week, Prime Minister John Briceño acknowledged that he was concerned about the sharp increases, while local media documented widespread complaints from consumers.

During Monday’s press conference, BEL Executive Chairman Lynn Young was asked specifically what would happen to customers, including middle-income households, whose bills had jumped by $300 or $400 and who genuinely could not find the money to pay before the due date.

Young said BEL routinely makes payment arrangements with customers facing such circumstances.

“We do a lot of payment plans,” Young said, explaining that BEL can arrange for customers to pay an unusually high bill over several months.

Government officials, meanwhile, said Cabinet is discussing what additional relief may be possible, with Public Utilities Minister Michel Chebat acknowledging that the public is facing genuine difficulty paying electricity bills.

BEL, however, maintained that it has so far found no evidence of a systemic billing problem responsible for the widespread increases.

Instead, Young said the company believes the unusually hot weather has been the primary driver of higher consumption. He explained that air-conditioning units and refrigerators must work significantly harder to maintain the same temperature when outside temperatures rise, while pumps, computers, routers and other electrical equipment can also consume more energy in hotter conditions. BEL acknowledged that it has received a higher number of high-bill complaints than usual this year.

Young said his own electricity bill increased by about $500 and that, after reviewing it, he determined that increased consumption was responsible. BEL says it is investigating complaints individually and can install monitoring equipment at a customer’s home to determine where electricity is being consumed.

The company also acknowledged that the ongoing rollout of new electronic or “smart” meters has contributed to sharp increases in some individual cases.

According to Young, some old meters had previously been estimated because meter readers could not access them, while others may have been under-recording consumption. When those meters are replaced and BEL obtains an accurate final reading, customers can see what the company describes as a one-time “catch-up” in their bill.

BEL insists it has found no evidence that the smart meters themselves are systematically overcharging consumers. Young said the newer electronic meters are more accurate than older mechanical meters and acknowledged that aging mechanical meters could have been under-recording electricity use.

That explanation is likely to remain under scrutiny, particularly because BEL also revealed that old meters are generally not tested after being removed; instead, the final reading is recorded and the old meter is destroyed. BEL says every new meter is tested before installation and that it is open to independent testing or investigation of the new meters.

Importantly, the recently introduced Cost of Power Adjustment, or COPA, does not by itself explain the enormous increases being reported.

The PUC approved an additional 1.5 cents per kilowatt-hour for August. That translates to only $1.50 more for 100 kWh, $3 for 200 kWh and $4.50 for 300 kWh of consumption.

The PUC has also confirmed there was an earlier increase of approximately three cents per kilowatt-hour in December 2025, but the extraordinary increases being reported in the latest billing cycle have gone well beyond the impact of the new 1.5-cent COPA charge.

For consumers who remain convinced that something is wrong with their bill, the PUC says they must first make a formal complaint to BEL. If the matter is not resolved, customers can lodge a written complaint with the PUC and should provide their bills and supporting documentation so the regulator can conduct its own investigation.

World.title: ‘Long overdue’
World.content:
Minister of National Security and Deputy Prime Minister Dr Horace Chang and Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange are all smiles as they receive the keys to the third Government-run shelter for women facing domestic abuse. (Photo: JIS)

LOCAL gender advocates have welcomed news that work has been completed on a third shelter for victims of domestic abuse.

Minister with responsibility for gender affairs Olivia Grange made the announcement last Friday as she toured the facility at an undisclosed location.

“We made a commitment that we would establish three centres, safe spaces for women, and we have achieved that,” said Grange as she pointed out that prior to the Dr Andrew Holness-led Administration there were no State-run shelters for women wishing to leave violent relationships.

In the last few years the Government completed, and is operating, two shelters for women. Grange said the addition of the third shelter will enable the ministry to offer up to 70 safe spaces for women and their children.

Grange said the completion of this third shelter, which is scheduled to begin providing a safe space for women after September 1, enables the Government to provide much-needed services to vulnerable females across the entire island.

“The completion of this space advances the gender agenda, because what we have been able to do now is to provide the spaces across the island, and we are now better equipped that when we get the call we are able to activate the kind of network that is necessary to move [women in abusive situations] into safe spaces,” said Grange.

On Sunday, gender and development practitioner Judith Wedderburn told the Jamaica Observer that the new shelter was long overdue.

“It is certainly very welcome because, not only from my experience but from the reports of women who do suffer, they have been beaten by a male partner and have experienced gender-based violence.
