In 2025, the project was presented directly to Mirziyoyev and fast-tracked without a tender, while the environmental assessment had not yet been fully completed. A foundation-laying ceremony took place on the day of the visit. Although Agalarov is no longer related to the presidential family by marriage, he continues to enjoy high-level political support.

The complex is planned for a 577-hectare site on the shores of the Charvak Reservoir. In 2025, the project was presented directly to Mirziyoyev and fast-tracked without a tender, while the environmental assessment had not yet been fully completed. A foundation-laying ceremony took place on the day of the visit. Although Agalarov is no longer related to the presidential family by marriage, he continues to enjoy high-level political support. PASHA Holding projects: The holding company, which has been linked to the president’s daughters Leyla and Arzu Aliyeva, as well as to Mehriban Aliyeva’s father Arif Pashayev, is building a Ritz-Carlton-branded hotel and residential complex in Tashkent. The group includes private lenders Kapital Bank and PASHA Bank. Banks linked to the family control a significant share of Azerbaijan’s banking-sector assets — more than 40%, according to some estimates.

The group includes private lenders Kapital Bank and PASHA Bank. Banks linked to the family control a significant share of Azerbaijan’s banking-sector assets — more than 40%, according to some estimates. SOCAR: Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal.

At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal. Other projects: Other businesses entering the Uzbek market include the Matanat-A gypsum plant, Landau STEAM schools, the Sur gold and silver processing plant, Gold Fresh Fruits orchards, the Baku City residential complex and other projects. Some are being implemented as public-private partnerships.

Statements by the two presidents

President Ilham Aliyev said in a statement to the press that relations between the two countries were built “on a very solid foundation, both spiritually and materially”. He said the range of projects under discussion in energy, transport, investment, tourism, mining, automotive manufacturing, agriculture, processing and banking gave the cooperation an “unprecedented character”.

Aliyev said that on every visit he was struck by the rapid development of Tashkent and Uzbekistan as a whole. He said increasing bilateral trade to $1bn was “no longer a dream of the distant future, but a target that can be achieved within a few years”. He also highlighted Mirziyoyev’s particular role in attracting investment to Karabakh and invited him to make a state visit to Azerbaijan at a time convenient to him.

Shavkat Mirziyoyev described Aliyev’s visit as a “historic event”, saying the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship” was evidence of this and that the provisions on strategic partnership and alliance were being backed up by concrete action. In his remarks, he highlighted a threefold increase in bilateral trade over the past five years, the goal of raising it to $1bn, the joint development of the Middle Corridor, and the idea of creating a separate Azerbaijani-Uzbek corridor across the Caspian Sea with a single operator.

Mirziyoyev also said the two countries spoke “with one voice” on the international stage. He described Azerbaijan’s full participation in the consultative meetings of Central Asian heads of state as a historic step and praised Aliyev’s policy of restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity, as well as the meeting in Washington and the declaration signed there.

Hikmet Hajiyev, a representative of the Azerbaijani presidential administration, said before and during the visit that relations between the two countries had reached a new level: moving from strategic partnership to alliance and then to “eternal friendship”. He said this was the first such step in the history of Azerbaijani diplomacy. According to Hajiyev, the “eternal friendship” that had already existed de facto between the two peoples had now been formally enshrined at the political level as well.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, villages and cities empty out.” Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”

The traditional pro-European “Saturday march” in Tbilisi on August 22 was dedicated to Georgian citizens who have left the country in search of work and better opportunities.

Participants said the growing emigration is driven by the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which they say have pushed the country away from the European integration path enshrined in the Constitution.

Many blame the party’s founder and honorary chairman, oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, personally.

“Villages and cities are emptying out when the state serves Ivanishvili” — this was the central message of the march, reflected in the slogans and statements by speakers.

Organisers announced that throughout September, the traditional “Saturday marches” will be held in support of Georgian emigrants.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament: balance of power, tools of government and opposition’s dead end
World.content:
Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

The parliamentary election results in Armenia have confirmed the continuity of the country’s political system while exposing deep structural contradictions. Political competition has shifted decisively towards intense polarisation. The National Assembly risks turning into little more than a platform for mutual accusations resembling a television talk show, rather than the country’s highest legislative body.

Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan’s assessment

Continuity of the system, limits of influence and a fragmented opposition

“The new National Assembly has retained the key feature of its predecessor. The Constitution allows the ruling Civil Contract party to make almost any decision on its own, except on issues that require a constitutional majority. The two opposition factions — former president Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance and businessman Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia — have access to the media and the parliamentary platform, and can openly express their views and criticise the government. However, they have no real leverage over current policy.

The opposition forces have undergone a reshuffle. In the eighth National Assembly, Kocharyan’s faction held the largest number of seats. In the new parliament, however, it is the smaller of the two opposition factions. They are also unlikely to build a stable coalition or an “umbrella” structure. Because of their different origins and the lack of a practical basis for cooperation, even if they unite, they will not secure 50% of the seats needed to take the initiative. A long-term alliance is impossible. In 35 years of the Third Republic, the opposition has never managed to produce a successful example of unity. The minority is therefore left with little more than keeping the protest movement alive.”

Legitimacy, voters and the government’s narratives

“The ruling party has significant external legitimacy. This includes recognition of the election results by the US, EU, Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Russia’s refusal to withhold recognition from Nikol Pashinyan. The ruling force also relies on support from the bureaucracy. In fact, bureaucratic legitimacy has grown stronger. Civil servants clearly understand their ties to the political leadership and recognise the risks that a change of elites could bring.

At the same time, the government’s social legitimacy remains low. Kocharyan won 10% despite his high negative rating, while Karapetyan’s party, hastily assembled over six months with its leader under arrest, won a quarter of the vote despite high turnout. This is a serious signal of the level of public dissatisfaction.

Realising that its support will not grow, the government abandoned any real ideology. Political strategists pragmatically discarded the “high-minded Yerevan intelligentsia”, which would not have voted for the government anyway and would not have gone to the polls. Instead, they focused on their target audience: residents of small towns and villages with lower levels of education, young people and older generations.

To maintain control, the government uses several narratives:

“Peace versus war” — portraying opponents as the “party of war” and frightening voters with the prospect that an opposition victory would lead to a new war in September.

“Democrats versus oligarchs” — selectively labelling businesses. Wealthy entrepreneurs who support the government are simply called “businessmen”, while any affluent opponents are automatically branded “oligarchs”.

“Europe versus Russia” — systematically linking the entire opposition to Moscow. Karapetyan is portrayed this way because he came from Russia, Gagik Tsarukyan because of his ties to Belarus, and Kocharyan as Putin’s personal friend.

Accusing voters of supporting the opposition solely for money. This new level of polarisation has emerged in official statements by the authorities.”

The government’s geopolitical narrative and the opposition’s dead end

“The government’s anti-Russian discourse found fertile ground. These sentiments had been developing for years, and the events of 2020 and 2023 — the war in Karabakh, followed by the exodus of the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh — only strengthened them.

At the same time, people across the post-Soviet space have traditionally associated the word “European” with quality and development: European healthcare, European education, European cars and so on. The government has effectively exploited this perception. Direct public support for Pashinyan from senior US officials, up to and including the US president, also played an important role.

The opposition has found itself in a strategic dead end. It cannot openly say “we are pro-Russian” or “we are not pro-Russian”. Unable to reject the geopolitical trend that enjoys broad public support, opposition parties have had to adapt and repeat that they are “also in favour of cooperation with Europe, but for a more carefully calibrated policy”.

Personal attacks instead of alternative programmes

“Instead of substantive work, the opposition is sliding into negative rhetoric and personal attacks: who is corrupt, who got their wife a job, who owns which flat and who once “didn’t even have a washing machine”. Armenian society knows perfectly well how the bureaucratic hierarchy works, so such “exposés” do not work. All these scandals only play into the government’s hands, allowing it to say: “Look who we have to work with in parliament.”

A constructive alternative would be to develop concrete programmes in different areas — healthcare, pensions, the economy, the army and so on. Even if the ruling majority rejects, say, 15 such professional programmes in a row, a systematic effort to offer solutions will eventually resonate with society. For now, trolling has replaced politics.”

Real state priorities: security, energy and meritocracy

“While parliament is busy trolling, the country’s key problems remain unresolved. One of them is security.

It is wrong to call the situation with Azerbaijan peace. You can see what real peace looks like on the border with Georgia, for example: people can cross freely using an ID card, while there are no transport corridors, European observers, military guards or concrete walls, even though 30% of the border remains undelimited. With Baku, however, there is only a state of “no war”. That is far from peace. At the same time, Azerbaijan is rapidly expanding its military capabilities in every sphere, including its air force.

Armenia needs to make foreign policy decisions and find ways to overcome the energy crisis.

Relations with all four neighbours — Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Iran — are in crisis. Meanwhile, the Armenian-American TRIPP “Trump Route” project — a transit route through Armenia — remains little more than a political narrative. At the same time, launching new facilities, such as an AI data centre in Hrazdan, could create an acute electricity shortage that talk of American small modular nuclear reactors alone cannot solve.

In the Armenian city of Hrazdan, Firebird AI’s artificial intelligence factory has begun operations. The facility is the largest AI data centre in the region. The first phase of the project, worth more than $500 million, uses advanced NVIDIA accelerators and server equipment from leading global manufacturers. Some experts believe the factory’s launch could put additional pressure on the country’s energy system. (firebird.ai)

The state needs a competent administration to overcome these challenges.

The country needs to embrace meritocracy, appointing people based on competence rather than loyalty.

Finally, the country’s leadership needs to reconsider its attitude towards citizens.

Nikol Pashinyan is the prime minister of all Armenians, not just the voters of Civil Contract. The claim that people could only have voted against the government in exchange for money is false and toxic. The government now faces a vast array of real problems. Its first task is to recognise the scale of those challenges and start addressing them.

Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

World.title: Anea the raccoon’s favourite activity at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

Raccoons love water. You can often see them swimming, wetting their fur or carefully washing their paws. Anea, a resident of Tbilisi Zoo, is no exception.

On hot days, Anea particularly enjoys dipping her paws in water and having a cool shower. So her keepers set up an improvised shower in her enclosure, which, as you can see in the video below, delighted her.

There is a metal container in her enclosure for drinking water, but who says she cannot take a bath in it too? Despite its small size, Anea fits perfectly inside, happily splashes around in the water and uses it to escape the summer heat. After noticing the raccoon’s love of bathing, her keepers have already ordered a bigger “bath”.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status.



The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo.



We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Opinion: ‘Moscow’s main fear is that Armenia will choose European Union’
World.content:
Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

In recent days, Russia‘s demand for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) or choose the European Union has increasingly been seen as a threat. Experts from the “Armenian Council” think tank made the assessment in an article.

Russia has long demanded such a referendum, including at the highest level. But there are now threats to initiate proceedings concerning Armenia’s membership of the EAEU. Decisions within the bloc require consensus, and Yerevan has the right to veto them.

“Russia’s main phobia is that the situation will deteriorate over time, leading the Armenian people to choose the European Union,” the authors argue.

They stress that this is not only Russia’s “main phobia”, but also its “main misconception”. The analysts believe that even the “economic pressure and blackmail” that Russia began applying to Armenia in May, during the pre-election period, have not changed Armenian public opinion. They cite the results of the parliamentary election on 7 June as evidence: Armenia’s ruling party won, rather than pro-Russian forces.

Ahead of Armenia’s parliamentary election, Russia imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian agricultural products. It also banned imports of flowers, Jermuk mineral water, certain alcoholic drinks and fish products. The authorities justified the measures by citing failures to meet required quality standards. However, Armenian experts and officials viewed the issue in the context of the election campaign. They therefore expected the pressure to end after the election. But that did not happen. Moreover, Russia introduced new restrictions after the election. At the same time, in early June, four EAEU member states called on Armenian authorities to hold a referendum as soon as possible on choosing between the Eurasian bloc and the EU. Yerevan responded that there were currently no grounds for such a vote because Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make a choice. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that Armenia should first obtain EU candidate status or, at the very least, put the issue on the agenda. However, Moscow continues to insist. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said the EAEU expects Armenia to hold a referendum by December. Otherwise, the bloc’s leaders would “take this fact into account when determining appropriate further joint steps”. He said a report on the possible consequences of suspending the EAEU Treaty in relation to Armenia would be discussed at the December meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council.

Armenia’s prime minister spoke about a referendum on EU membership

“No one in Armenia has ever talked about holding a referendum on EAEU membership or an alternative in the form of the EU.

On 9 January 2025, when the Armenian government discussed and approved a bill to launch the EU accession process, Prime Minister Pashinyan said:

“Armenia can begin the process of joining the EU only if a certain number of referendum participants vote ‘yes’ in accordance with the procedure established by the Constitution.”

Senior Armenian officials later repeated this point on various occasions.

The key point is that Armenia will hold a referendum on joining the European Union, not on whether to remain in or leave the EAEU.

This fundamental difference significantly changes the forecasts for the expected outcome. However, if Armenia votes to join the EU, it will inevitably leave the EAEU at some stage of the subsequent process.”

Russia is pushing for a referendum on a different question

“Armenia’s willingness to hold a referendum on EU membership is fundamentally different from what Moscow wants to impose.

Russia is clearly manipulating the situation by demanding a referendum on the EAEU now, when Armenia is at least a decade away from joining the EU.

We need to understand the real reason for this urgency.

The Kremlin understands that if EU membership becomes a genuine possibility, no rational society could vote against it.

Therefore, to keep Armenia in the EAEU and have a chance of stopping its move towards the EU, a referendum must take place as soon as possible, while the prospect of EU membership remains unclear and uncertain.”

Moscow is trying to “beat” Europe by exploiting Armenian businesses’ dependence

“The EAEU mechanisms currently work in favour of Armenian businesses, creating influence and dependence.

At the same time, Armenia is steadily diversifying its economy, reducing that influence and dependence.

The question of whether to remain in the EAEU directly affects many companies with specific interests in Russia. By contrast, EU membership remains a more abstract issue for them for now.

Moscow does not expect to “beat” Europe in economic competition over the next few years or even decades and offer Armenia more attractive conditions. It therefore believes it still has an opportunity to influence the situation now. That is why it is in such a hurry.”

Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

World.title: Mother of teen allowed to leave hospital before suicide calls for change
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

A Perth teenager who took her own life within hours of leaving hospital had attempted suicide 25 minutes before being allowed to leave, a review has found, as her mother calls for improvements to mental health care.

Hailee Hildebrant, 18, was a mental health inpatient at Fiona Stanley Hospital when she died on January 13, sparking the clinical incident review.

The teenager also made "explicit statements" that she planned to take her own life before going on planned overnight leave, the report said.

Hailee Hildebrandt, 18, took her own life after she was released from Fiona Stanley Hospital. (Supplied: Stacey Hildebrandt)

It also stated the patient had told staff to notify her mother to collect her belongings, but there was no phone number available as she had been removed as the next of kin.

After leaving the hospital alone she sent several text messages to her mother saying she was going to kill herself.

Her mother called police who traced her phone and found her unresponsive.

Hailee's mother Stacey Hildebrant told 102.5 ABC Perth Radio, she should not have been allowed to leave the hospital.

Hailee Hildebrandt was an inpatient at Fiona Stanley Hospital. (ABC News)

"I cannot figure out how they couldn't recognise the crisis she was in and still let her go," she said.

" In a mental health facility they can intervene, sometimes they're on 15-minute checks, that's enough to save somebody's life. "

Stacey said the hospital had previously contacted her so should have had her phone number, and that she had not been notified when she was removed as a next of kin.

"I'm unsure how somebody that mentally unwell was able to remove a next of kin," she said.

Recommendations accepted

The clinical incident report made 21 recommendations for further reviews, training, processes and policies.

This included that the South Metropolitan Health Service (SMHS) develop a process for identifying a support person when there is no next of kin identified, as well as a 'red flag' process for leave or discharge planning when there is no next of kin identified.

A SMHS spokesperson said it accepts all of the recommendations and is working to put them into practice.

A memorial for Hailee in West Perth. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

"The death of Hailee is tragic. Our thoughts remain with her family, loved ones and everyone affected by her loss," the spokesperson said.

"While no system can eliminate all risks associated with complex mental health conditions, every recommendation represents an opportunity to strengthen care and improve outcomes for young people and their families, carers and significant others."

Mental Health Minister Meredith Hammat said she expected all recommendations from the review to be implemented in full.

"I acknowledge the immense pain her family continues to endure, and I want to assure Stacey that the findings of this review are being treated with the seriousness they warrant," she said.

Teen dies hours after release from Perth hospital The mother of a teenage girl who took her own life a few hours after being released from a Perth mental health ward says a series of systemic failures is responsible for her daughter's death.

"No review can undo the devastating loss of a child, but it is vital that we learn everything we can from tragedies like this to improve the care provided to other Western Australian families.

"I have written to the chief psychiatrist asking that they undertake a further investigation."

WA's chief psychiatrist has engaged a child and adolescent psychiatrist from New South Wales to lead the review of Hailee's care, the circumstances surrounding her death, and opportunities for improvement.

Stacey said she wanted the outcomes of the reviews to be concrete.

"(We need to) learn from it, make the changes," she said.

World.title: Asylum's temporary closure labelled an 'economic catastrophe'
World.content:
Business owners in regional Victoria say the closure of their town's abandoned asylum will be an "economic catastrophe".

The Aradale asylum was a psychiatric hospital that operated until 1993 in Ararat, about two and a half hours north-west of Melbourne.

The state government owns the popular tourist attraction and leases it to Melbourne Polytechnic, which shut down the site on Friday due to safety concerns.

Ararat, population 8,000, is the only Australian town that is home to two former mental asylums.

The town's other asylum, J Ward jail, remains open.

Aradale opened in 1865 and housed the state's mentally ill for 126 years. (ABC News: Eden Hynninen)

Dark history of gruelling treatments

The Aradale asylum opened in 1865 and housed the state's mentally ill for 126 years.

The patients brought to Aradale were deemed either too sick or too dangerous to remain in society and were subjected to gruelling treatments including restraint and electroshock therapy.

Business owners say Aradale has fallen into disrepair. (ABC News: Eden Hynninen)

The abandoned asylum is made up of 64 buildings spread over more than 40 hectares.

The hospital closed in 1993 following a decision from the state government to deinstitutionalise patients in the mental hospital system.

Since then, Aradale has become a popular "dark tourism" site where visitors learn more about the death, trauma and suffering that existed in its walls.

Locals say the closure of Aradale will be catastrophic for the town. (ABC News: Eden Hynninen)

Repair requests ignored

Nathaniel Buchanan, the owner of Aradale Ghost Tours, said the closure would cause hundreds of thousands of dollars in economic loss for the town.

He said the asylum had been allowed to fall into disrepair despite continual requests for maintenance.

"A small hole quickly becomes a big hole and then you get water coming in pretty quickly," he said.

He said multiple requests for maintenance through Melbourne Polytechnic had been ignored.

"[About four years ago] they ceased communication, pretty much," he said.

The abandoned swimming pool at Aradale. (ABC News: Eden Hynninen)

Mr Buchanan said the town would be devastated by the decision and that Ararat "will suffer". He has suspended bookings and begun processing refunds for tours he cannot honour.

"This is an economic catastrophe," he said.

"The flow-on effect from that is enormous, because you've got cafes for breakfast, lunch and dinners, shopping and other attractions.

" This building is a national treasure. "

In a statement to the ABC, Melbourne Polytechnic said it had suspended access to affected areas of the site.

"The inspection identified a number of safety concerns requiring further investigation and assessment," the statement said.

"We recognise the disruption this decision may cause. However, the safety of our community must take precedence."

It said the closure applied only to the affected areas of the site and that other areas of the broader Aradale site remained open.

Visitors can see inside the asylum's mortuary. (ABC News: Eden Hynninen)

Tourism economy anxiety

A government spokesperson confirmed Melbourne Polytechnic had closed the site to ensure public safety.

"While further assessments are underway, Melbourne Polytechnic is working directly with affected community groups and keeping them informed," the spokesperson said.

Labor MP and member for Ripon Martha Haylett said she was not warned about the impending closure and that many people were blindsided.

She said she had been working with Mr Buchanan "for years" to improve communications with Melbourne Polytechnic.

Martha Haylett says she has been working to get better transparency from Melbourne Polytechnic. (ABC Central Victoria: Sarah Lawrence)

"They just point-blank ignored me for years. They've been operating in really bad faith for a long time," she said.

"I'd gone out there and checked it out and raised it with Melbourne Polytechnic and they just ignored my letter.

"It's like they have just cut [Mr Buchanan] off at the knees.

"As the caretakers … I just hope [Melbourne Polytechnic] will be able to get it up and running in the long term."

The ABC has received emails from other concerned businesses who said Friday's immediate closure had already delivered a "noticeable effect" on business.

Parts of the site are closed due to safety concerns. (ABC News: Eden Hynninen)

Tourism businesses said about 80 per cent of weekend bookings were from people wanting to visit the asylum.

Ararat Rural City Council said it recognised the heavy toll the closure would have on local businesses.

"While safety concerns surrounding the site make this a complex issue, the resulting strain on our tourism sector is very real, and we remain fully committed to supporting our local business community," the council said.

World.title: 'A dangerous individual': Ex-snooker champ convicted of child sex abuse
World.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been convicted of sexually abusing two primary school children in Scotland in the 1990s and early 2000s.

Dott, 49, was found guilty of abusing a girl from 1993-96 and a boy from 2006-10 after a five-day trial at the High Court in Glasgow. The judge ordered Dott to be held in custody ahead of his sentencing on September 29.

The woman, now in her 40s, testified that Dott sexually abused her on multiple occasions, "caressing" her bottom over her clothing, exposing himself and touching her with parts of his body, including his penis.

The man, now in his late 20s, said he was abused on multiple occasions, with Dott touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts.

Dott with his wife Elaine after winning the snooker world championship in 2006. (Getty Images: Rui Vieira)

"Dott is a dangerous individual, and I hope this conviction provides some measure of comfort to those impacted by his crimes," Detective Inspector Gary Smillie from Police Scotland said.

Snooker's governing body suspended Dott in April 2025 after he was charged in the case. The Scot was ranked number 56 in the world at the time and dropped from the rankings after the season.

On Monday, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association revoked Dott's membership following an emergency board meeting. The WPBSA also said it wrote to the World Snooker Tour to request his immediate removal from the WST Hall of Fame.

Dott won the World Snooker Championship in 2006 and was a runner-up twice.

AP/Reuters

Prominent WA federal Liberal MP Andrew Hastie says his party is fighting for its life in the upcoming by-election in the state seat of Secret Harbour.

"We are fighting for our lives and we should be fighting for every single vote in Secret Harbour," Hastie told 7.30.

Hastie, whose electorate of Canning includes parts of Secret Harbour, has warned the state Liberal leader Basil Zempilas against not going hard enough in the election campaign.

"I don't accept this idea that a win for One Nation is a win for the Liberal Party," Hastie said.

"Basil Zempilas said that a win for One Nation would be an opportunity. I don't see that at all. I think we should be fighting to win in every contest we enter, or we shouldn't enter the contest. "A lesson from the 2021 state election is you don't wave the white flag. Voters sense weakness and they will go to the strong horse if you signal weakness."

Hastie said people in his electorate are turning to One Nation as they are hurting in a housing crisis. He said the major parties should do a better job of responding to people's needs.

"If you come down to the beach here in my electorate, sadly you will find people sleeping in their cars because they can't get into a home, and that's why people are frustrated."

He said the state Liberal Party had had time to prepare for the by-election and should support the Liberal candidate against One Nation.

"We've known about this by-election since December of last year. I announced in my Canning division in January that we should expect a by-election, so we've had time to prep the ground."

World.title: 'Ghost' home open before realtor used shell company to buy client's home
World.content:
A Perth real estate agency which allegedly ran a "ghost" home open before using a shell company to purchase the property it had been hired to sell has been reprimanded by consumer authorities.

The home owner believes more should have been done, with the case prompting calls for stronger penalties to be applied for breaches of conflict of interest rules.

Home owner Chao "Jack" Wu believes he received almost $100,000 less than his house was worth when his property was sold in 2024 by Ideal Realty WA to the firm's own real estate agents.

The real estate agents — Roy Li, whose legal name is Liang Li, and Lynn Ding, who goes by Lynn Ting but whose legal name is Lin Ding — deny they failed to disclose that they were the real buyers before making an offer on the property.

They also dispute they paid less than it was worth.

Jack sells his first home

Jack purchased his first home in Western Australia in 2020, six years after settling in Perth from China.

He invested tens of thousands of dollars in the property, a brick and tile 1970s build in the eastern suburb of Kenwick, renovating the driveway and installing a granny flat out the back.

In 2024, Jack signed an exclusive sales agreement on April 23 with Ideal Realty, who advertise themselves as a multi-award-winning boutique agency with more than a decade operating in Perth.

Mr Wu signed the offer contract for the sale of the house on April 29. (Supplied: Jack Wu)

Six days later, he received an email from Ms Ding, copying in Mr Li, saying they had received three offers for his home, the highest of which was from a company called Generation Two PTY LTD.

"The buyer is almost a cash offer, we recommend to accept the offer and get it secure, or the buyer will offer another property," the email said.

Mr Li also sent Mr Wu a few texts that day, telling him:

29 April 2024 12:20pm Roy Li: "The buyer has no finance issue and we can accept it or the buyer will offer others after compared (sic)".

29 April 2024 1:24pm Roy Li: "Will do the best to deal with the buyers. No worries".

29 April 2024 1:24pm Roy Li: "Not easy to hold the buyers too long :)"

Jack said he signed a sale contract with Generation Two later that afternoon after making a counter offer for an additional $20,000.

'Weird' feeling

But a few weeks later, he said he had a "weird" feeling an adjustment had been made to the name of the buyer on the sale contract after it had already been countersigned by both parties.

Jack then decided to try to find out more details about Generation Two, and ordered corporate documents from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) which revealed the owners were Mr Li and Ms Ding.

The documents also showed Generation Two was established and registered at Ideal Realty WA's office address on the same day the offer was made on Jack's home.

On the sale contract, the company was listed as registered at a different, residential address, being Mr Li's postal address.

Jack received an offer to buy his home from a company 'Generation Two', which corporate records show was owned by his real estate agents. (ABC News: Rebecca Trigger)

Jack said when he confronted them with these details, Mr Li and Ms Ding agreed to pay him another $10,000 and to also waive the agents' sale fee of $10,000.

He said that only then, almost six weeks after the initial sale contract was signed, did Mr Li send him a disclosure form to sign, acknowledging their interest in the purchase.

In WA, it is against the law for a real estate agent to be a party in a transaction for a property they have been hired to sell, unless they obtain prior written consent from the owner.

Jack said he went ahead with the sale because he believed, as he had already signed a sale contract, he would be liable for damages if he pulled out of the transaction.

Agent denies not disclosing he was buyer

When the ABC asked Mr Li why he had referred to himself as "the buyer" in his texts and emails with Jack, he said he could not recall the specifics of these messages, but believed he would have communicated about himself in the third person because he was also the agent.

Mr Li also said he had told Jack before making the offer that he and Ms Ding were the buyers and had negotiated the purchase price directly with him.

"Before the settlement, before we are doing the finance, before everything, he knows we're the buyer," Mr Li said.

He did acknowledge, however, that Jack only signed the disclosure form weeks after the sale contract was signed.

He initially claimed Jack refused to sign the disclosure form as a way of negotiating a higher price for the property, something Jack denies.

"The timing of the written disclosure was an administrative oversight, and our procedures have since been reviewed to ensure this does not occur again," Mr Li said in a later statement to the ABC.

Mr Li says he listed a residential address alongside Generation Two on the sale contract, instead of its true registered address which was the same as Ideal Realty's office address, because that was his postal address at the time.

'Ghost' home open prompts questions

Jack is unclear on what home opens were conducted before Mr Li and Ms Ding made the offer on his home.

He alleges Ideal Realty held a "ghost" home open designed "to suppress my price expectations".

Mr Li sent Jack a text message the day before he presented the Generation Two purchase offer saying 13 groups had joined a home open and two groups had been booked for private viewings.

Many potential buyers don't need to inspect the property themselves, Mr Li said. (ABC News: Graeme Powell)

Jack said he later spotted a Google review on Ideal Realty WA from a punter complaining that they had showed up to a scheduled home open at that address but were told it was cancelled.

The ABC spoke with that potential buyer, who confirmed when she arrived at the property that day the agent present told her that the home open had been cancelled.

In response to the allegation, Mr Li told the ABC the rental tenant had refused to allow access to the inside of the property, so potential buyers were only able to view the outside.

But he said he held private viewings at the property before presenting the offers.

He also said potential buyers had become more comfortable with making offers based on seeing videos and photos since the COVID pandemic.

"So many investors they don't need to see the property," Mr Li said.

"They just check up the floor area, … from the photos they can see the property condition."

Conflicting valuations

Last year, Jack obtained legal advice and had the property retrospectively valued at the point of sale.

He said it put the value of the property at $800,000, or $95,000 more than what Mr Li and Ms Ding paid.

The annual growth of house prices in Perth still sits at 22.7 per cent, though it has slightly softened in recent months. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

Mr Li also said he had the property retrospectively valued, which put its price at between $680,000 and $705,000.

He said he believed Jack was disappointed because shifts in the market meant the property was now worth more.

" He feels he lost money," Mr Li said. "But sorry man, that's your choice. You made a final decision. "

Consumer watchdog issues formal warning

Jack complained to Consumer Protection, which investigated his case and issued a formal warning to Ideal Realty relating to an alleged conflict of interest.

A formal warning is issued by the department when it believes there is a prima facie case of a contravention of consumer law.

It also found Ideal Realty allegedly breached sections of the real estate code of conduct dealing with the requirement for agents to act in the best interests of their clients, duty of care, duty for honesty and misleading or deceptive conduct.

The department issues warnings when it believes consumer law was breached. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Breaches can result in fines of $5,000 for individuals and $25,000 for companies, but Ideal Realty WA was not issued a fine.

Consumer Protection does not publish details of administrative warnings and said it could not comment directly on their investigation.

A spokesperson, however, said in general it was lawful for a real estate agent to buy a property from their client, however they must disclose the interest to the seller before any negotiations take place, so the seller can make an informed decision.

Real estate lawyer, academic and commentator Tim O'Dwyer said there was a clear risk of a conflict of interest when an agent wanted to buy their client's home.

He described the Consumer Protection warning as a "slap across the knuckles with a feather" and urged sellers not to agree to offers in these circumstances without seeking independent legal advice and an independent property valuation.

"A buyer wants to pay the lowest possible price, and an agent's duty is to get the highest possible price," Mr O'Dwyer said.

World.title: 'Buy a tent': Single mother turned away by crisis services
World.content:
Tiffany Emmerson and her four children started couch surfing in December 2025 after she separated from her partner.

The single mother said the looming threat of having to live out of her car filled her with fear.

The 33-year-old said she tried to protect her children from the reality of their situation but said they were confused by the instability.

"You can't really explain to a two-year-old, a four-year-old and a seven-year-old what's going on," Ms Emmerson said.

"They just have questions of, 'Why are we at this person's house? Why are we staying here? Why are we staying there?'"

Her youngest is six weeks old.

Tiffany Emmerson packs a bag for her children. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

'Dire' situation

Ms Emmerson said she had reached out to every homeless and housing service across Townsville but had been knocked back by each one.

She said one told her to "buy a tent and find somewhere to go and pitch it".

"There's just no houses available, there's just nothing. Apparently, there's no shelters for people to go to, there's no emergency accommodation," she said.

" There's absolutely nothing. People are living in tents. "

Ms Emmerson said RentConnect, a service helping people find private rental housing, told her they could not help her because she did not meet the financial threshold.

For now, she is staying with her aunt, Kristy Emmerson, who lives in public housing.

Kristy Emmerson tries to keep a sense of normalcy for the children, keeping them entertained with toys and puzzles. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

It is a temporary fix with no long-term solution and, if her aunt decided to move out of the property, Ms Emmerson and her children would have nowhere to go.

Kristy said she felt terrible about the situation and it was affecting her mental health.

"This is Australia. When was it ever OK for people to not have a home, a roof over their heads?" she said.

Although Tiffany has an approved application for public housing, she still does not know when or if a property will become available.

She said many others were in a vulnerable position similar to hers.

Every time Tiffany Emmerson moves to a different location, she has to repack all her belongings, including a steriliser and clean bottles for her bottle-fed newborn baby. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

'Huge gap' in Townsville

Townsville Housing and Homeless Network (HaHN) chair Kym Musumeci said, despite lobbying for a dedicated homeless shelter for more than two years, no progress had been made.

"We've taken it to Canberra, we've taken it to the [housing] department, we've taken it to any local member that will listen to us, basically anyone who will listen to us," she said.

She warned there was a huge number of people seeking support.

"We have families sleeping in cars, we have seen an increase in tents popping up around Townsville," she said.

Last Thursday, more than 1 tonne of "rubbish, abandoned belongings, and other waste" was cleared from three "unoccupied, illegal" camps across the city, according to Mayor Nick Dametto.

The photo was posted to social media by Mayor Nick Dametto. (Supplied)

Ms Musumeci said 50 to 80 people turned up to the Red Cross homeless hub each day, but it did not have the resources to support them.

Seeking somewhere safe to sleep

"If we've got a stable shelter where people can go to be safe and secure and access supports whenever they need them, it's going to go a long way," she said.

HaHN has launched a petition for a shelter.

In response, a spokesperson for Queensland Housing Minister Sam O'Connoll, thanked the community for their advocacy but did not clarify whether the government planned to establish a homeless shelter.

The spokesperson said in Townsville, the government had added 110 social and affordable homes since being elected, with construction on a further 349 homes underway.

In 2025-26, $32.6 million was allocated to fund 17 specialist homelessness services in Townsville, providing 175 places of temporary supported accommodation, alongside outreach and support services, according to the statement.

Statewide, there are more than 44,000 people on the public housing list.

In Townsville, there are 3,558, down from 4,023 last year.

Funding cuts

The opposition's housing spokesperson, Meaghan Scanlon, said the government had changed the rules around eligibility for crisis accommodation.

Meaghan Scanlon says the state government is actively cutting the supports that would help people who are struggling right now. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"There's a number of people who are being exited from social housing, and so that's why Queensland is experiencing homelessness in our streets and in our parks," she said.

"It's so frustrating that the Crisafulli government have decided to cut $42 million of funding from crisis accommodation in just this year alone."

She said the government was trying to suggest everything was OK but said she had spoken to many single mothers and their kids who were sleeping in cars.

"It's just not acceptable that a mum and her kids are being told there's nothing the government can do to help," Ms Scanlon said.

" That is just not OK in a wealthy state like Queensland. "

Tiffany Emmerson says she has seen other mums posting on social media about their struggles to find housing. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

Tiffany Emmerson said it had all been an "absolute stressful nightmare".

"We need more emergency temporary housing that's safe and suitable for families until they can get back on their feet and find a place," she said.

World.title: Researchers dodge crocs to probe coral bleaching after technology failed
World.content:
Reef research off the coast of the Northern Territory's Groote Eylandt has revealed the latest technology may not always be able to accurately predict coral bleaching events.

Anindilyakwa Land and Sea Rangers first noticed coral losing its colour in 2024 and voiced their concerns to researchers from the University of Technology Sydney (UTS).

The underwater system was then mapped for the first time in history, creating a baseline for ongoing monitoring of the reef's health, and the collaboration ultimately confirmed the Indigenous rangers' suspicions of coral bleaching.

The project was driven by local Indigenous rangers, who worked with UTS researchers to document the reefs. (Supplied: Hadley England)

UTS researcher Emma Camp said the 2024 instance was the result of high-temperature waters but, unlike other bleaching events, predictive technologies failed to pick it up.

"We have global models that help us predict when reefs are going to bleach, but those models didn't predict we would have had bleaching in Groote Eylandt at that time," she said.

" Only by having connections on the ground were we able to see why that was happening. "

Dr Camp said the project revealed a need for ongoing reef mapping, as well as further research into the current technology to uncover why this event was not predicted.

Emma Camp says connections on the ground helped when the modelling failed to predict the 2024 coral bleaching event. (Supplied: Hadley England)

Crocs, stingers and cyclones

The project was conducted with the Anindilyakwa rangers, making it the first in-depth recording of Groote Eylandt's coastal reef system.

Anindilyakwa Land Council's Kirsten Eden said unique challenges navigating NT waters were part of the reason such research had not been done before.

Rangers and researches had to stay sharp as they navigated crocodile-inhabited waters. (Supplied: Hadley England)

"The Northern Territory is filled with crocodiles, stingers [and] the weather can become quite unfavourable at times," she said.

"You've really got to have your wits about you.

" It becomes quite an in-depth operation with drones in the air, spotters standing up on the roof of the boats and making sure we can get as close to those reefs as possible. "

Dr Camp echoed her sentiment on severe weather, explaining the reef had also suffered cyclone damage in addition to the bleaching.

Tropical Cyclone Megan reached category three intensity off the coast of Groote Eylandt in 2024, with strong winds causing significant damage to local vegetation and the wharf.

Dr Camp said cyclones often moved across the ocean with such force they could break up a reef's architecture.

Research teams had to keep their wits about them in order to safely survey the reefs. (Supplied: Hadley England)

"That's actually part of the job of the reef, the reef stops those big waves from crashing into shore and causing coastal erosion," she said.

" But there's a cost and consequence to that … cyclones can have significant impacts on reefs, and you can see the impact quite immediately. "

Researching coral species

During the project, a variety of unrecognised coral species were catalogued — research is now underway, with the aim of either identifying the samples or having them acknowledged as new discoveries.

In mapped Groote Eylandt's reef system, researchers discovered uncategorised coral species. (Supplied: Hadley England)

"I'm almost certain there's a few that haven't been found before," Ms Eden said.

"It just opens up this whole other realm of knowledge, not just for us but for other ranger groups who are in the same boat as us, without that knowledge of what's actually in our sea country.

World.title: Major travel delays in Sydney’s north after train wiring issue
World.content:
A wiring fault on Sydney’s T1 North Shore Line is causing mass delays for city-bound commuters on Tuesday, with urgent repairs expected to last the morning peak.

The loss of tension in an overhead wire near Chatswood Station has resulted in the cancellation of city bound services from Gordon to North Sydney. Limited bus services will replace trains from Gordon to Chatswood, where commuters can travel towards the city on the Metro. The problem was due to a failure in the cutaway mechanism on the wires, causing them to sag.

Repair crews have been on the scene since Monday night when the issue was discovered.

Sydney Trains chief executive Matt Longland expects the repairs to continue for the entirety of the morning peak, and advised commuters to consider alternative train or Metro routes.

World.title: Ralph Carr to learn his fate on rape, sex assault charges
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Ralph Carr to learn his fate on rape, sex assault charges Erin Pearson August 25, 2026 — 7:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Talent manager Ralph Carr will on Tuesday learn how long he will spend in jail for the rape and sexual assault of a woman more than 30 years his junior. Carr, 66, will appear for sentencing on Tuesday, with the County Court taking the unusual step of live-streaming the proceedings. Ralph Carr and his connections. Aresna Villanueva It follows a three-year suppression order, obtained in March 2023, which concealed Carr’s identity on the basis that the safety of his mental health was at risk if he were publicly named. Carr has been in custody since last month when a jury convicted him of two counts of rape and one of sexual assault. Rape carries a maximum penalty of 25 years in jail.





Defence barrister Dermot Dann, KC, said Carr was experiencing profound shame and nightmares since being jailed, where he is in lockdown for 23 hours a day. Carr has also applied for a stay, or deferral, in serving his sentence after what Dann described as “the shortest incidents of rape” the legal system had ever seen. Related Article Justice Psychiatrists cast doubt on court secrecy orders that protect accused The barrister said that after lifting the suppression order over Carr’s identity, the risks to his client’s mental health became “so much more dire”, with his risk of self-harm elevated by his perceived damage to his reputation and identity. Dann said his client’s declining mental health warranted mitigation of his sentencing along with Carr’s lack of criminal history, prior good character, and the significant contribution he had made to the community.



No victim impact statement was filed and the woman did not attend the pre-sentence hearing. Judge Frank Gucciardo will hand down his sentencing remarks from about 11.30am, followed by his ruling on Carr’s stay application. If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: ‘Violent white men’: Washington Post ordered to reinstate opinion writer fired after Charlie Kirk posts
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing ‘Violent white men’: Washington Post ordered to reinstate opinion writer fired after Charlie Kirk posts Corey Williams August 25, 2026 — 7:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An arbitrator has ordered The Washington Post to reinstate a black opinion writer fired over social media posts about violent white men following last year’s killing of American influencer and MAGA supporter Charlie Kirk. The ruling said the newspaper did not have sufficient cause to terminate Karen Attiah, who at the time was the last black full-time member of the Post’s opinion desk. The arbitrator, Sarah Miller Espinosa, also ordered the Post to award Attiah full back pay and lost benefits. After Kirk’s killing, Attiah, the founding global opinion editor for the Post and the newspaper’s only black female opinion writer, made several posts to her Bluesky account. Ashara Wilson via AP Kirk, 31, who rose from a teenage conservative campus activist to become a top podcaster and ally of US President Donald Trump, was shot and killed on September 10 during a public appearance at Utah Valley University. Kirk launched Turning Point USA in 2012 and made provocative statements about race, gender and politics. He was critical of the black movement on college campuses and called George Floyd, the black man whose 2020 murder at the hands of Minneapolis police sparked protests, a “scumbag”.



His death elicited a torrent of comments about him, both pro and against, and some who spoke out against him in the days after the killing faced sanctions or dismissal at work. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America It’s OK to speak ill of the dead. In fact, sometimes we must Jenna Price Columnist Attiah posted after Kirk’s killing After Kirk’s killing, Attiah, the founding global opinion editor for the Post and the newspaper’s only black female opinion writer, published several posts on her Bluesky account. One post read: “Refusing to tear my clothes and smear ashes on my face in performative mourning for a white man that espoused violence is … not the same as violence.”



“If anything, the rush to coddle violent white men is self-protective – that we know they are not used to feeling vulnerable and mortal – and will react violently out of fear. And we will all suffer,” read another post. Attiah was emailed a termination letter on September 11, accusing her of “gross misconduct”. Charlie Kirk speaks before he was shot during Turning Point’s visit to Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah. AP “Your public comments on social media regarding the death of Charlie Kirk violate the Post’s social media policies, harm the integrity of our organisation, and potentially endanger the physical safety of our staff,” the letter read. But Espinosa found that the newspaper, in a June 4 hearing, failed to establish that Attiah “engaged in gross misconduct” and that the Post “did not have good and sufficient cause to terminate” her employment, which violated the collective bargaining agreement with the newspaper’s union.



Related Article Updated

Media & marketing ‘Sad and disgusted’: Jeff Bezos shakes up Washington Post with radical shift “After wrongfully firing me last year, an independent arbitrator has ordered the @washingtonpost to reinstate me immediately, with back pay,” Attiah posted on Instagram on Monday. “It’s been a year-long fight, but this is a victory for journalists everywhere. More to come soon.” Ruling welcomed as a landmark moment The Democracy Defenders Fund, which, along with Washington-Baltimore News Guild, represented Attiah, said the ruling was a landmark moment for press freedom, “confirming that corporate media institutions cannot use retaliatory discipline to silence journalists who address uncomfortable truths.” The Post said in a statement that it respected the arbitration process, but declined to comment further.



Jeff Bezos, the billionaire owner of The Post, caused a stir in February 2025 when he announced changes to the newspaper’s opinion pages to limit what he described as viewpoints opposing “personal liberties and free markets”. US President Donald Trump arrives to speak at a memorial for Charlie Kirk in Arizona on September 21. AP At the time, Attiah’s firing was among dozens of others across various professions stemming from comments about Kirk’s assassination, igniting a debate over First Amendment rights as Trump vowed retribution for remarks he considered disparaging. The National Association of Black Journalists, the nation’s largest professional advocacy organisation for journalists of colour, added at the time that Attiah’s firing had “raised an alarm about the erosion of black voices across the media.” During the organisation’s annual convention this month in Atlanta, the NABJ gave The Post a “Thumbs Down Award” because the newspaper had laid off black journalists and eliminated race and culture beats.

World.title: ‘Who started the fire?’ UK backs Ukraine with seismic deal on AI weapons
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Who started the fire?’ UK backs Ukraine with seismic deal on AI weapons David Crowe Updated August 25, 2026 — 6:54am ,first published 5:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Britain will develop new defence systems with Ukraine by gaining access to battlefield data that can help train artificial intelligence programs that support future weapons, despite warnings from Russia against the deepening cooperation. The pact will also see Britain share confidential missile designs so that Ukrainian companies can make the weapons inside their country in the hope of countering Russian airstrikes, amid new warnings about a shortage of air defence systems. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, left, with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Monday. Getty Images Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that the country faced a “funding gap” of €27 billion ($44 billion) and needed help such as bringing forward European Union loans, as he marked the nation’s independence day on Monday. Zelensky welcomed leaders including British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to ceremonies in Kyiv at a time of mounting risks for Ukrainian civilians, as the country confronts a shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles to counter Russian attacks.



Burnham promised help on this front by agreeing to give Ukraine the designs for the Storm Shadow missile, a weapon that is launched from a jet fighter to reach a target as much as 250km away. The move is a significant show of support for Ukraine at a time when Zelensky is seeking help from US President Donald Trump to share the design of the Patriot systems in the hope they can be manufactured in Ukraine, alleviating the missile shortage. Burnham plays the guitar in the mobile recording studio of a military and artistic unit that perform on the front lines, in hospitals and at rehabilitation centres. Getty Images Burnham is shown the rubble at the site of a strike near the Lukanivska market in Kyiv. Henry Nicholls/Pool AFP via AP The missile plans dominated media coverage of Burnham’s visit to Kyiv – his first as prime minister – to join other western leaders at the ceremonies, while a Kremlin spokesman declared that Britain was adding “fuel to the fire” in conflict.



When reporters asked Burnham about the Kremlin’s comment, he responded: “Who started the fire? That’s the question, isn’t it?” Only after the headlines about the missile deal, however, did the news emerge that Britain would receive battlefield data from a Ukrainian tech centre, known as the Avengers Labs, to develop AI systems that can power drones and autonomous weapons. “The platform provides real-world data and insights to train AI models, collected by thousands of daylight cameras and infrared sensors across the battlefield in Ukraine,” the UK government said. “Those sensors and cameras capture millions of objects, such as tanks, artillery, air defence systems, infantry, and aerial targets, including Shahed drones and reconnaissance UAVs, feeding back data to the Avengers Lab to train new AI models.”



One project will explore the development of low-power AI chips designed to power future drones, robotics and autonomous systems. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Ukraine pins hope on new era of AI drones to transform the face of war “If successful, the technology could underpin a new generation of intelligent machines capable of operating for longer, responding faster and functioning in environments where conventional systems struggle,” the UK said. Developers in Ukraine have been working on AI software to create autonomous drones for some time, telling this masthead about their plans in Lviv last year. Russian developers are keeping up in the drone arms race, however, and have deployed autonomous drones at targets in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, according to The New York Times, which reported this week on Russian drones fitted with AI chips and computer systems from US tech giant Nvidia.



In an attack on July 6, the newspaper reported, three Ukrainians were killed by a Russian drone that was “self-targeting” and using AI components, in what would be the first documented case of this technology being used against civilians in the war. On Monday, Burnham visited a Kyiv shopping centre hit by a Russian strike in May, before being given a guitar by a Ukrainian soldier. The prime minister played the guitar briefly before hearing Ukrainian troops sing an Oasis song. View post on X While Britain is sharing valuable missile designs, the move is not expected to bolster Ukrainian defences in the near-term because of the challenge of manufacturing the weapons. Zelensky is urgently seeking help from Trump to ensure Ukraine can make its own versions of the Patriot interceptors, which are now in short supply after being heavily used to counter Iranian missile and drone attacks in the Middle East.



Arun Dawson, a researcher at the Freeman Air and Space Institute at King’s College London, told the Associated Press that the UK plan would not help Ukraine through the coming northern winter and would probably not have an effect until next year, at the earliest. “What Ukraine needs is protection from Russian ballistic missile attacks,” he said. The Storm Shadow is known as the SCALP when made and deployed in France. The missile design is used by the British, French and Italian air forces. The missile would give Ukraine a deeper offensive capability, Dawson told the Associated Press.



“You can use it to take out the Russian sites from which they are launching these ballistic missiles,” he said. With AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ASX set to edge up, Wall Street weighed down by tech stocks; Trump bought SpaceX shares
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to edge up, Wall Street weighed down by tech stocks; Trump bought SpaceX shares Stan Choe Updated August 25, 2026 — 6:22am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks drifted to a mixed finish as the countdown ticks toward potentially market-moving events coming later in the week. The areas of the bond market that the US Treasury Department is trying to calm down, meanwhile, eased a bit. The S&P 500 slipped 0.3 per cent and pulled a bit further from its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 140 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.8 per cent. Most stocks rose, but tech giant Nvidia weighed on the market. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to edge higher, with futures at 6.05am AEST pointing to a rise of 9 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.47¢. Reporting season continues, with Coles and Woodside Energy among companies set to release results today. Tech stocks led the way downward following big swings through the summer on worries that the frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high and that the huge demand for AI chips won’t be sustainable if they don’t produce enough profits.



Related Article Medicine Big pharma’s next $10 billion gamble: Ozempic for your brain Chip giant Nvidia has been a tremendous winner of the AI boom and become Wall Street’s largest and most influential stock because of it. It will deliver its latest quarterly earnings report on Wednesday, which could dictate the next big move for AI-related stocks. Nvidia sank 2.9 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500, where the majority of stocks rose. Drops of 5.8 per cent for Micron Technology and 2.6 per cent for Broadcom also helped drag the index lower. All told, the S&P 500 fell 21.51 points to 7,652.86. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 140.15 to 53,417.16, and the Nasdaq composite sank 200.26 to 25,980.19. The other big factor moving stocks recently has been the bond market, where longer-term Treasury yields climbed through the summer on worries about high inflation, huge government debts and other factors. High yields make it more expensive for everyone to borrow, not just the government, and have already pushed up mortgage rates and hurt the housing industry.



The US Treasury Department announced a surprise move last week to increase the size of planned buybacks of Treasurys, which could help contain the rise in yields for 10- and 30-year Treasurys. But analysts warned the move may have only a limited effect because of how small the size of the buybacks are and how they do not fix the fundamental problems of too-high debt for the US government and expensive oil prices because of the war with Iran. On Monday, the yield of the 10-year Treasury eased to 4.70 per cent from 4.74 per cent late Friday and is back below where it was late Tuesday, before the US Treasury Department made its surprise announcement. Helping to bring yields down on Monday was a drop in oil prices. Brent crude fell 2.3 per cent to $US90.54 per barrel. Last month it zigzagged between $US72 and $US102 as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. The United States on Monday announced new sanctions aimed at Iran, which helped drag the value of Iran’s currency to a record low against the US dollar. Despite Monday’s easing of Treasury yields, analysts warn the US government’s attempts to influence the bond market could ultimately mean higher pressure on inflation. Inflation already is worse than nearly everyone would like and has been for years.



That raises the pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise the federal funds rate, which affects very short-term overnight loans. When the Fed raises that rate, it could help keep a lid on inflation by trying to slow the overall economy and undercutting prices for stocks and other investments. Related Article Opinion

Big four accountants KPMG’s sackings are just the start of the fallout for the firm Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The Fed’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, is set to deliver a speech Friday at an economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. The mountain setting has been the backdrop for major Fed policy announcements in the past, but investors are unsure of what they may get from Warsh this time around. Warsh has insisted that he wants to give financial markets fewer clues about what the Fed will do with interest rates, hoping that markets react more to incoming data about the economy and inflation than to what the Fed is signalling. But with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announcing his move last week, Warsh now holds the ball, according to economists at Bank of America. Expectations are high among investors for Warsh to talk about inflation and how the Fed could potentially react, and a failure to deliver could lead to bond yields rising further, they said.



Elsewhere, a public financial disclosure has revealed US President Donald Trump invested as much as $US50,000 ($70,000) in Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June, giving him a financial stake in a major government contractor run by his former adviser. He bought between $US15,001 and $US50,000 in shares on June 23, according to a financial disclosure signed by him on August 12 and made public on August 22. The purchase was part of more than a thousand stock trades the president made in June. Trump’s investment in SpaceX adds a new financial link between the president and Musk’s rocket company at a time when the administration is making decisions that could affect the firm’s fortunes. SpaceX is a US military contractor, and ​often seeks approvals from federal agencies. Trump last week directed his team to help drastically increase ‌the number of US commercial space launches. SpaceX is a dominant player in that sector. In stock markets abroad, indexes dipped around much of the world. South Korea’s Kospi fell 3.1 per cent, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 1.9 per cent for two of the biggest moves.



Seoul has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings this summer because it is dominated by two tech titans benefiting from the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: US launches ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ to isolate Iran from the world
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war US launches ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ to isolate Iran from the world Michael Koziol Updated August 25, 2026 — 5:33am ,first published 4:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The US is issuing deadlines to countries to stop all financial dealings with Iran as part of a new “Operation Economic Outcast” aimed at isolating the Islamic regime in Tehran from the rest of the world. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said President Donald Trump was calling his global counterparts with specific demands regarding their commercial interactions with Iran. If they fail to comply, their institutions face exclusion from the US financial system. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the launch of “Operation Economic Outcast” against Iran. AP “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent said at a news conference in Washington on Monday (US time). “It is no longer acceptable to operate in the grey spaces of this conflict … Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking.”



In a speech that was heavy on threatening rhetoric, Bessent likened the announcement to “D-Day” – the start of the allied invasion of Nazi-controlled Europe during World War II. But he provided few specifics, and did not unveil any immediate secondary sanctions against other countries or banks. He said it was likely that a major financial institution would be hit with sanctions by the end of the week. The move comes just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to meet Donald Trump at the White House. Getty Images Asked why the US was not imposing secondary sanctions straight away, Bessent said: “We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behaviour. Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” The US has so far resisted targeting Chinese banks and intermediaries, which process the bulk of Iranian oil sales. Trump has a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House next month.



When asked, Bessent suggested Chinese banks were not immune from sanctions, but said the US preferred to engage in “quiet diplomacy”. “If they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money – into repression – they will be targeted,” he said. Motorcyclists in Tehran pass a billboard depicting Donald Trump with the words: “Great Victory! Strait of Hormuz.” AP Several new measures were announced on Monday, including sanctions against nearly 60 Iran-linked entities, individuals and vessels. That included a procurement scheme for Iran’s ballistic missile development and nuclear research, a malicious cyber group and a network of brokers and vessels transporting Iranian oil, according to US Treasury.



And the US expanded its list of sectoral sanctions against Iran. Anyone operating in the fields of digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping was now liable to be sanctioned. Related Article Iran sanctions Trump announces ‘economic D-Day’ of Iran sanctions, moving war to new phase Bessent said that every branch of Iran’s Bank Melli – the largest regime-controlled commercial bank – must be “shuttered and dark”. The move signals a transition in the war against Iran from primarily a military conflict to an economic battle where the US will try to use the weight of its financial system to cut Tehran off from all revenue. Friday will mark the six-month anniversary of the war, which Trump initially said would last four to six weeks. Although fighting has subsided for most of that time, a peace deal to end the conflict has proved elusive.



Trump pulled back from a threatened military offensive against Iran’s energy infrastructure and bridges, but reinstated a naval blockade on all Iranian ports in July. Meanwhile, the US is trying to establish safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz for the rest of the world’s ships. Iran’s trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don’t take these statements into account anywhere,” Ghalibaf said on X. Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked Trump and Bessent for the move. “You justly exact a steep price from that cruel dictatorship and from those who assist its continued aggression,” he said.

World.title: Major travel delays in Sydney’s north after train wiring issue
World.content:
A wiring fault on Sydney’s T1 North Shore Line is causing mass delays for city-bound commuters on Tuesday, with urgent repairs expected to last the morning peak.

The loss of tension in an overhead wire near Chatswood Station has resulted in the cancellation of city bound services from Gordon to North Sydney. Limited bus services will replace trains from Gordon to Chatswood, where commuters can travel towards the city on the Metro. The problem was due to a failure in the cutaway mechanism on the wires, causing them to sag.

Repair crews have been on the scene since Monday night when the issue was discovered.

Sydney Trains chief executive Matt Longland expects the repairs to continue for the entirety of the morning peak, and advised commuters to consider alternative train or Metro routes.
