World.title: Ralph Carr to learn his fate on rape, sex assault charges
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Ralph Carr to learn his fate on rape, sex assault charges Erin Pearson August 25, 2026 — 7:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Talent manager Ralph Carr will on Tuesday learn how long he will spend in jail for the rape and sexual assault of a woman more than 30 years his junior. Carr, 66, will appear for sentencing on Tuesday, with the County Court taking the unusual step of live-streaming the proceedings. Ralph Carr and his connections. Aresna Villanueva It follows a three-year suppression order, obtained in March 2023, which concealed Carr’s identity on the basis that the safety of his mental health was at risk if he were publicly named. Carr has been in custody since last month when a jury convicted him of two counts of rape and one of sexual assault. Rape carries a maximum penalty of 25 years in jail.





Defence barrister Dermot Dann, KC, said Carr was experiencing profound shame and nightmares since being jailed, where he is in lockdown for 23 hours a day. Carr has also applied for a stay, or deferral, in serving his sentence after what Dann described as “the shortest incidents of rape” the legal system had ever seen. Related Article Justice Psychiatrists cast doubt on court secrecy orders that protect accused The barrister said that after lifting the suppression order over Carr’s identity, the risks to his client’s mental health became “so much more dire”, with his risk of self-harm elevated by his perceived damage to his reputation and identity. Dann said his client’s declining mental health warranted mitigation of his sentencing along with Carr’s lack of criminal history, prior good character, and the significant contribution he had made to the community.



No victim impact statement was filed and the woman did not attend the pre-sentence hearing. Judge Frank Gucciardo will hand down his sentencing remarks from about 11.30am, followed by his ruling on Carr’s stay application. If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: ‘Violent white men’: Washington Post ordered to reinstate opinion writer fired after Charlie Kirk posts
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing ‘Violent white men’: Washington Post ordered to reinstate opinion writer fired after Charlie Kirk posts Corey Williams August 25, 2026 — 7:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An arbitrator has ordered The Washington Post to reinstate a black opinion writer fired over social media posts about violent white men following last year’s killing of American influencer and MAGA supporter Charlie Kirk. The ruling said the newspaper did not have sufficient cause to terminate Karen Attiah, who at the time was the last black full-time member of the Post’s opinion desk. The arbitrator, Sarah Miller Espinosa, also ordered the Post to award Attiah full back pay and lost benefits. After Kirk’s killing, Attiah, the founding global opinion editor for the Post and the newspaper’s only black female opinion writer, made several posts to her Bluesky account. Ashara Wilson via AP Kirk, 31, who rose from a teenage conservative campus activist to become a top podcaster and ally of US President Donald Trump, was shot and killed on September 10 during a public appearance at Utah Valley University. Kirk launched Turning Point USA in 2012 and made provocative statements about race, gender and politics. He was critical of the black movement on college campuses and called George Floyd, the black man whose 2020 murder at the hands of Minneapolis police sparked protests, a “scumbag”.



His death elicited a torrent of comments about him, both pro and against, and some who spoke out against him in the days after the killing faced sanctions or dismissal at work. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America It’s OK to speak ill of the dead. In fact, sometimes we must Jenna Price Columnist Attiah posted after Kirk’s killing After Kirk’s killing, Attiah, the founding global opinion editor for the Post and the newspaper’s only black female opinion writer, published several posts on her Bluesky account. One post read: “Refusing to tear my clothes and smear ashes on my face in performative mourning for a white man that espoused violence is … not the same as violence.”



“If anything, the rush to coddle violent white men is self-protective – that we know they are not used to feeling vulnerable and mortal – and will react violently out of fear. And we will all suffer,” read another post. Attiah was emailed a termination letter on September 11, accusing her of “gross misconduct”. Charlie Kirk speaks before he was shot during Turning Point’s visit to Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah. AP “Your public comments on social media regarding the death of Charlie Kirk violate the Post’s social media policies, harm the integrity of our organisation, and potentially endanger the physical safety of our staff,” the letter read. But Espinosa found that the newspaper, in a June 4 hearing, failed to establish that Attiah “engaged in gross misconduct” and that the Post “did not have good and sufficient cause to terminate” her employment, which violated the collective bargaining agreement with the newspaper’s union.



Related Article Updated

Media & marketing ‘Sad and disgusted’: Jeff Bezos shakes up Washington Post with radical shift “After wrongfully firing me last year, an independent arbitrator has ordered the @washingtonpost to reinstate me immediately, with back pay,” Attiah posted on Instagram on Monday. “It’s been a year-long fight, but this is a victory for journalists everywhere. More to come soon.” Ruling welcomed as a landmark moment The Democracy Defenders Fund, which, along with Washington-Baltimore News Guild, represented Attiah, said the ruling was a landmark moment for press freedom, “confirming that corporate media institutions cannot use retaliatory discipline to silence journalists who address uncomfortable truths.” The Post said in a statement that it respected the arbitration process, but declined to comment further.



Jeff Bezos, the billionaire owner of The Post, caused a stir in February 2025 when he announced changes to the newspaper’s opinion pages to limit what he described as viewpoints opposing “personal liberties and free markets”. US President Donald Trump arrives to speak at a memorial for Charlie Kirk in Arizona on September 21. AP At the time, Attiah’s firing was among dozens of others across various professions stemming from comments about Kirk’s assassination, igniting a debate over First Amendment rights as Trump vowed retribution for remarks he considered disparaging. The National Association of Black Journalists, the nation’s largest professional advocacy organisation for journalists of colour, added at the time that Attiah’s firing had “raised an alarm about the erosion of black voices across the media.” During the organisation’s annual convention this month in Atlanta, the NABJ gave The Post a “Thumbs Down Award” because the newspaper had laid off black journalists and eliminated race and culture beats.

World.title: ‘Who started the fire?’ UK backs Ukraine with seismic deal on AI weapons
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Who started the fire?’ UK backs Ukraine with seismic deal on AI weapons David Crowe Updated August 25, 2026 — 6:54am ,first published 5:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Britain will develop new defence systems with Ukraine by gaining access to battlefield data that can help train artificial intelligence programs that support future weapons, despite warnings from Russia against the deepening cooperation. The pact will also see Britain share confidential missile designs so that Ukrainian companies can make the weapons inside their country in the hope of countering Russian airstrikes, amid new warnings about a shortage of air defence systems. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, left, with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Monday. Getty Images Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that the country faced a “funding gap” of €27 billion ($44 billion) and needed help such as bringing forward European Union loans, as he marked the nation’s independence day on Monday. Zelensky welcomed leaders including British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to ceremonies in Kyiv at a time of mounting risks for Ukrainian civilians, as the country confronts a shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles to counter Russian attacks.



Burnham promised help on this front by agreeing to give Ukraine the designs for the Storm Shadow missile, a weapon that is launched from a jet fighter to reach a target as much as 250km away. The move is a significant show of support for Ukraine at a time when Zelensky is seeking help from US President Donald Trump to share the design of the Patriot systems in the hope they can be manufactured in Ukraine, alleviating the missile shortage. Burnham plays the guitar in the mobile recording studio of a military and artistic unit that perform on the front lines, in hospitals and at rehabilitation centres. Getty Images Burnham is shown the rubble at the site of a strike near the Lukanivska market in Kyiv. Henry Nicholls/Pool AFP via AP The missile plans dominated media coverage of Burnham’s visit to Kyiv – his first as prime minister – to join other western leaders at the ceremonies, while a Kremlin spokesman declared that Britain was adding “fuel to the fire” in conflict.



When reporters asked Burnham about the Kremlin’s comment, he responded: “Who started the fire? That’s the question, isn’t it?” Only after the headlines about the missile deal, however, did the news emerge that Britain would receive battlefield data from a Ukrainian tech centre, known as the Avengers Labs, to develop AI systems that can power drones and autonomous weapons. “The platform provides real-world data and insights to train AI models, collected by thousands of daylight cameras and infrared sensors across the battlefield in Ukraine,” the UK government said. “Those sensors and cameras capture millions of objects, such as tanks, artillery, air defence systems, infantry, and aerial targets, including Shahed drones and reconnaissance UAVs, feeding back data to the Avengers Lab to train new AI models.”



One project will explore the development of low-power AI chips designed to power future drones, robotics and autonomous systems. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Ukraine pins hope on new era of AI drones to transform the face of war “If successful, the technology could underpin a new generation of intelligent machines capable of operating for longer, responding faster and functioning in environments where conventional systems struggle,” the UK said. Developers in Ukraine have been working on AI software to create autonomous drones for some time, telling this masthead about their plans in Lviv last year. Russian developers are keeping up in the drone arms race, however, and have deployed autonomous drones at targets in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, according to The New York Times, which reported this week on Russian drones fitted with AI chips and computer systems from US tech giant Nvidia.



In an attack on July 6, the newspaper reported, three Ukrainians were killed by a Russian drone that was “self-targeting” and using AI components, in what would be the first documented case of this technology being used against civilians in the war. On Monday, Burnham visited a Kyiv shopping centre hit by a Russian strike in May, before being given a guitar by a Ukrainian soldier. The prime minister played the guitar briefly before hearing Ukrainian troops sing an Oasis song. View post on X While Britain is sharing valuable missile designs, the move is not expected to bolster Ukrainian defences in the near-term because of the challenge of manufacturing the weapons. Zelensky is urgently seeking help from Trump to ensure Ukraine can make its own versions of the Patriot interceptors, which are now in short supply after being heavily used to counter Iranian missile and drone attacks in the Middle East.



Arun Dawson, a researcher at the Freeman Air and Space Institute at King’s College London, told the Associated Press that the UK plan would not help Ukraine through the coming northern winter and would probably not have an effect until next year, at the earliest. “What Ukraine needs is protection from Russian ballistic missile attacks,” he said. The Storm Shadow is known as the SCALP when made and deployed in France. The missile design is used by the British, French and Italian air forces. The missile would give Ukraine a deeper offensive capability, Dawson told the Associated Press.



“You can use it to take out the Russian sites from which they are launching these ballistic missiles,” he said. With AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ASX set to edge up, Wall Street weighed down by tech stocks; Trump bought SpaceX shares
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to edge up, Wall Street weighed down by tech stocks; Trump bought SpaceX shares Stan Choe Updated August 25, 2026 — 6:22am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks drifted to a mixed finish as the countdown ticks toward potentially market-moving events coming later in the week. The areas of the bond market that the US Treasury Department is trying to calm down, meanwhile, eased a bit. The S&P 500 slipped 0.3 per cent and pulled a bit further from its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 140 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.8 per cent. Most stocks rose, but tech giant Nvidia weighed on the market. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to edge higher, with futures at 6.05am AEST pointing to a rise of 9 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.47¢. Reporting season continues, with Coles and Woodside Energy among companies set to release results today. Tech stocks led the way downward following big swings through the summer on worries that the frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high and that the huge demand for AI chips won’t be sustainable if they don’t produce enough profits.



Related Article Medicine Big pharma’s next $10 billion gamble: Ozempic for your brain Chip giant Nvidia has been a tremendous winner of the AI boom and become Wall Street’s largest and most influential stock because of it. It will deliver its latest quarterly earnings report on Wednesday, which could dictate the next big move for AI-related stocks. Nvidia sank 2.9 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500, where the majority of stocks rose. Drops of 5.8 per cent for Micron Technology and 2.6 per cent for Broadcom also helped drag the index lower. All told, the S&P 500 fell 21.51 points to 7,652.86. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 140.15 to 53,417.16, and the Nasdaq composite sank 200.26 to 25,980.19. The other big factor moving stocks recently has been the bond market, where longer-term Treasury yields climbed through the summer on worries about high inflation, huge government debts and other factors. High yields make it more expensive for everyone to borrow, not just the government, and have already pushed up mortgage rates and hurt the housing industry.



The US Treasury Department announced a surprise move last week to increase the size of planned buybacks of Treasurys, which could help contain the rise in yields for 10- and 30-year Treasurys. But analysts warned the move may have only a limited effect because of how small the size of the buybacks are and how they do not fix the fundamental problems of too-high debt for the US government and expensive oil prices because of the war with Iran. On Monday, the yield of the 10-year Treasury eased to 4.70 per cent from 4.74 per cent late Friday and is back below where it was late Tuesday, before the US Treasury Department made its surprise announcement. Helping to bring yields down on Monday was a drop in oil prices. Brent crude fell 2.3 per cent to $US90.54 per barrel. Last month it zigzagged between $US72 and $US102 as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. The United States on Monday announced new sanctions aimed at Iran, which helped drag the value of Iran’s currency to a record low against the US dollar. Despite Monday’s easing of Treasury yields, analysts warn the US government’s attempts to influence the bond market could ultimately mean higher pressure on inflation. Inflation already is worse than nearly everyone would like and has been for years.



That raises the pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise the federal funds rate, which affects very short-term overnight loans. When the Fed raises that rate, it could help keep a lid on inflation by trying to slow the overall economy and undercutting prices for stocks and other investments. Related Article Opinion

Big four accountants KPMG’s sackings are just the start of the fallout for the firm Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The Fed’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, is set to deliver a speech Friday at an economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. The mountain setting has been the backdrop for major Fed policy announcements in the past, but investors are unsure of what they may get from Warsh this time around. Warsh has insisted that he wants to give financial markets fewer clues about what the Fed will do with interest rates, hoping that markets react more to incoming data about the economy and inflation than to what the Fed is signalling. But with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announcing his move last week, Warsh now holds the ball, according to economists at Bank of America. Expectations are high among investors for Warsh to talk about inflation and how the Fed could potentially react, and a failure to deliver could lead to bond yields rising further, they said.



Elsewhere, a public financial disclosure has revealed US President Donald Trump invested as much as $US50,000 ($70,000) in Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June, giving him a financial stake in a major government contractor run by his former adviser. He bought between $US15,001 and $US50,000 in shares on June 23, according to a financial disclosure signed by him on August 12 and made public on August 22. The purchase was part of more than a thousand stock trades the president made in June. Trump’s investment in SpaceX adds a new financial link between the president and Musk’s rocket company at a time when the administration is making decisions that could affect the firm’s fortunes. SpaceX is a US military contractor, and ​often seeks approvals from federal agencies. Trump last week directed his team to help drastically increase ‌the number of US commercial space launches. SpaceX is a dominant player in that sector. In stock markets abroad, indexes dipped around much of the world. South Korea’s Kospi fell 3.1 per cent, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 1.9 per cent for two of the biggest moves.



Seoul has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings this summer because it is dominated by two tech titans benefiting from the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
