World.title: US launches ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ to isolate Iran from the world
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war US launches ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ to isolate Iran from the world Michael Koziol Updated August 25, 2026 — 5:33am ,first published 4:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The US is issuing deadlines to countries to stop all financial dealings with Iran as part of a new “Operation Economic Outcast” aimed at isolating the Islamic regime in Tehran from the rest of the world. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said President Donald Trump was calling his global counterparts with specific demands regarding their commercial interactions with Iran. If they fail to comply, their institutions face exclusion from the US financial system. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the launch of “Operation Economic Outcast” against Iran. AP “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent said at a news conference in Washington on Monday (US time). “It is no longer acceptable to operate in the grey spaces of this conflict … Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking.”



In a speech that was heavy on threatening rhetoric, Bessent likened the announcement to “D-Day” – the start of the allied invasion of Nazi-controlled Europe during World War II. But he provided few specifics, and did not unveil any immediate secondary sanctions against other countries or banks. He said it was likely that a major financial institution would be hit with sanctions by the end of the week. The move comes just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to meet Donald Trump at the White House. Getty Images Asked why the US was not imposing secondary sanctions straight away, Bessent said: “We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behaviour. Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” The US has so far resisted targeting Chinese banks and intermediaries, which process the bulk of Iranian oil sales. Trump has a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House next month.



When asked, Bessent suggested Chinese banks were not immune from sanctions, but said the US preferred to engage in “quiet diplomacy”. “If they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money – into repression – they will be targeted,” he said. Motorcyclists in Tehran pass a billboard depicting Donald Trump with the words: “Great Victory! Strait of Hormuz.” AP Several new measures were announced on Monday, including sanctions against nearly 60 Iran-linked entities, individuals and vessels. That included a procurement scheme for Iran’s ballistic missile development and nuclear research, a malicious cyber group and a network of brokers and vessels transporting Iranian oil, according to US Treasury.



And the US expanded its list of sectoral sanctions against Iran. Anyone operating in the fields of digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping was now liable to be sanctioned. Related Article Iran sanctions Trump announces ‘economic D-Day’ of Iran sanctions, moving war to new phase Bessent said that every branch of Iran’s Bank Melli – the largest regime-controlled commercial bank – must be “shuttered and dark”. The move signals a transition in the war against Iran from primarily a military conflict to an economic battle where the US will try to use the weight of its financial system to cut Tehran off from all revenue. Friday will mark the six-month anniversary of the war, which Trump initially said would last four to six weeks. Although fighting has subsided for most of that time, a peace deal to end the conflict has proved elusive.



Trump pulled back from a threatened military offensive against Iran’s energy infrastructure and bridges, but reinstated a naval blockade on all Iranian ports in July. Meanwhile, the US is trying to establish safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz for the rest of the world’s ships. Shortly before Bessent’s speech, Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who signed the now-expired memorandum of understanding with the US, said no one was buying America’s “bombast”. “The United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries. Iran’s trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don’t take these statements into account anywhere,” Ghalibaf said on X. Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked Trump and Bessent for the move. “You justly exact a steep price from that cruel dictatorship and from those who assist its continued aggression,” he said.



But American analysts drew attention to the gulf between the Trump administration’s rhetoric and Bessent’s failure to announce any immediate secondary sanctions. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America How is Trump weakening American power? Let me count the ways Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Aaron David Miller, a former State Department negotiator and Middle East expert, said time would tell if the administration would actually cut off China, Turkey, India, Pakistan and others from the US financial system, initiating a trade war. “This really doesn’t seem to be D-Day,” he said. “This is D-Day plus however many days the administration is going to give all these countries … It’s hard for me to believe, on the eve of Xi’s visit here, that that’s the way they’re going.” Miller said Iran’s enablers were unlikely to comply with US sanctions. And “the Iranians are not going to sit around like some potted plant and just suffer this”, he added. “They’re going to strike back.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Congestion charges: Three options for Auckland commuters revealed
World.content:
Auckland councillors will today confirm three options for charging commuters to drive in and out of the city during peak times.

One option was to charge commuters entering the city centre during rush hour, while another included city fringe suburbs like Newmarket and Newtown, and possibly Ponsonby and Parnell.

A third option would also include core motorways such as from the Harbour Bridge to Point Chevalier and Mount Wellington.

Waitākere Ward councillor Shane Henderson said any charges would need to be balanced with investment in transport alternatives.

Waitākere Ward councillor Shane Henderson. Auckland City Council / Supplied

"In West Auckland that means the northwestern busway will need to be committed to by the government ... because people need proper alternatives."

Henderson said it was important to get Aucklanders feedback on the three proposals.

City Centre Cordon is described as the "fairest, simplest" and "most feasible scheme", saving four minutes of travel time. Supplied / Auckland Council

"We're putting it out to the people, and saying 'what do you think about this?' And we'll go from there."

After the options are confirmed by the Transport and Infrastructure Delivery Committee on Tuesday, initial public consultation will start in mid-November before an option is decided on in 2027.

Council documents described the city centre option as the "fairest, simplest and likely most feasible scheme", but noted it would raise limited revenue to improve public transport.

The city-fringe option was described as "significantly improved effectiveness compared to the city centre cordon", but noted it would include Auckland Hospital.

Option 2: City Fringe Cordon would charge drivers entering via Newmarket, Newton, Parnell and Ponsonby during peak hours. Supplied / Auckland Council

The option including the core motorways was described as "providing significant net revenue to fund improved public transport alternatives" such as rapid bus transit routes next to motorways.

The charges would range between $2 and $7 per trip, depending on which areas were included.

Council documents estimated the charges could save drivers four minutes per trip for the city centre option and up to 12 minutes per trip if core motorways were included.

After an option is confirmed in 2027, it would be ratified and get ministerial approval in 2028.

World.title: Online radio stations beat the algorithm to cater to some niche tastes
World.content:
Popularity of sleep radio booms in recent years Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Would you like to fall asleep to birdsong or relive the first time you heard your favourite band?

The internet has allowed anyone to start their own station - catering to some niche tastes from era-specific-only music to local gossip.

John Watson started Sleep Radio in 2012, after being diagnosed with depression from having to make people redundant at his corporate HR job.

"And of course, with depression comes insomnia. And I often get out of bed at night feeling completely awake, go and watch TV until about six in the morning and then be like a zombie for the rest of the day."

He said he tried relaxation CDs - which were difficult to find - and online radios - which would wake him up with adverts or station IDs.

"And I thought, I've got to do something better than this. So I basically created my own playlist."

He said he wondered how many people suffered with insomnia: he found millions through support groups on Facebook.

From there, Watson started a website then launched his own online radio station to share the music that had helped him.

"We had I think about 10 listeners on the first night, and within a week it was over 1000 and I was quite astounded."

A year ago, he did another count and found he had 50,000 regular listeners every month in 190 countries.

Artists and listeners send him music to broadcast as it is difficult to find the right kind.

He told RNZ the music most "conducive to sleep" was ambient, slow, instrumental and wordless.

This was also why the station has a global appeal, he said, and because someone was always trying to sleep somewhere in the world.

The testimonials page on his website showed this best: a commentator in Antarctica said it helped him sleep during six months of daylight.

"Every week, we get fantastic emails and messages from people telling them how it's helped them in their battle with insomnia. And I get a real buzz out of that."

One childcare centre told him they put his station on at naptime.

"I never, ever thought that I would be able to help so many people," Watson said.

80s and 90s only - Nostalgia

Niche radio stations seemed ideally suited for nostalgia: playing the tunes audiences had grown up with.

Bradley "B-Man" Simmonds started Keep Laughing Forever Radio, playing only songs from the 80s and 90s, after being diagnosed with myalgic encephalomyelitis chronic fatigue syndrome, which causes debilitating fatigue.

After becoming housebound, he decided to revisit an old dream of becoming a radio DJ, which he had let go of to work at a bank.

"I quickly discovered that peddling term deposits and insurance wasn't quite as rock'n'roll as being a radio DJ."

Bradley "B-Man" Simmonds of Keep Laughing Forever Radio. Supplied

He said his goal was to make his listeners nostalgic.

"It was a time before everyone was glued to a screen 24/7, before auto-tune became a thing and before deciding what song to listen to involved scrolling through thousands of options.

"There was something magical about hearing a song come on unexpectedly and thinking, I haven't heard this in years. That feeling is something that I really want to bring back."

Simmonds broadcast music all day and played his shows - Powerzone with Paul Rands, All About The 80s with Rob Charles - which released every fortnight.

He also added jingles, TV themes and movie quotes from that era.

"Those little moments that made radio feel like a friend in your room. Back then radio wasn't just something that you listened to, it was something that made you smile."

His app reached more than 10,000 downloads.

"The response has been amazing," he said.

James McKenzie told RNZ he had been listening to Simmonds' radio station since it began three years ago.

"I'm nearly 50 years old and so that era that he is focusing on is totally what I grew up [with] - the 80s and 90s."

He said listening to the show sends him back in time.

"And you think about: 'Oh, what was I doing when I was, you know, 15 years old, when I heard this song for the first time?'"

During the 80s and 90s, he said, there were more cultural touchstones people could bond over, like music.

"You don't go to school and talk about what happened on that episode of ALF or whatever, you know. Because kids have such variety and exposure to so much these days."

And it turned out nostalgia did not only work for those who had lived through the 80s and 90s.

Seventeen-year-old Luka Harrop joined Keep Laughing Forever Radio as the "Gen Rock Guy".

He said his family raised him on music from that time.

"When I was young, in Australia, we went to see Kiss, who have been one of my biggest idols."

He told RNZ being part of the Keep Laughing Forever helped him connect with people who loved the same music he did.

"I suppose it's quite special to me because not too many people my age still listen to it."

He said he liked how upbeat the music was and its counter-cultural, alternative aesthetic.

Being on the radio sparked an interest in a media career, he said.

Keep Laughing Forever Radio has been broadcast in more than 30 stations around the world, including on Retro Hit Radio in Auckland, which also only played songs from the 80s and 90s.

Richard Phelps has been running the station for more than two decades.

He said his radio station featured the "uniquely Kiwi flavour" New Zealand artists brought to the genre, which he believed had been overlooked by mainstream radio at the time.

"So we had a really unique blend of music and that's not replicated anywhere these days," he said.

He described the Dunedin music scene in the 80s and 90s as "rock heavy, it's a little punky, it's a little alternative".

He said online radio stations could give audiences more than an algorithm: they offered story-telling and connection.

World.title: SkyCity receives and rejects two cheap takeover offers
World.content:
Casino and gaming company SkyCity said it has received two takeover offers in the past few months and rejected them for being too low.

The company made the disclosure after media speculation that it was talking to a US private equity company, Oaktree Capital.

It said it had been approached in May by Oaktree with a non-binding, conditional and unsolicited offer of 70 cents a share, while another unnamed party had offered 75 cents a share.

SkyCity shares last traded at 66 cents each in response to the speculation and has traded between 46 and 99 cents over the past year. The offers valued the company at between $770m and $825m.

"Both indicative proposals were subject to numerous conditions, including a period of at least 8 weeks due diligence and arranging debt financing," SkyCity said in a statement to the NZX.

"The proposals were also conditional on agreement on transaction structure, negotiation of binding documentation, unanimous SkyCity board support, SkyCity shareholder approval, regulatory approvals, and acquirer internal approvals, amongst other matters."

It said the suitors also wanted to be exclusive bidders and undertakings that SkyCity would not sell any assets.

Up your bids

"The Board unanimously determined that these proposals did not adequately reflect the underlying value of the company, and that the conditions were problematic.

"Accordingly, the parties were advised that SkyCity was not prepared to proceed on the terms proposed."

It said it offered to consider engagement if revised and improved offers were tabled, but none had been submitted.

Last week, SkyCity reported a fall in its full year profit, possible job losses, and plans for asset sales.

World.title: Mackenzie District mayor feels let down by bed tax backtrack
World.content:
Mackenzie District contemplates revenue without levy Morning Report Download MP3 6m

The Mackenzie District mayor says public toilets are being left in shambles from tourists driving through and feels let down by the government after it shelved the possibility of bed taxes.

On Sunday the National Party ruled out the idea of a bed tax, promising that there will be "no new taxes" if it's re-elected.

It comes after Prime Minister Christopher Luxon spoke publicly a fortnight ago about the possibility of three new taxes under National - a bed tax, a bank tax, and a fuel excise increase.

Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said policies like a bed tax would only hurt those booking weekends away and the party would instead look at existing mechanisms to help councils cope with tourism costs. She said the party would continue to invest in front-line services.

But Mackenzie District mayor Scott Aronsen told Morning Report revenue from the taxes would not only have helped fund fixing and maintaining the region's creaking sewage system but also make improvements to public amenities.

"At least the bed tax should have some form of consistent income," he said.

"When we talk about IVL (International Visitor Conservation and Tourism Levy), we've really tried hard to get a share of that on an annual sort of a basis, but the reality is most of that money has gone to DOC (Department of Conservation) and we've missed out."

The Auckland and Queenstown Lakes District mayors had also expressed their disappointment with National's announcement

Aronsen said some of the IVL funding was needed for basic operating costs, including cleaning toilets.

He said that was especially the case in Tekapo, but Burkes Pass was overlooked.

"Now Burkes Pass is a little very small village between Tekapo and Fairlie and we've got one single public toilet on the side of the road there and it gets absolutely hammered," Aronsen said.

"We now have problems in the Burkes Pass service system, whereby it's running at capacity all the time now and we're getting those big pink stickers from ECan (Environment Canterbury) saying that you're exceeding your consent limits, you've got to do something about it.

"So that's just a real classic example, we take the eyes off Tekapo and look at Burkes Pass for instance."

Aronsen said a bed tax would have allowed them to build it into their budgets.

We would have some sort of idea based on bed nights every year, what we could derive from it, he said.

"But the problem with IVL is one minute you're in favour and the next you're not and then you've got to go begging with cap in hand to try and get some or you've got to be continually beating the drum," Aronsen said.

"If we had a bed tax at least we would know exactly what was more or less going to come in each year based on visitor numbers."

Aronsen said they had been let down by the government.

"Well of course we are because we've been promised a loaf of bread and we've been given a rock, you know, that's the reality," he said.

"It's election year and politicians are doing what they do best and quite frankly we're pretty annoyed about it.

World.title: National goes it alone on social media ban for under-16s
World.content:
National alone on social media ban for under-16s Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The prime minister and education minister's announcement the government has introduced a bill to ban social media for under-16s has caused two of the three parties in government to distance themselves from it, while it also appears to have caught Labour on the hop.

National is progressing its efforts to ban under-16 year olds from social media platforms, but so far is going it alone, unable to gather the support of its coalition partners, and Labour holding its support until it gets some more answers.

The bill puts the pressure on social media companies to take "reasonable steps" to check users are of-age, and includes the establishment of an online safety regulator and penalty regime.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon with students at the government announcement of a plan to ban social media for under 16 year olds. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The bill was introduced to Parliament on Monday as a government bill, and announced through a government press release, even though New Zealand First and ACT confirmed they had invoked the agree to disagree provision.

With 11 sitting days to go, the prime minister admitted the bill would not get its first reading before the election.

"We've got a lot of important bills to get out the door, but then we'll pick this up on the other side of the election. But I think now this is the right thing to do," Christopher Luxon said on Monday.

Minister Stanford on proposed social media ban Morning Report Download MP3 8m

With New Zealand First and ACT long making it clear they opposed a ban, and without Labour's guaranteed support, it meant Erica Stanford brought the bill to Cabinet for sign-off knowing that National did not currently have the numbers to progress it past first reading.

It left Labour free to push out its decision on the bill until after November, or for New Zealand First and ACT to fight against it should there be another round of coalition negotiations.

Labour, which had released a list of 79 questions it wanted answered, was likely to discuss the bill further at Tuesday's caucus meeting, with leader Chris Hipkins open to coming to a position before the election.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Hipkins said his party would continue to engage with National on the bill "in good faith", even though the prime minister's admission the bill would not get its day in Parliament any time soon came as a surprise.

"We were working on the basis that we thought they were asking us to support it before the election. It's clear, I now understand from the press conference, not from any communication with them on it, that they don't intend to progress it," Hipkins said.

Weekly interview with opposition leader Morning Report Download MP3 9m

Speaking to Morning Report's John Campbell on Tuesday, he said Labour did support the idea behind the legislation.

"As a parent myself, as a former minister of education I'm really worried about what kids are being exposed to online. Social media can do significant harm and we've got to provide parents with extra tools to keep their kids safe and to make sure that we're keeping up with what has been a massive issue that's arisen over the last 10 years or so."

"We recognise that this is a real issue but we also recognise that there aren't any easy answers."

He said the Australian approach which National's proposal was based on "by and large hasn't worked".

"It has had some benefit, but it hasn't worked on the main."

National's coalition partners were even more unimpressed with the way the bill was announced, with New Zealand First leader Winston Peters going through great pains to stress it was a National bill, not a government bill.

"Here we are having to tell a coalition partner how MMP works, and this is not how it works on this occasion. You've got two parties that aren't agreeing," he said.

ACT leader David Seymour. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

Deputy PM David Seymour on proposed social media ban First Up Download MP3 6m

David Seymour, meanwhile, said it was National's right to "go it alone" and put the bill out before the election, and wished the party luck, but he did not believe it was a serious solution.

"I think people can judge for themselves, one party pushing through what is really an election campaign policy for themselves, at exactly the time the government needs to stick together," he said.

Seymour acknowledged on First Up that social media caused serious harm to young people.

But he said proposals such as fining social media company 10 percent of its global revenue didn't make sense.

"If you take Meta, which is Facebook and Instagram, their global revenue is $200 billion. That means that the New Zealand government would be demanding $20 billion. That's about $33 billion," he said.

Social media harm billed as a generation's biggest challenge Morning Report Download MP3 3m

"Now, if they were going to pay us that for some breach, that would be fantastic, that would put the New Zealand government way back out of deficit and into surplus for a few years, which would be great.

"But I don't think anyone seriously thinks that they would pay many times more than they've ever made doing business in New Zealand."

Seymour said France and Australia have had little success with their approach.

He said change would need to be driven by larger markers and larger governments, like what was happening in several American states.

New Zealand will benefit from the social media industry changing, but we're not actually in a position to force that, Seymour sad.

"If the New Zealand government was going to do something, I think it would be far more effective if it was to put a restriction on selling and supplying smartphones, that is something small enough to fit in a pocket, touchscreen, internet access, camera, restrict under-16s from having those.

"Let them have dumb phones so they can still keep in touch with their parents and so on. But that would be something the New Zealand government can practically enforce. It's something it could physically do within its own territory."

Minister Stanford on proposed social media ban Morning Report Download MP3 8m

Stanford said the government couldn't sit back and do nothing

Not only for their mental health, but their physical health as well, she told Morning Report.

"A third of our teens are on social media for five hours a day or more. Grandparents can see it," Stanford said.

"We see our kids changing. It's our job to protect them from this stuff and we are completely powerless to these big algorithms.

"As the Prime Minister said today it's not going to be a silver bullet. It is going to be a generational shift where the expectation is for those young people coming through who are currently 9, 10, 11, 12 that they will not be on social media."

She said Australia had got 20 to 30 percent of their kids off social media in under a year.

Stanford said it would have to be a "generational shift".

She said there had to be meaningful legislation in place to make social media companies take notice.

"That's why you've seen the UK do the very similar thing and the EU as well and Australia have very quickly realised that their penalties and fines for example were way too low," Stanford said.

"There is a cascading range of things we would do right from warnings, corrective notices, enforcement undertakings, there's a whole lot including tiers of penalties before you got to that one but we want to be firstly in lockstep with our partners but secondly we want to say we're serious about this.

"We know that if we put $20 million or $30 million they're not going to pay any attention to that. Our kids are far too profitable for them to worry about that.

"We need to say actually we're serious about protecting our kids from the harms that you are causing with your algorithms and we take this seriously."

Luxon said it was "perfectly reasonable" that parties formed their own view of the bill, but insisted the bill was "not a political thing".

"It's actually a Kiwi thing, and that's what this is really about, and that's what we really want the other parties to think about too."

Stanford rejected an allegation from Peters that New Zealand First had only been made aware National wanted to introduce the bill on Friday, and had first seen the Cabinet paper over the weekend.

"The bill has been circulated for a number of weeks. It's been with all parties. In fact, I offered New Zealand First a full briefing with my officials, which they accepted, so they certainly have had the Cabinet papers for a really long time."

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Hipkins said it had been "difficult" to get information out of the minister, but he did not want the matter to become a political football.

"My comments here are relatively moderate. I'm a little frustrated, but they're moderate because I do want to find a way forward."

Luxon and Stanford were also keen to put politics aside, with Stanford saying Labour would get a response to its questions shortly.

"It was quite a long, detailed list. Nothing particularly insurmountable. They're just actually intelligent questions, but nothing of serious concern," she said.

"We're happy to engage with any political party on this, because it's about the kids, not about political parties per se," Luxon added.

Hipkins said National had provided further answers to Labour's questions late on Monday night.

Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong promised to back the legislation as far as Select Committee, if elected, saying children were being exposed to real harm online and regulation had not kept pace.

However, the government's own analysis said the evidence that an under-16 age restriction will be effective is mixed.

"Opportunity supports stronger obligations on platforms to address harmful algorithms, addictive design, behavioural profiling, data leaks, and other systemic risks. Stronger protections should commence alongside this legislation, not be deferred to a later phase. An age restriction isn't a substitute for making the platforms themselves safer."

She said the party would reserve full backing for the legislation until the committee had seen evidence about age restrictions, privacy implications and broader platform regulation.

Despite the political back-and-forth, the policy is popular with the public, even amongst supporters of parties that oppose it.

A RNZ-Reid Research poll from June 2025 had 57.8 percent of respondents say they supported a ban, with 31.6 percent opposed.

National supporters overwhelmingly agreed with a ban - 75.1 percent - while even ACT and New Zealand First supporters were also in favour.

Those invited to the announcement included students, principals, and members of the B416 campaign group, which has lobbied the government extensively for a ban.

Whangaparāoa College principal Steve McCracken, who is also chair of the Secondary Principals' Council, said there had been some success in Australia of children disengaging with social media, which he said was a good sign.

"This is a step towards trying to help our young people actually just reconnect with each other, and become better citizens overall."

Whangaparāoa College principal Steve McCracken. Supplied / Whangaparāoa College

A government fact sheet released alongside the announcement said around three in 10 children in Australia no longer had social media accounts.

The prime minister said the government was trying to make it the new normal.

"I came through an era in schooling where actually you didn't have to have a bike helmet in primary and intermediate school, and then eventually at intermediate school it became a law, or became normal, that actually everyone wears their bike helmet, and then it became abnormal when you didn't have a bike helmet on, and it's no different here."

Dr Maneesh Deva, a paediatrician but also an adviser for the B416 group, said he welcomed any action to protect children against big tech.

Paediatrician Dr Maneesh Deva is an adviser for the B416 group. Supplied / B416

"We've moved from a play-based generation to a phone-based generation. What we're seeing is really high rates of anxiety, self-harm presentations, sleep disturbance, and attention problems," he said.

"I think the kids describe it well when they say that, what are you seeing on social media? They call it brain rot. And I think they've pretty much got it right."

Not everyone in attendance was convinced.

"I don't think it's going to work. I strongly believe that people are going to find ways around it," said Naenae College student Josiah Scott.

"I think a ban is quite a privileged stance. People that can't interact, like marginalised communities, a big part of their ability to interact with each other. Disabled people who can't get out of the house as easily as most people, people who can't afford to do extra activities, aren't going to be able to connect with these people anymore," said student Lily Sang.

She said a better step would be to fund 'third spaces' better, and give teenagers a place to go and build connection.

"If you're going to take away one form of connection, you need to be able to build up spaces and make them more accessible for people."

But Queen Margaret College (QMC) student Biju Kim said she often found herself scrolling instead of studying.

Fellow QMC student Ana Bareta agreed, saying while social media could bring good things like connection, she also found herself scrolling without realising how long she had been scrolling for.

"I could have been doing study, I could have been outside, I could have been hanging out with my friends. But no, I've just been scrolling, or just on social media."

Attendees received a short heads up, with Stanford's office confirming to RNZ they were invited to an "update to the work being done to reduce online harm" late last week.

RNZ has approached TikTok and Meta. Meta declined to comment.

Stanford had pre-emptively dismissed any opposition the ban was likely to get.

"I've met with some of the tech companies, and they make all the same excuses that you would expect them to make: 'oh, but we're trying, oh, but there's worse things out there'. At which point, I say, 'what? Worse than learning how to self-harm on your platform?'.

World.title: PNG's tinder-dry Central Province and NCD struggle under El Nino
World.content:
Papua New Guinea's Central Province is feeling the brunt of prolonged drought caused by the El Nino weather phase.

Central and the National Capital District which is located within it, is extremely dry, its communities struggling with damaged crops and water sources in short supply.

Port Moresby communities meanwhile have been experiencing frequent water outages due to malfunctioning of the city's water infrastructure.

There' also been at least one bad bout of frost, which has worsened the crop damage.

The ongoing weather disruptions have prompted the Central Province government to conduct an assessment of the scale of the province's food and water security problems.

The National Disaster Centre warned months ago that the El Nino phase could increasingly impact many parts of the country, and other regions such as the Highlands and Western province have been suffering for months.

Now much of PNG's central region is tinder dry, and fires are a common sight in the arid hills around the capital

And further into Central Province, many water sources have dried up, forcing closures of schools.

The Central Governor Ruffina Peter said the provincial executive has allocated K5.3 Million to respond to the drought and help communities.

World.title: Neonatal nurse on why infant mental health matters
World.content:
NICU nurse on the importance of infant mental health Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Dressed in colourful scrubs and yellow Crocs, neonatal nurse practitioner Fiona Dineen is a pop of colour against the stark white hospital walls.

Wellington Hospital's Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) can be a scary place for families, awash with bright lights, beeps, monitors and feeding tubes.

But nowadays, infant mental health is treated as equally important to physical symptoms, meaning parents are tasked with playing a big role in hospital-based care.

Dineen has been caring for sick newborns for nearly three decades, two of those in Wellington.

A baby in Wellington Hospital's NICU. Supplied / Health NZ

She was 2025's Neonatal Nurses College of Aotearoa Quality and Innovation Award winner, for leading work to ensure babies in NICU were cared for not just physically, but emotionally and relationally too.

She told RNZ that, although "infant mental health" might conjure images of a baby lying on a therapist's couch, the first thousand days of their lives were crucial for their brain development.

"Within the neonatal unit, some of our babies can be here for up to six months and very seldom sometimes a year," she said, when RNZ visited the unit one Friday morning in August.

"So we have this opportunity of supporting babies with their brain growth, their emotional status, their connections, their attachments with their parents. And that's what infant mental health is."

That hadn't always been a priority, she said.

"Thirty years ago, parents weren't allowed into the neonatal units. They had viewing platforms where they would come and look at their baby through a window and they weren't allowed to have hands-on touching with their babies."

Paediatric nurse Fiona Dineen in front of Wellington Hospital. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

But these days, parents formed an integral part of the care team.

"Yes, you need the technology," said Dineen. "Yes, you need the medicine. But with the parents being the main caregivers to their babies and teaching them how to do that, it makes the trajectory even more complete and babies get discharged a lot quicker when we have parents more active."

Alex and Zach Thompson from Wairarapa were new parents to twins, Isabella and Leo.

"So we're mostly here all day," said Alex. "The only time I really leave is to eat food. I spend most of the day with them, sometimes cuddling one or the other, and sometimes we do double cuddles, which is nice."

She said it wasn't how she had pictured starting life as a parent. She had spent the first few days in hospital herself, and now they were staying in the Ronald McDonald House across the road from the hospital.

"It's still hard," Alex said. "Having that different routine because you do expect to just go home with your baby and start life as a family, but we've had to do it slightly differently."

Wellington Hospital's Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU). Supplied / Health NZ

One-on-one time with the babies was important, and it was clear the babies thought so too.

"They realise that it's been a certain amount of time since we last had a cuddle and they either get fidgety or grumpy - and you can tell."

And their personalities were already shining through.

"Leo is definitely a mama's boy," she said. "He's quite soft, you know, he is really just a sweetie. Whereas Isabella, she's tiny but she's fierce and she'll tell you how it is even if she can't talk yet."

Jaydene Latu has a baby girl, Shekinah.

She was born at 23 weeks, the length of her mother's forearm, weighing 335 grams - the nappies she wore when she arrived would fit in the palm of your hand.

Her birth 10 weeks ago had been touch-and-go.

World.title: Pensioners' growing tax bill
World.content:
People who are over the age of entitlement to NZ Super are contributing 15 percent of all personal taxes, data shows, but economists say even as that amount grows, it won't help balance the books.

Data released under the Official Information Act showed there were 268,800 working superannuitants in the most recent tax year for which data was available, and 632,300 non-working.

The working group paid $6.6 billion in tax on all income and $1.56b in tax on NZ Super.

The non-working group paid $4.24b in tax on all income and $2.6b on tax on NZ Super.

People staying in work longer and paying more tax Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Across non-working and working superannuitants, they paid $9.84b in income tax in the 2024/2025 tax year. Of that, $4.166b was tax paid on super.

Inland Revenue said the "working" group in 2024/2025 received $772 million more in net superannuation than they paid in income tax on their other earnings, to a net transfer of an average $2872 per person.

For the non-working group, the figure was a net transfer of $19,018 per person on average.

At the other end of the scale, 14 and 15-year-olds paid $9.9m in tax in the 2024/25 year, and $7.3m in progress data for the most recent tax year.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said the amount of tax paid by older taxpayers was likely to continue to grow as more people stayed in the workforce longer.

He said Stats NZ population projections were that the percentage of people aged 65 would rise from 16.5 percent in 2024 to closer to 19 percent in 2031 and just over 20 percent in 2036.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold. Supplied / LinkedIn

"There's more of them so, in principle, you've got the potential there for there to be more taxpayers. The other thing is that there has been a rising employment rate and participation rate of over 65s in the workforce.

"Since 2016, the proportion of the employment rate, so that's the proportion of over 65s that are in employment, has risen from 23 percent to around just under 27 percent ... that's a reasonably significant increase in the proportion of older New Zealanders that are actually working, presumably because perhaps the labour market's getting a bit easier for them relative to before. Maybe they need to work for longer. Maybe they just want to work for longer as well."

He said, because New Zealand did not reduce a person's NZ Super entitlement if they were still working, there was not the disincentive to keep working that might be there in other countries.

He said while young people's employment had dropped in recent years, that was likely to reflect the economic environment and would change again as it improved. Older people working were more of a structural shift, he said.

Shamubeel Eaqub, principal economist at the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research Supplied

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said some older people were working because they wanted to but others had little choice.

But he said the net effect was still that over 65s consumed more in public services than they contributed in taxes.

Treasury work showed children and people aged over 65 generally received more in government support than they paid in tax, while working age people paid more than they received.

That would continue even as the number of working older people increased. "The sheer volume of people in those older and especially oldest age groups balloons the costs.

"Rising older people's participation in work and thus increased tax contributions via income tax and also GST - because they are likely to spend more - helps improve the revenue side of the ledger. Just not enough to fix the fiscal math - which still doesn't work."

Eckhold agreed. "The reality is that even though there'll be more people working over 65, there will be a limit to when you can work to. And healthcare costs are rising … we're getting better treatments, more expensive treatments, people have higher expectations about what they can do now. So that all costs money."

World.title: Zak Butters trade rumours dominate Port Adelaide's turbulent season
World.content:
It's been a tumultuous year for Port Adelaide.

Its newly-appointed coach Josh Carr had to navigate a new system with an injury riddled list; using 39 of its 44-listed players and finishing the season with 15 unavailable.

He also had to build chemistry and belief despite a contract decision overshadowing his campaign.

Its vice-captain and dual All-Australian Zak Butters has dominated headlines all season as one of the biggest free-agents available this off-season; and has now confirmed the worst-kept secret in football that he has requested a trade to Victoria.

"I've made a decision to head home. It's obviously been one that I've wrestled with for a while now. It's been a tough decision and one that I haven't taken lightly," Butters said on Monday.

"Although I've loved my time in Adelaide … I'm probably at a stage in my life where I'd like to get back around some family and friends and enjoy some more time with them."

Butters denied reports in June that he had begun telling those close to him he was eager to move east after a trip back home during the round 12 bye; another chapter in a compendium of updates on the dual Showdown medallist's future.

So why was the club so protective of Butters when he had a foot out the door?

There are two key foundations of any negotiation in any industry. Value and relationships.

Growing speculation

As the weeks progressed and the speculation grew, the four-horse race between Richmond, Geelong, Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs intensified as the coverage evolved into a public bidding war; increasing Butters' contract terms and giving the Power fuel for higher trade demands.

Every story has a source … and every source has an agenda.

Zak Butters to leave Port Adelaide Star Port Adelaide midfielder Zak Butters has informed the Power he wants to return to Victoria.

Player agents are looking to maximise demand and clubs want their outgoing stars to leave at a high price.

Relationships between the two parties are also incredibly important in future dealings. Clubs are constantly trying to find the balance between fair compensation and long-term favours.

For Port Adelaide this was the case two years ago when Dan Houston was desperate to move to Collingwood but the Magpies didn't have the capital for a reasonable return.

The Power settled for Picks 13, 29 and 36 plus forwards Jack Lukosius and Joe Richards in exchange for its dual All-Australian defender and a future first round pick.

It was a move that was widely panned at the time but hasn't done much damage given rising key forward Jack Whitlock was taken at 29 and Joe Richards is developing into a handy midfield option.

But Dan Houston and Zak Butters are different cases.

The Power is hoping to maximise its draft haul in moving its triple best-and-fairest winner given it has rarely had early selections in recent years leading to a gulf in young talent depth.

It also has a litany of upcoming academy and father-son draftees it will need to match bids on, such as expected number one pick Dougie Cochrane and Zemes Pilot.

Matthew Richardson spoke about the Butters trade rumous in May. (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

Back in May, Port chief executive Matthew Richardson flagged on ABC Sport that the club would match any bid on Butters to force a trade given the star is a restricted free agent.

"There will be offers that we can match and we will match. It does give the club a fair bit of control in what happens," he said.

The issue is Butters current suitors have a diverse availability of picks at their disposal and the Power's best option Richmond doesn't quite align with the values Butters claimed he was eyeing when I asked him back in March what would dictate his decision.

"I think you're stupid if you don't want to win premierships," he said.

"I want to win. Family is important as well … but you can't look too far ahead."

THE CONTENDERS (As of current ladder position, all four clubs have all future picks available) Geelong: 17, 35, 53, 71

Western Bulldogs: 10, 28, 46

Collingwood: 16, 34, 63, 66, 70

Richmond: 2, 20, 38, 56

While Port navigates its way through the 20 out-of-contract players it has held fire on due to the Butters decision, there will be time for Josh Carr to reflect on his inaugural season at the helm.

Season highlights

Despite double ups with four sides who missed finals; the Power managed seven wins in 2026 and had a clear narrative throughout; it could match it with the best but could rarely beat them.

Its campaign ended with an equal league record five losses by five-points or less and eight by as much as 14-points.

A Showdown win over Adelaide in June was the highlight, plus its April upset over Geelong; but its only road wins were against fellow bottom four sides West Coast and Richmond.

It finished 16th for ball movement from D50 to F50 but defensively was a powerhouse until the final month where 10-goal losses to the Lions, Swans and Demons blew out the team's average points against to 89, dropping it down from a Top 4 side into 10th.

The other positive was its clearance work. Despite missing Connor Rozee for the majority of the campaign, and Zak Butters for the final month, the side finished second for clearance differential, blooding future stars in Jase Burgoyne, Joe Richards and Miles Bergman on ball.

Port Adelaide won seven games in the 2026 season. (ABC Riverland: Catherine Heuzenroeder)

From a list perspective it was the only side not to have a player named in the AFL's 22-under-22 squad and some of the long-term signings from the Hinkley era like Todd Marshall and Brandon Zerk-Thatcher barely featured.

Former Port midfielder and four times Showdown medallist Josh Francou believes 2026 was a free hit for Josh Carr.

"It has been a difficult campaign … the way they're defending the ground is a real plus for them but they struggle to move the ball," he said.

"Next year things start to ramp up on Josh Carr and he's got to get it right."

Despite all the adversities, it feels like Josh Carr has laid the foundation for success but a critical off-season awaits as he looks to reshape the list and keep his stars healthy for the 2027 campaign.

World.title: Cyclists run for cover as hailstorm forces La Vuelta stage cancellation
World.content:
A torrential hailstorm in the French Pyrenees forced the abandonment of the third stage of the Vuelta a España on Monday.

With 15 kilometres remaining of the 174-km route from Gruissan to Font-Romeu, the skies darkened as the peloton neared the top of the Col de Mont-Louis and huge hailstones began bouncing off the tarmac and pelting the riders.

Mats Wenzel (Kern Pharma) and Lorenzo Fortunato (XDS Astana) were 25 seconds ahead of the peloton when the elements intervened, as race leader and favourite Tadej Pogacar was seen indicating to the peloton to pull off the course.

Bedraggled riders were then seen getting off their bikes and shuffling into a hotel for shelter.

Shortly afterwards, race organisers, ASO, announced the stage would not resume, leaving fans frustrated at the finish where thick layers of hail blanketed the road.

Slovenia's Pogacar (UAE Emirates-XRG) retained his overall lead of nine seconds from Belgium's Wout van Aert (Dutch Visma-Lease a Bike) with Britain's Matt Brennan 10 seconds back.

Earlier it had been warm and sunny on the flat approaches to the mountainous finish with no sign of the chaos to come as a five-man breakaway group stayed out ahead.

Pogacar, bidding to complete his Grand Tour collection by winning the Vuelta for the first time, was always near the front of the pack with his team setting the pace.

Sadly, his expected challenge for the stage victory fell foul of the weather in an anticlimactic finish.

He will get his chance to underline his superiority again on Tuesday, though with stage four featuring three first-category climbs as the race starts and finishes in Andorra la Vella.

Reuters

World.title: From almost drowning as a child to the pinnacle of surf lifesaving
World.content:
Under an expansive blue sky and bathed in the type of sunshine that typifies Queensland's mocking parody of winter, the ocean at Surfers Paradise is made to look incredibly inviting, even on a Thursday morning in August.

But the crashing of waves into the hard-packed sand offers a reminder that beyond the beauty of the scene, the power of the ocean remains a potent force.

Australian Iron Series athlete Tiarnee Massie knows about this more than most.

The 24-year-old is a third-generation surf lifesaver at Maroochydore Surf Life Saving Club on Queensland's Sunshine Coast.

Not only that, but she is the reigning and defending Iron Series champion and will wear the yellow number 1 seed bib when the series gets underway in October with the Coolangatta Gold.

Tiarnee Massie will look to once again win the overall title when the series finishes at Surfers Paradise early next year. (Getty Images: Iron Series/Chris Hyde)

Her story could have been very different, though.

"I think I was nine months old," Massie tells ABC Sport on the Gold Coast.

"I was at home and my older sister was playing in the pool with her friends.

"Someone left the pool gate open and I found myself in the pool and drowning at the bottom of the pool."

The scenario is one that is all too painfully familiar for far too many Australian families.

The 2025 National Drowning Report, published by Royal Life Saving Australia and Surf Life Saving Australia, identified 15 fatalities of children aged four or younger, eight of which occurred in a swimming pool.

In total, the report noted that there were 357 drowning deaths over the past 12 months, a 27 per cent increase on the 10-year average.

Tiarnee Massie is aware she could have become a statistic for Australia's downing deaths. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

"My mum was actually on the phone and she had this gut instinct that something was wrong, so she hung up and she came out and she found me in the water," Massie says, knowing how fortunate she is to not be a contributing statistic to the nation's drowning tally.

"She started doing resuscitation and she saved my life that day."

That near-death experience didn't seem to do Massie any long-term harm.

Even in the short term it seems the young Massie was relatively unperturbed by the experience — she tells ABC Sport she was back in the water the very next day.

"It didn't affect me at all," Massie says.

"But it certainly affected my mum," she adds with an infectious and earnestly cheeky grin.

"Still now, when she's watching me in the ocean, she just can't watch. She's actually fainted a few times.

"She's got demons there, but she knows that I'm capable and she knows that I love it.

"I have the best family who support me. They are always coming to all of my competitions, we stay together and to be able to share these incredible experiences and moments with them, it's a dream come true."

Tiarnee Massie says her mum sometimes struggles watching her race. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

That day sparked something in Massie's mother too, who has gone on to become a CPR trainer at the Maroochydore Surf Club, joining a club that her uncle, Ashley Massie, competed for in surf lifesaving competitions.

"She never was involved [in surf lifesaving] to the extent of being a trainer until the moment that I drowned in the pool," Massie says.

"You don't know if you are someone that deals well in those situations until you're literally in the situation.

"You know, you can do all the training, but unless you actually are in that situation, you don't know whether you can do it. And my mum did it."

And incredibly, that ability to remain calm under the intolerable pressure of a life or death situation, clearly passed on to her daughter.

"I was 15, I was on a family holiday in Thailand and we were out surfing with my friends and I actually noticed that this man was struggling in the water," Massie says.

"My mum signalled me from the beach saying he's in trouble and my friend and I went over and helped him and we saved his life that day."

Competing is serious for Tiarnee Massie, but so too is the bigger picture of saving lives. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

The magnitude of that moment may have passed the then-teenage Massie by somewhat: "I was so young that I actually didn't understand the importance of what I did, I was just doing what I was trained to do," Massie says.

"I was doing what I knew how to do, I was in the ocean, I understand the ocean and I didn't understand that he couldn't."

The enormity soon struck home when the man she saved wrote her a letter.

"Later on he wrote a letter to myself and my friend, Grace, saying how grateful he was for us saving his life and that we have changed his life forever and all of this incredible stuff," she says.

"It was from that moment on that I realised how important the work that we were doing is.

"You know, I may be training to be the best ironwoman in the ocean, but most importantly, I'm training to be the best person to save a life on the beach.

"I think that is so rare in sport and that is such a special gift that we have as surf lifesavers. We are literally training to save someone's life."

Tiarnee Massie (right) will lock horns with number two seed Lily O'Sullivan (left) in the Iron Series. (Supplied)

Massie will start the defence of her title at the Coolangatta Gold, an event she came into as favourite last year, only to suffer the heartache of a broken paddle on the ski leg.

Despite that disappointment, Massey was still able to claim the series title.

Now she looks forward to honouring that yellow jersey over the course of the Iron Series, with events taking place in Coolangatta, Thirroul, Newcastle and the season final at Surfers Paradise on February 7.

"I feel so honoured to be wearing the yellow jersey this season," Massie says.

"I have looked up to every woman and man before me who has worn this jersey and to be actually in those yellow togs with the number one on them is such an honour.

"I'm just so grateful, I did all the hard yards as a young girl and stuck it out through the highs and lows of sport and all the triumphs and failures and I finally got to achieve my dream of becoming the Iron Series champion."

World.title: England drop fast bowler Carse after nightclub incident
World.content:
England fast bowler Brydon Carse has been dropped from the squad for the second Test against Pakistan following an investigation into an incident at a club in Derby, the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) says.

"Following a referral from the ECB, the Cricket Regulator has confirmed that they will investigate events on Saturday night in Derby," the ECB said in a statement.

Bazball's complex legacy Brendon McCullum deliberately set out to make England's men's Test team a less complicated team to play cricket for. After four years of Bazball's highs and lows, it leaves a very complicated legacy.

"Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the second men's Test while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained."

Carse, who did not play in the opening Test victory at Headingley, will be replaced by Sonny Baker.

Videos circulated on social media appearing to show the 31-year-old Durham bowler in handcuffs being spoken to by police officers outside a venue.

According to reports, Carse was not arrested, and no charges were brought.

BBC reported that Derbyshire Police confirmed a man in his 30s was arrested, but then de-arrested shortly afterwards.

"A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night, 22 August," a police statement said, according to the BBC.

"However, the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards, having agreed to leave the area."

It has been a busy summer for England's Cricket Regulator, the body set up to investigate alleged breaches of the ECB's code of conduct.

In June it concluded an investigation into former Test captain Ben Stokes and fast bowler Gus Atkinson after a nightclub incident following the first Test against New Zealand.

Both were left out of the second Test before the regulator ruled that there was insufficient evidence to establish that any regulatory breach occurred.

The latest investigation came less than a week after England's returning Test captain, Joe Root, spoke of the players being "really good role models and human beings" following a series of incidents and accusations of a drinking culture.

Controversy has followed England in recent times, with off-field issues during last winter's tours, including Harry Brook being fined £30,000 ($57,200) following an altercation in Wellington, as well as reports of drinking during a mid-Ashes series trip to Noosa.

Stokes eventually announced his retirement from international cricket while Brendon McCullum was sacked as Test coach, with Root confirming that the team had done away with the curfews under new coach Stephen Fleming.

Reuters

World.title: Manu's talks with PNG PM helped lock in Chiefs deal
World.content:
Joey Manu has revealed how a conversation with Papua New Guinea's prime minister helped convince him to return to the NRL and join the Chiefs in 2028.

The two-time premiership winner will be 31 by the time the two-year deal starts, and will arrive with the ability to play fullback, centre or even five-eighth in the club's first year.

Manu toured PNG last month and met with Prime Minister James Marape while there, before signing the deal from France on Sunday.

Manu unveiled as PNG signing The PNG Chiefs confirm Joey Manu will join them, ending the former Roosters star's dream of playing for the All Blacks.

"Talking to the prime minister and how passionate he was about making it not just a PNG team, but a Pacific team and trying to get the Pacific nations behind this team, I think it's going to be special," Manu said.

"I'm a really proud Cook Island and Māori man, and I know my family's real proud back in Tokoroa in New Zealand and also in the Cook Islands too.

"It's a big decision to make, but bringing that positive impact to PNG but also young Pacific Island kids (is big).

"There's so much talent in the Pacific Islands, and rugby league is taking over the islands, so it's really cool to have a Pacific team."

Manu's signing means he follows Jarome Luai, Alex Johnston, Connor Watson, Brian To'o, Zac Lomax and English Test prop Matty Lees as Chiefs signings.

The PNG outfit will officially be able to hit the open market in November, with all eyes on whether Nathan Cleary or Sam Walker will still be available at that point.

Canberra second-rower Hudson Young also shapes as a potential target, given he is yet to agree to terms for an extension at the Raiders.

"Just joining the Chiefs is pretty special in the first year," Manu said.

"With how it can affect the country, that's why I wanted to go there.

"It's got a lot of positives about how passionate the country is, and what we can do for the country and how we can make a positive impact on people's lives."

Manu left the Sydney Roosters for rugby union at the end of 2024, initially to Japan's Toyota Verblitz before moving to Racing 92 in France.

His current deal expires next May, meaning it is possible he could sign for an NRL club for the second half of next season before joining PNG.

"I still keep a close eye on a few games and I get to watch a few games when I can," Manu said.

"You miss certain things when you're watching. I'm just grateful that I get to come back and play.

"I really enjoy playing rugby league, so I'm excited.

"Rugby league is a special game for myself, and to come back and play in the NRL is very special."

AAP

World.title: Swans assistant takes over as Essendon coach
World.content:
Mark McVeigh, a former Essendon player and Sydney assistant coach, will take over as Essendon's senior coach after what the club said was an "extensive" and "deliberate" selection process.

McVeigh, 45, won the role ahead of Bombers great and ex-coach James Hird, as well as Jaymie Graham and Murray Davis.

Essendon confirmed the announcement on Monday afternoon, a day after the stricken club's narrow loss to Port Adelaide.

McVeigh would take over "effective immediately", the club said in a statement.

James Hird (L) and Dean Solomon (C) speak with Mark McVeigh (R). (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

The official announcement came following a day of speculation and a message of congratulations from former teammate and Bomber's legend, James Hird.

"I put my heart and soul into the effort, but obviously fell short and that's the way it goes," Hird said on Nine yesterday night.

Brad Scott was sacked on May 25, with Dean Solomon taking over as interim coach for the rest of the season.

Solomon rounded out the Bomber's worst season in club history with a 10-point defeat to Port Adelaide on Sunday.

McVeigh commits to building Essendon's 'next great era'

The search for a new coach has involved a tumultuous selection process, with opinion sharply divided on whether Hird should win another tenure in the role.

Club president Andrew Welsh, who played at Essendon alongside McVeigh and Hird, said the appointment was a unanimous board decision.

"Mark was clearly the best candidate for what this role demands," Welsh said on the club website.

"We are building the next successful era for Essendon, with a view to playing finals, winning finals and competing for premierships.

"We weighed every candidate against what this role actually demands, and Mark was the clear stand-out."

Hird congratulates McVeigh A 'very disappointed' James Hird congratulates former teammate Mark McVeigh, as the Bombers prepare to unveil their new coach.

McVeigh played 232 games for Essendon and returns to the club on a three-year contract after nearly 14 years away, which also included working as an assistant coach at the Greater Western Sydney Giants.

He also acted as caretaker coach at the Giants in 2022.

"We're not looking backwards, we're building the next great era of this football club," McVeigh said.

"That's not built on promises. It's built on our standards, our actions and the work we put in every single day."

AAP/ABC

World.title: Matildas star receives rousing welcome in return after mother's death
World.content:
Matildas midfielder Kyra Cooney-Cross has played her first match in more than five months after taking time away from football to spend time with her mother before her death.

Cooney-Cross was sent on in the 63rd minute as Arsenal recorded a 1-0 pre-season win over Paris FC in Borehamwood.

The 67-time international recorded her first minutes since the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup final in March, when she started in the Matildas' 1-0 loss to Japan in Sydney.

Cooney-Cross announced on January 8 via Instagram that her mother Jessica Cooney was diagnosed with terminal Stage 4 bile duct cancer. She died on July 10.

Arsenal manager Renee Slegers confirmed on March 28 Cooney-Cross was granted indefinite compassionate leave and would remain in Australia after the Asian Cup to be with her mother.

"You're my biggest inspiration and the person I aspire to be," Cooney-Cross wrote on social media after her mother's death.

"Mum, my favourite part is knowing that I'm a little piece of you."

The 24-year-old returned to Arsenal's pre-season training on August 17, with the Gunners' Women's Super League campaign set to begin on Sunday evening against former Socceroo Dario Vidosic's Brighton & Hove Albion.

Cooney-Cross received a rousing ovation at Meadow Park as she was substituted on alongside compatriot Steph Catley.

Loading Instagram content

The former A-League Women's star with Melbourne Victory and Western Sydney Wanderers was involved in the build up to Canadian attacker Olivia Smith's 91st minute winner.

Arsenal's final pre-season match is against Charlton Athletic on August 26.

The Addicks signed Australian trio Emily van Egmond, who marked a national record 170 international appearances during the AFC Women's Asian Cup, alongside fellow Matildas midfielder Leah Davidson and youth international Grace Johnston, following the club's promotion from the Women's Super League 2 in May.

Meanwhile, goalkeeper Jada Whyman is returning to A-League club Sydney FC after a stint in Sweden.

Whyman is yet to play for the Matildas but has been selected in multiple national squads.

Tech.title: The cat-and-mouse game over 3D-printed guns has begun
Tech.content:
The creator of the world’s first 3D-printed gun claims he’s developed a way to thwart government-mandated software meant to block 3D printers from making firearms. It’s an opening volley in what’s shaping up to be an evolving battle between regulators trying to stem the tide of ghost guns and individuals trying to create workarounds.

Cody Wilson, who claims to have made the detection-defying tool, is calling it “Hochulization” as a direct jab at New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who pushed through the nation’s first law mandating gun file detection software on new printers earlier this year. “New York is trying to reach into the internet and police how open-source 3D printing is done,” Wilson, who’s based out of Austin, Texas, told The Verge. “I think of it as a self-defense measure.”

The tool is designed to break a relatively simple approach to a 3D-printed gun ban. Wilson’s company, Defense Distributed, runs DEFCAD, the world’s largest 3D gun file repository, which he says hosts over 200,000 files of gun designs and components, such as suppressors. Each of those files can be identified by a hash, a unique string of numbers that’s created by running the file through an algorithm. In theory, a gun file detection system that uses a hashing-based identification method would look for those exact hashes to determine whether a file is a potential gun, flag it, and prevent it from printing.

Hochulization mucks up that process by automatically changing those hashes. It adds a series of bytes to each file that changes the hash without altering the function of the end product. A 3D-printed suppressor or gun, in other words, would still work as intended. “Hochulizaiton is a de minimis policy to change the hash of every file that gets created and downloaded to where there is never going to be a complete library of hashes,” Wilson says.

Wilson says he wants to apply the Hochulization treatment to all files hosted on DEFCAD by default as a means of “self-defense” against growing calls for gun detection software, which he describes as invasive digital surveillance. Wilson says he will make the tool available to DEFCAD users, though he says he also intends to make it open source, which would let an individual user with a gun file apply the tool to scramble the hash and potentially sidestep detection.

Image: Cody Wilson

“I think all the files in the repository, the 3D files anyway, should be Hochulized,” he adds. “And so that is what we’ll do.” He claims he has begun this process.

Wilson’s approach is an early indicator of the resistance to 3D-print-blocking tech. In this case, the momentum is coming from a Second Amendment advocate, but that might not always be the case. Groups of makers, digital rights experts, and members of the entertainment industry who aren’t focused on guns have all spoken out against the tech, expressing fears that requiring file scanning on printers introduces a new level of digital surveillance into the process that could limit what everyone can create.

3D-printed firearms are growing in number but remain an evolving public threat. In 2021, the New York Police Department confiscated just one 3D-printed gun. That jumped to 109 in 2024. Prominent gun policy group Everytown found similar upticks across 20 other cities. Still, when compared with the percentage of conventional firearms confiscated around the country, 3D-printed models remain comparatively small. The total number of firearms in the US has been estimated to outnumber people.

Policymakers and gun control advocates argue cases like this demonstrate a glaring gap in the legal system. People with prior felony convictions and others who aren’t legally allowed to own guns can do so anyway with the help of a 3D printer. And while many states regulate the making and selling of so-called “ghost guns,” actually enforcing those laws is notoriously difficult. This new approach, which requires 3D printers to install mandatory file-blocking software, attempts to close that gap by stopping a print before it ever starts. Industry experts are still debating whether that’s technically feasible at scale. Gov. Hochul, who pushed through the country’s first law mandating print-blocking software on new printers as part of the state’s FY 2027 budget, says it’s necessary to close what she calls a black-market “plastic pipeline.”

Hochul’s office did not respond to our request for comment regarding Wilson’s Hochulization workaround.

New York isn’t alone. A similar bill in California, AB 2047, is gaining momentum and is advancing to the Senate floor for a vote. Like in New York, this bill would require new printers manufactured or sold in the state to be equipped with print-blocking software. The state Department of Justice would publish a roster of compliant printer models, and those not on the list would be banned from sale or transfer in the state starting in December 2029.

A spokesperson for California Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, who introduced and coauthored AB 2047, declined to comment when asked about Wilson’s project.

Neither of these efforts explicitly details what print-blocking software should look like. That’s being left up to groups of industry experts with backgrounds in manufacturing technology, artificial intelligence, firearms regulation, and other relevant fields. A purely hash-matching approach would limit the number of non-guns mistakenly identified as guns, but as Wilson’s project shows, it may be trivially easy to bypass. More expansive approaches that use AI to analyze a file’s geometry and predict whether it’s a gun would almost certainly prevent more guns from being printed, but they also risk introducing more false positives.

Wilson’s hoping his tool will make its way into those working group conversations. By showing just how simple it is to complicate a purely hashing-based approach, he’s essentially trying to force policymakers’ hands into choosing between a more aggressive scanning scheme or the status quo of nothing.

“You are going to have to do more than create a database of known files and check against hashes because that’s too easy to defeat,” Wilson says.

Dartmouth College associate professor of engineering Solomon Diamond told The Verge Hochulization would likely work on a technical level to bypass a hash-based detection model. Still, he said that doesn’t necessarily make the approach useless as a policy path. In reality, it’s not clear that every 3D printer user would go the extra step to change a hash. Downloading gun files from DEFCAD also requires setting up an account and linking an email address, which is another barrier to entry. The hashing approach, in other words, is better than nothing and might stop the casual, less motivated user from downloading a gun.

Moving beyond hash matching, Wilson says his team found other ways to bypass more sophisticated detection using “adversarial noise.” To do this, his team first created their own AI detection model designed to classify guns and gun parts, trained partly on both public and non-public files from DEFCAD’s database. They based their model on claims made by other companies, such as the Spain-based Print&Go, which is working with lawmakers in New York and California.

Wilson claims he was able to get files past their own system using techniques like re-saving the same gun part as a slightly different mesh (a digital representation of the object’s surface) or adding “a small extra lump of unused geometry.” Overall, Wilson says their gun detection system, even when trained on high-quality data, still had a 30 percent false positive rate. He says that false positives speak to issues inherent to more prediction-based systems.

Wilson approaches the scanning debate as a self-described crypto-anarchist and an aggressive Second Amendment advocate. He’s a leading voice in arguing that gun files should be considered constitutionally protected speech under the First Amendment. He also created the platform Hatreon as an alternative to Patreon to thwart its speech policies, a platform that attracted extremists, white supremacists, and neo-Nazis until it was shut down in 2018.

But concerns over this proposed change to the way 3D printing works aren’t limited to gun owners. Makers and hobbyists previously told The Verge they fear this new paradigm will falsely label non-guns, like this e-reader case, as dangerous weapons and limit their freedom of expression in the process. Others are concerned a process that earnestly starts with gun file increments could be expanded by corporations looking to enforce IP and copyright protections.

Wilson isn’t new when it comes to picking fights over 3D-printed gun laws. After posting the first Liberator files online, the State Department ordered him to remove them and threatened him with jail time for allegedly violating ITAR export-control rules. Wilson and Defense Distributed sued the agency, claiming they attempted to stop him from publishing computer code, which he says is constitutionally protected under the First Amendment. That set in motion a complex web of legal fights over the broad claim that the gun file codes aren’t constitutionally protected speech, an issue that’s still being debated in courts.

Tech.title: Zillow and Redfin settle FTC antitrust case over their rental listings partnership
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The FTC and Zillow have announced a settlement that ends the case alleging that a 2025 “partnership” between Zillow and Redfin violated antitrust laws. The FTC had alleged Zillow agreed to pay Redfin to syndicate its listings, while Redfin would end its own advertising contracts and promise not to compete with Zillow for multifamily listings.

The FTC’s settlement proposal allows Redfin to continue syndicating rental listings from Zillow “unencumbered by the anticompetitive restraints” in the original deal, but also requires Redfin to restart its own rental listings advertising business, which it wound down as part of the partnership.

Daniel Guarnera, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Competition, said the deal “delivers better, quicker, more certain results for both renters and property management companies than we would have been able to achieve after prevailing at trial.” The state attorneys general of Arizona, Connecticut, New York, Virginia and Washington also agreed to the proposed settlement.

This ending also follows other recent settlements from the Trump administration in high-profile cases of companies behaving badly, like the Live Nation-Ticketmaster case, and its case against Realpage.

Tech.title: Robotaxis are real now — so is the pushback
Tech.content:
Robotaxis are expanding. So is the fight over the rules governing them.

In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul withdrew a proposal earlier this year that would have opened the door to driverless robotaxis outside New York City after taxi drivers, unions, and state lawmakers opposed it. Six months later, commercial driverless service remains illegal in the state, and legalization efforts are stalled.

In DC, labor unions are fighting legislation that would legalize commercial robotaxis, while lawmakers are weighing a 200-vehicle cap and a 15-cent-per-mile fee that would fund Metro upgrades and aid workers displaced by autonomous vehicles. A July City Council hearing on the proposal stretched for a grueling 10 hours.

In San Francisco, Mayor Daniel Lurie, a vocal supporter of robotaxis, is now calling for tougher robotaxi regulations after Waymos repeatedly snarled traffic during emergencies and major events. And as of July, California police can now formally cite autonomous-vehicle manufacturers when their driverless cars break traffic laws.

And while Congress has yet to pass comprehensive robotaxi legislation, federal regulators have stepped up their scrutiny.
