Tech.title: ChatGPT vs. Gemini: Which Chatbot Is Better at Seeing the World Around You?
Tech.content:
ChatGPT is the most well-known AI chatbot around, but Gemini has been gaining popularity for the past few years. Both models are great with text, but we’re in a multimodal world now, and using your camera to help AI identify objects is becoming increasingly common.

Both ChatGPT and Gemini Flash have seen upgrades in the multimodality department, and it’s been a long time since I tested the visual AI recognition on Gemini Live, so it was a good time to revisit its prowess and see how it compares to the world’s most popular AI chatbot.

Below are a few tests, none of which were overly complex, to test how well ChatGPT and Gemini can “see” the outside world. To keep things consistent, I only used photos and not live video, and I uploaded the same photo to both chatbots with identical prompts.

Which chatbot came out on top? Find out below.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Test 1: Scribbled notes

I sloppily wrote a page from a book on my e-ink tablet to see which chatbot could read it better. Blake Stimac/CNET

For an easy starter test, I quickly scribbled in the notes app on my Boox Note Air 5C with the pen. It looked like a mess, which is what I was going for. I copied the words from a random page from The Hound of the Baskervilles by Arthur Conan Doyle:

“’A moderate walk along this moor-path brings us to Merripit House,’ said he. ‘Perhaps you will spare an hour that I may have the pleasure of introducing you to my sister.’ My first thought was that I should be by Sir Henry’s side. But then I remembered the pile of papers and bills–” (I ran out of room to complete the sentence, so I left it at that.)

ChatGPT

ChatGPT missed this one. The first line, “a moderate walk along this moor-poor path brings us to Merripit House,” was almost completely wrong, with the chatbot transcribing it as, “A moment will always this moment — [Henry’s?] to Merritt House.”

Its analysis said the handwriting contained notes about a memory involving Henry, Sir Henry and the writer’s sister. It also pointed out that some of the words were hard to determine, so it marked words with uncertain words in brackets.

Gemini

Gemini nailed it. It translated my sloppy text word for word, identified the source and even offered specific handwriting characteristics from the image, like “open loop formations on the letters like y, g, and f.”

The fact that Gemini was able to correctly identify the source may also have affected the accuracy of the translation. Nonetheless, compared to ChatGPT, it’s a night-and-day difference.

Test 2: Chess

Both ChatGPT and Gemini tried to give their best guesses for the next move for this chess game at the Esports World Cup. Esports World Cup YouTube/Blake Stimac/CNET

To get an idea of how both chatbots interpret an ongoing chess match, I snapped a photo from a game on the Esports World Cup YouTube channel and asked both Gemini and ChatGPT what the next best move was for black.

Gemini

While I’m not a chess expert by any means, Gemini’s answer was long and elaborate.

Its final answer was Bxf4.

ChatGPT

ChatGPT’s approach to responding was initially different. It was showing its thinking process, and one of the lines said it “installed chess libraries and searched for a local Stockfish engine,” which is an open-source chess engine used to calculate moves. However, it took over 4 minutes to get to the response.

Its final answer was c5 to d4.

It did offer a secondary best move: Bxf4, the same as Google’s suggestion.

I reached out to the US Chess Federation to humor me and get some insight about what they thought of the test, but did not receive a reply.

To look for another party’s interpretation of each chatbot’s response, I decided to ask… Claude. I uploaded the same image and included the original prompt as well as both responses from Gemini and ChatGPT. Claude’s conclusion, without going into detail, was that Gemini read the board incorrectly and ChatGPT was the more appropriate answer.

Test 3: Sick plant

ChatGPT and Gemini tried to identify the type of plant and why one of the traps was turning black. Blake Stimac/CNET

The third test was of a photo of a Venus flytrap I own. I asked the chatbots to identify what type of Venus flytrap it is (it’s a towering giant) and why one of the traps was turning black. I knew this would be a particularly tricky one, given that most Venus flytraps look similar.

Gemini

Gemini didn’t identify the correct name of the flytrap, but I didn’t really expect it to. As far as the blackening trap, it listed a variety of ways why it could be happening, including the correct one: The trap attempted to consume an insect that was too large.

ChatGPT

ChatGPT gave a similar, but more detailed reply. It said it wasn’t confident in assigning a particular cultivar for the specific trap itself, but it did give more information about how the one trap could be blackening, as well as a section of “what I’d do” that provided some helpful tips.

Overall, both chatbots provided decent answers, but ChatGPT’s more detailed response won this round.

Test 4: Movie art

Gemini managed to figure out which movie inspired this art. ChatGPT was at a total loss. Blake Stimac/CNET

This was a fun one: I took a photo of three pieces of art that depicted the mouths of the Sanderson sisters from the movie Hocus Pocus. The hand-painted pieces are from an artist and not official movie merchandise.

ChatGPT

ChatGPT was unable to identify the movie, though it was able to accurately describe the image I uploaded: “Three diamond-shaped paintings that look like custom artwork.” It asked for additional details, like the year the film was made, to identify it.

Gemini

Gemini was easily able to identify what I showed it. “This artwork features the iconic smiles of the Sanderson Sisters from Disney’s Hocus Pocus (1993).”

From there, it went into detail about what character was in what position and the actresses who played the characters.

Gemini seems to be the winner

While I preferred ChatGPT’s response for the Venus flytrap test, Gemini’s consistency and ability to correctly identify sources in both the notes and the movie art tests makes me favor it overall. Since I couldn’t get a real answer from an expert about the chess test, I’ll leave that one out of the final tally.

Either way, if you’re looking for the best AI chatbot that can most accurately “see” and describe the world around you, Gemini takes the cake — for the most part.

Tech.title: People’s Picks: Our Readers Say These Mobile Carriers Are Better Than the Industry Giants
Tech.content:
Switching to a new mobile carrier shouldn’t be taken lightly. There’s a lot that goes into narrowing down which one can give you the best cellular service and customer satisfaction for a reasonable price.

Major network carriers come with perks and programs. Take the new Apple Upgrade for example. The program lets you lease an iPhone with AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile. Some even offer monthly savings on your phone bill and subscriptions to streaming services, like Apple TV and Netflix.

But mobile virtual network operators have a lot to offer, too. CNET’s People’s Picks is a community awards program that surveys our readers to get their opinions on the tech gadgets and services they use and love the most. The latest round focuses on what readers think about their mobile carriers — that includes everything from price to signal reliability and even data. And CNET readers have a few favorites that aren’t among the big three.

CNET’s People’s Picks: Mobile carriers’ overall satisfaction rating

Overall winner: Mint Mobile

J. Hazelwood/CNET

CNET readers chose Mint Mobile as CNET’s People’s Picks overall mobile carrier winner. It has a strong overall satisfaction average rating of 4.68 out of 5.

“Customer satisfaction in general is a fuzzy metric, and Mint Mobile has done an excellent job of reinforcing to its customers that they’ve made the right choice,” said Jeff Carlson, CNET senior editor. “I chalk a lot of that up to its marketing, led by actor and former part-owner Ryan Reynolds, which elevates Mint in a crowded market. But Mint remains affordable and reliable, which solidifies its customers’ choice.”

Value for money

Mint Mobile beats out other MVNOs and major network carriers, giving you the best bang for your buck. It offers flexibility without costing a fortune.

Mint Mobile offers several phone plans depending on your term and data needs. It offers three, six and 12-month plans starting at $15 per month for some plans, but an upfront payment is required. Mint Mobile also offers family plans that let you choose the data amount for each included line at one set price. You’ll also have the option to use your existing phone or buy one through Mint Mobile.

“The position of Mint Mobile and the other MVNOs on this list really shows how much people value simplicity in pricing and features,” said Carlson. “Yes, Mint requires up-front payment to get the best value, but customers can see what that is. They can budget a set amount for the next six months, pay it, and then not worry about fluctuations during that time.”

Carlson also noted that Mint Mobile isn’t trying to load up its plans with features to justify higher costs. It has core features such as 5G coverage and high-speed data, which is what most people are looking for.

Comparatively, major networks struggle in this category. For comparison, Verizon and AT&T are 2.98 and 3.05, respectively. It’s also worth noting that readers are happy with Mint Mobile’s pricing — 90% say their bill has remained consistent over the past year, and 5% say it has decreased.

Cellular data connection

Usually, if your carrier’s cellular data connection isn’t reliable enough, you’ll go looking for a Wi-Fi network. Most CNET readers with Mint Mobile service (70%) give the mobile carrier high ratings for how well they’re able to rely on Mint Mobile’s cellular data without connecting to a Wi-Fi network.

Over half (59%) of CNET readers with Mint Mobile service rarely have that problem, and for some, not at all. Eleven percent of CNET readers with Mint Mobile service say they leave Wi-Fi off entirely because their cellular data is faster.

Carlson said it is surprising that MVNOs, including Mint Mobile, win against major network categories for cellular data connection, but there are many reasons people connect to Wi-Fi instead of relying on their mobile carrier — like downloading files quickly or watching YouTube videos.

Runner-up: Consumer Cellular

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Consumer Cellular wins a few categories in CNET’s People’s Picks, including signal reliability, customer service and the mobile carrier that’s least likely to drop calls. It also comes close to winning in two categories: cellular data connection and unlimited data.

Signal reliability

Consumer Cellular wins in signal reliability, with the highest average rating of 4.60 out of 5. US Mobile and Mint Mobile trail closely behind, with averages of 4.56 and 4.53, respectively.

But that’s not the whole story, because all the MVNOs use the big carriers’ infrastructure – they don’t have their own cell towers. Most are tied to a single carrier, like Mint Mobile, which uses T-Mobile’s network. On its website, Consumer Cellular says, “When you 

If you’re curious about coverage, Consumer Cellular has an interactive map that shows which areas are covered based on your zip code or address. Most areas have 5G or 4G LTE, and Wi-Fi calling is also available.

Least likely to drop calls

If you’re constantly dealing with dropped calls, CNET readers with Consumer Cellular give it high marks compared to other mobile carriers. Most (70%) of Consumer Cellular readers say they rarely or never lose service. Close to 23% experience call drops in rural areas and on road trips — the lowest among mobile carriers. Even fewer experience call drops inside their home. Carlson said that could be because CNET readers with the service are getting the best coverage in their area, which is also why readers have high signal reliability ratings.

Customer service

Consumer Cellular also wins in customer service, with an average rating of 4.72 out of 5, compared to US Mobile’s 4.34. There are two ways to reach Consumer Cellular for assistance: call (888) 345-5509 or use its online chat feature. Consumer Cellular also receives high rankings from CNET readers for its service and fast resolution times. Most say they were able to resolve issues with Consumer Cellular over the phone in fewer than 30 minutes.

T-Mobile

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Most popular

T-Mobile is the most popular mobile carrier among CNET readers (29%), followed by Verizon (18%). T-Mobile has several phone plans to choose from, but CNET editors recommend the T-Mobile Essentials Saver 2.0, which starts at $55 per month if you need only one line; the T-Mobile Experience More 2.0 may be ideal if you’re looking to save money from other perks. We like that T-Mobile’s autopay discount qualifies you for a lower price when you use an eligible payment method.

T-Mobile has a few features that make it worth considering if you’re looking for a new mobile carrier. CNET editors say it has a robust 5G network and some money-saving perks, like plan savings with a new line and T-Mobile Tuesdays — the carrier’s weekly appreciation program. And T-Mobile recently unveiled a three-year phone installment plan to make new phones more affordable.

“One advantage T-Mobile has right now is its visibility – customers respond to T-Mobile Tuesdays, its sponsorship of things like a large section of the Formula One Las Vegas Grand Prix and its broad marketing,” said Carlson. “It feels like a place to be, and its mobile plans are well-received. They aren’t the cheapest, but their position here makes me think people are responding to T-Mobile giving them plenty of features for what they’re paying for.”

US Mobile

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Data speeds

US Mobile earns a nearly perfect average of 4.65 out of 5 from CNET readers who use it, making it the highest among popular mobile carriers. MVNO competitors Mint Mobile and Consumer Cellular come close to winning this category, with average ratings of 4.63 and 4.48, respectively.

Several factors go into determining data speeds. If you own a phone that’s capable of the highest 5G speeds and you’re in an area that can deliver them, you’ll see the best performance. That could be a device such as an iPhone 17 connected within a pocket of T-Mobile’s 5G Ultra Capacity (its name for 5G millimeter-wave spectrum) signal, which can download files much faster or deliver movies at 4K resolution smoothly.

Like Consumer Cellular, US Mobile isn’t tied to a specific carrier for its infrastructure. It’s able to use the best network available in your area – but US Mobile lets you choose which one to use. For example, if you travel to a location with a stronger network (like an extended vacation or for work), you can switch to that network for a fee. It uses its own names for the networks: Dark Star is AT&T, Light Speed is T-Mobile, and Warp is Verizon.

US Mobile’s ability to leverage the best network in your area likely gives it the edge in this category. US Mobile’s Broadband Facts break down each plan’s data speeds. All three Unlimited plans (Flex, Starter and Premium) have unlimited data, but your download and upload speed will depend on which cellular network you’re connected to. US Mobile’s Dark Star has download speeds up to 389 Mbps, while the Light Speed and Warp networks have download speeds up to 357 Mbps and 702 Mbps, respectively. Upload speeds are much different. Dark Star, Light Speed and Warp have upload speeds up to 33, 32 and 702 Mbps.

Fair pricing

Fair pricing eliminates month-to-month surprises — giving you predictability and peace of mind when paying your bill. That’s why US Mobile also wins for CNET’s Fair Pricing category of People’s Picks, with 98% of US Mobile users saying their bill “remained perfectly consistent” or “actually went down” in the last 12 months. While other mobile carriers reported base monthly prices increasing, US Mobile didn’t report any new fees, perks going away or changes.

US Mobile’s plans start at $25 per month for the Unlimited Starter plan, including taxes and fees, whereas the Unlimited Flex is an annual plan that starts at $17.50 per month, including taxes and fees.

Visible by Verizon

J. Hazelwood/CNET

For unlimited data

Visible by Verizon gets the highest marks from readers who use the mobile service for its no-data-throttling policy. CNET found that 73.3% of Visible by Verizon users say their data is truly unlimited and has never been throttled, whereas 72.9% of readers with Consumer Cellular service say the same. Comparatively, 61% of Verizon postpaid users say the same. You may notice slower internet speeds if you reach your monthly high-speed data limit.

Visible by Verizon offers unlimited data across all three plans, with premium (high-speed) data included on Visible Plus and Visible Plus Pro. Customers don’t need to worry about hitting a cap and seeing their speed dropped (though Visible and all carriers reserve the right to slow data if needed). While the Visible plan is listed as the most popular, the Visible Plus and Visible Plus Pro plans also offer unlimited data when roaming in Mexico and Canada, but speeds drop after 2GB per day of use.

Google Fi Wireless

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Roaming features

Most (63%) of readers who have Google Fi Wireless are satisfied with its roaming features, the highest among mobile carriers. There are no reports of dissatisfaction or frustration from CNET readers.

CNET’s director of content, Patrick Holland, says Google Fi is one of Google’s best-kept secrets. “Its competitive pricing, international roaming (at no extra charge) and flexible data plans are some of the main reasons that it’s been my carrier of choice for most of the past decade,” said Holland.

Google Fi Wireless has a few standout roaming features among other competitors. International service is available with Google Fi Wireless’ Unlimited Premium and Unlimited Standard plans. The Unlimited Premium plan includes free texts and calls at 20 cents per minute. Some calls to other countries (over 50) are free. Google Fi Wireless also offers 50GB of high-speed data to over 200 destinations, with 256kbps thereafter. Many other providers offer minimal international features.

Did you agree with these findings? CNET’s People’s Picks is community-driven and helps us spread the word about the tech and services you love. Take our ongoing phones survey to tell us what you love about yours.

Methodology

CNET commissioned Alchemer to conduct the People’s Picks survey to compile data. The survey was carried out online, and all figures are from Alchemer. The total sample comprised 1,198 adults. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus). Fieldwork was undertaken July 1 to July 26, 2026.

Tech.title: How to Stop AI Chatbots From Training on Your Personal Data
Tech.content:
If you’re reading this, there’s a good chance you’ve used the likes of ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude or some other AI chatbot. People continue to use them for day-to-day help with writing, generating images and for vibe coding apps and games. And that’s not even talking about the capabilities of agentic AI.

However, to get the best results, AI chatbots tend to need more context and information from you — some of which may be personal information — to complete the task. This data is stored on the chatbot’s parent company’s servers, such as OpenAI’s and Google’s, and can be used to train AI models. If you’re using a chatbot for something sensitive, like personal health, you might not want that info to be regurgitated to someone else asking a similar question.

By default, many chatbots will use your data to train their AI models, but most allow you to turn this option off. If you want to take back your data and even go as far as to delete it, we have a few steps to help you get the job done.

Gemini

You’ll need to turn off a few settings in your Google account and in Gemini to prevent your data from being used to train AI models.

Google

Go to myactivity.google.com.

Click Web & App Activity and turn it off.

Turning off Web & App Activity will prevent your new searches, location and other data from being recorded to your Google account and used for AI training. However, turning this off does not delete the existing activity already on your account. You’ll still need to click the delete button on the same page and select to delete your data from either all time or your specified range.

Gemini

Gemini has its own settings that you’ll need to disable in order to prevent Google from using your data for model training:

Log in to Gemini.

Click the Settings cog.

cog. Click Activity .

. Click the drop-down and set it to Off.

Similarly, you’ll also need to manually delete the existing Gemini activity (your conversations) by clicking the delete button and selecting a time range.

Claude

If you’re looking to remove your data or prevent Anthropic from using your data in Claude, it’s a little more straightforward.

Change Model Improvement settings:

Log in to your Claude account.

Click your profile icon .

. Click Settings .

. Click Privacy .

. Set the toggle for Help improve our AI models to off.

While you’re here, you might also want to toggle the Location metadata off for good measure.

Deleting your conversations in Claude is also easy:

Log in to your Claude account.

Click Chats on the left sidebar.

on the left sidebar. Click Select Chats .

. Click Select all .

. Click Delete.

Per Anthropic’s privacy policy, deleted chats are stored for up to 30 days in its back-end systems. If you’ve previously allowed Anthropic to use your data, and you turn the setting off, new and existing chats won’t be used to train models going forward, but your data will be used in training that is in progress and won’t be removed from models that have already been trained.

ChatGPT

ChatGPT is the world’s most-used chatbot. If you’ve been using it for a while without adjusting your settings, you’ve probably given OpenAI a lot of data.

Turn off model improvement in ChatGPT:

Log in to your ChatGPT account.

Click your profile icon.

Click Settings .

. Click Data controls .

. Click improve the model for everyone .

. Switch the toggle to improve the model for everyone off.

This pop-up menu contains two additional settings to include your audio and video recordings, but toggling the main switch at the top will disable both of these settings.

To delete all of your chats, there’s a dedicated button in the Data controls menu. Like Anthropic’s policy, OpenAI also stores deleted chats for up to 30 days.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Meta

The TL;DR for trying to get Meta to stop using your data to train its AI is that there’s no guarantee. There’s no elegant solution, and you’ll have to submit a form, which Meta may take action on.

Making your profiles private and limiting your posts will shield you the most from AI training. Or you can just delete your Instagram and Facebook profiles.

Instagram users looking to get away from the fact that others can reuse their own media can opt out to avoid the deepfake apocalypse.

Aside from that, all else you can do is mute Meta AI.

I was unable to find the specific setting to get Meta to stop using your data, and Meta did not respond to a request for comment when asked for a guaranteed way to opt-out of AI model training.

Grok

It’s almost surprising that Grok will allow you to turn off AI model training on X, but you can. Here’s how.

Log in to your X account.

Click the More button.

button. Click Settings and privacy .

. Click Privacy and safety .

. Click Grok & Third-Party Collaborators.

Uncheck the box next to “Allow your public data as well as your interactions, inputs, and results with Grok and XAI to be used for training and fine-tuning.”

While you’re at it, you might want to uncheck Allow X to personalize your experience with Grok and Allow Grok to remember your conversation history. You can also choose to delete your conversation history with Grok in this menu.

There are plenty of other AI tools that you may need to do this for if you’re a habitual user. We’ll continue to add to them here over time. The settings may be a bit obscured and hard to find, but if the option is there, you’ll typically find it in the data or privacy settings of the selected chatbot.

Tech.title: My Guaranteed Steps to Tell if a New Device Is a Flock Camera
Tech.content:
As I’ve covered Flock Safety’s AI camera and license plate tracking technology, including cities choosing to cancel their surveillance contracts while others adopt even more, I’ve come across a common problem. Many people don’t actually know what a Flock camera looks like.

That’s one reason I’m not the biggest fan of crowdsourced Flock-spotting apps like DeFlock, which make it a bit too easy to give conflicting information about what people think is a Flock camera. This led to so much confusion in my own city that the city council had to put out a bulletin explaining that local government no longer uses Flock cameras, and what people are seeing probably aren’t Flock cams in the first place.

So, how do you know if you’re seeing a mounted Flock camera, or a traditional traffic cam, or a competitor camera, or just a new cam from a friendly neighbor? I’m rounding up the exact ways you can tell.

Look for the telltale Flock camera shape

You can still identify most Flock cameras by their distinctive design. Allen J. Schaben/Contributor/Getty

Flock Safety’s brand has a very clear camera shape, so with a closer look, it’s typically easy to tell if it’s a Flock automatic license plate reader camera or something else.

Watch for the classic oval, hooded shape of the camera with a circular lens, a near-universal mark of Flock camera.

Notice this competitor brand Obvio has a distinctly different design than Flock, and may not offer the same surveillance services.

Not all license plate cameras are Flock, and that can matter for your privacy. Chip Somodevilla/Staff/Getty

Keep in mind, Flock offers a variety of additional camera features, including AI person detection and sound detection, like listening for gunshots, so not every model looks exactly the same. But this is still one of the first and simplest ways to detect a Flock brand camera. If you get very close, you can also small, shiny, stem-like Flock logo on the front of the cameras.

Some Flock cameras don’t have the slim hood, but the color, general design and logo still give them away. Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

I have seen reports of other ALPR cameras hidden inside objects like fake plants, but this doesn’t appear to be Flock’s typical approach and is very rare so far.

Best DIY Home Security Systems of 2026: Install Them Yourself Dodge installation fees and take security into your own hands with these super smart security kits.

Look for Flock’s visible solar panel arrays

Flock’s solar panels often have a distinctive look. Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

Next, look for Flock’s large, dark-colored solar panels, which are typically angled above the camera or close by on the same mount. Many ALPR cameras use solar panels so they can be installed nearly anywhere, but Flock’s have a unique design that’s more noticeable the longer you look at the cameras.

If you see what you think is a surveillance device without a solar panel, it probably isn’t one, or at least not one associated with Flock and its camera competitors like Axon or Obvio.

For example, red-light or speed cameras may be wired into traffic-light mounts, but they are used for traffic enforcement and don’t carry the same surveillance baggage as general ALPR cameras. While they automate certain aspects of traffic enforcement and take pictures of license plates, they don’t typically have the AI recognition, broad police search capabilities, or ways to recognize individual vehicles and people like Flock can (although they can still make communities uncomfortable).

Red light and traffic cameras aren’t Flock, and don’t have the same surveillance capabilities as Flock. Robert Daemmrich Photography Inc/Contributor/Getty

Remember, Flock and ALPR solar panels are always larger and more public than the panels people use for their home security cameras. Fortunately, there are other ways to make sure.

Check what surveillance equipment local law enforcement has bought

Searching the Atlas of Surveillance by city or county can surface Flock Safety camera locations, contract details and any reported data-sharing agreements with federal agencies. EFF

I recommend confirming your community is using Flock cameras even if you think you’ve spotted one. One of the best ways is with the Atlas of Surveillance website, which uses dedicated research to collect the different surveillance technologies that cities, police and sheriff departments have bought and are using.

The Atlas of Surveillance tries to stay as current as possible, and you can search by town or county in just a few seconds. It links to reports or public records to confirm use if possible. I’ve used it frequently to trace Flock activity in certain areas, not only with cameras but with growing numbers of surveillance drones, too. It works with multiple types of devices and platforms that law enforcement uses, making it one of the most dependable ways to corroborate that your local government recently started using Flock cameras.

When I talked to senior research Beryl Lipton from the Electronic Frontier Foundation about using the website, she said, “People should start by searching for their town and county to see what technology is in play close to home. While folks may expect some larger cities to use some of these devices, I think people will be surprised to see how common they’ve become in mid-sized and rural areas too.”

Lipton also recommended using a similar tool, the Street-Level Surveillance hub, which is more focused on the complex ways today’s agencies use surveillance technology. With both tools together, you should have a good idea what your community is facing.

Check who owns the property and what contracts they may have

Private companies like Home Depot can use Flock too, which makes it confusing when cameras are posted around parking lots. Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

Flock doesn’t just contract with cities or police departments. That means that while a city government may have canceled Flock Safety cameras, local businesses can use them on their private property, which can cause a lot of confusion among worried people.

If it doesn’t appear your local government is using Flock cameras, try to find out who owns the property with a camera on it, and if they contract with Flock. Home Depot and Lowe’s, for example, are very open about using ALPR cameras, including Flock’s, in their parking lots, and sometimes share that data with police.

Local businesses and neighborhood entities like HOAs can also contract with Flock, but you can often ask them directly if they have AI surveillance cameras and why.

Ask your city council

Asking your city government and showing up to meetings is a great way to find out what’s going on with Flock. The Washington Post/Contributor/Getty

Going to your city council, especially in person, can also be helpful (even Darth Vader thinks so). You can find out about present or future connections with Flock and make your opinion heard. You may also discover that, as I’ve seen before, cities have canceled their Flock contracts and no longer use the cameras, but they still stay up because no one is sure how to legally remove them.

I’ve also seen city councils unsure what Flock cameras are or how police use them, essentially signing off on police and sheriff budgets without knowing what they’re paying for, which is a sign that auditing and accountability practices are lacking. Or, I’ve noticed some cities announce new camera or surveillance programs but carefully avoid using the word “Flock” even though they are contracting with Flock Safety.

Asking direct questions to public servants can help handle issues like these. Look for council meetings where the public is welcome, and try writing or calling your city council to ask about their plans for Flock, if any.

File a public records request

Check if your city or state supports public records requests. You may be able to use a government website to formally request access to information about ALPR cameras, installations and contract documents.

Depending on the public records portal, you may have to be very specific about the kind of information you want, and which government body has it — the police department vs. the city, for example. My other steps are a good start to the research you need if you want to access public records like this.

While not every camera is from Flock, knowing which are — and which have ALPR or person detection capabilities — is a key step in avoiding confusion and protecting your privacy.

Tech.title: Watch the Highest-Ever Resolution Video of the Sun’s Surface
Tech.content:
New video and simulations of the sun’s surface can now bring you a closer look than we’ve ever had before.

The images were captured by the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, the largest of its kind in the world, located atop the volcano Haleakalā on Maui, which translates to “house of the sun” in English.

These new images of swirling plasma provide evidence that seems to confirm a long-predicted theory about what may be occurring on the sun’s surface.

As liquids of different densities flow past one another, they swirl together at the point where they meet, creating motion that resembles hurricanes or the mixing of ocean waves.

Understanding these complex interactions on the sun may help predict space weather, particularly severe disturbances called coronal mass ejections, which can overwhelm Earth’s protective magnetic field and damage Earth’s infrastructure, including power grids and communications networks.

To see the sun’s newest and most extreme close-up yet, check out the video embedded in this article.
